cia-0000102960:
Corrective Labor Establishment Number 9 at Bakal is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102960, dated July 5, 1987. The heading in the catalog shortens the place name to Bakl. The sample text covers camp years from 1981 to 1984 and gives the site a physical layout.

Prisoner living and working areas formed a rectangle inside three fences, one wire and electrified, one wood, and one reinforced concrete. Each fence stood about six meters high, with guard posts every twenty meters between two fences. Outside stood barracks for about two hundred MVD troops with automatic weapons, plus the camp office building.
cia-0000119760: A September 1956 briefing for the National Security Council brings late news from Hungary. The Council received the freshest items ahead of formal papers, and that autumn Hungary was the most watched story in Washington's crisis reporting. Late-news briefings filled the gap between daily papers, carrying raw items to the Council before analysts had settled on a firmer shared judgment.
cia-0000126960: A January 1965 CIA report covers political and economic strains in Colombia, spelled Columbia in the agency's heading. The South American nation was under pressure on both fronts at once. The paper measures those strains as the agency saw them in the middle of the decade. Strain papers measured pressure before it broke into headlines, and Colombia's mid-sixties pressures included rural violence that would shape the country for generations afterward.
cia-0000132160: Situation report 477, from January 1991, covers Saddam speaking in public and two terrorist incidents, the heading breaking off. The Iraqi leader's public words were read closely for signs of his plans. The report sets out that day's events in the crisis watch. Saddam's speeches were mined for bluff and intent alike, since his public line often set the terms that diplomats then spent days trying to move.
cia-0000132260: Situation report 567, dated January 1991, reports an outbreak of disease in Iraq that was not caused by biological weapons, the heading breaking off. Ruling out a germ warfare cause mattered in a war shadowed by such fears. The report sets out the finding. Disease appears in most long wars, and ruling out a weapons cause quickly mattered for troop morale as much as for the medical picture in the south.
cia-0000132460: Caribbean tensions are surveyed in a CIA document dated February 4, 1960. Cuba was the main source of the strain, but the troubles spread across the island chain. Washington feared that another island might follow Cuba's path into revolution. The short document surveys those strains country by country, giving readers the agency's regional picture at the start of 1960.
cia-0000132660: Cuba and North Korea stating that their views are the same fills a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The phrasing was the formal language of full accord between two states. Havana and Pyongyang were both clients of Moscow with the United States as a foe. The short paper notes the joint statement and the ties standing behind it.
cia-0000135860: Dated 3 June 1952, one CIA document in the open files deals with the Guatemalan situation in mid 1952, watched by the agency two full years before the coup. PBSUCCESS was the code name for the CIA effort to bring down President Jacobo Arbenz of Guatemala, which ended with his fall in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136260: The cable dated 6 May 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with Instruction 11 for broadcasts, the script series running without a gap for LANGEVIN. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136860: A disturbance like the Bogotazo might hit Caracas during the Tenth Inter-American Conference, warns this 15 February 1954 field report, rated from a usually reliable American observer. The ambassador to Costa Rica told President Remon he had information on good authority that such trouble was planned; Remon expressed grave concern for his wife, who was scheduled to attend. Romulo Betancourt, Venezuela's exiled former president living in Costa Rica, is named the likely cause of the trouble.
cia-0000141160:
JMWAVE, the CIA station in Miami, sent headquarters a cable on 4 November 1961 about the bodies of dead air crew from a crashed plane linked to the Cuba operation. Officers had talked the matter over by phone. The question was stark: bury the men quietly in Nicaragua, or bring the bodies back and risk the story breaking open.

The cable leans toward a quiet burial. Bringing the bodies home, it warns, could stir bad press and revive what it calls the April business, meaning the failed April invasion. It also notes the families had likely already given the men up for dead, and telling them now could cause fresh pain.
un-ga-res-1760:
Pressure on Britain over Southern Rhodesia mounts in Resolution 1760, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 31 October 1962. The Assembly recalls its 1960 call to end colonial rule, which it says applies in full to the colony. Four months before, it had ruled that Southern Rhodesia is a land not yet self-governing under the Charter. It also backs the people's fixed right to rule themselves and to form a free African state.

The Assembly had heard people who came to plead the case in person. It notes with deep regret that Britain had still not moved to call a meeting on a new constitution, with full African voice in the room. Votes like this one built the long UN campaign against the white minority regime in Rhodesia.
un-ga-res-3160:
Eight years of drift over the Falkland Islands, called the Malvinas by Argentina, draw a rebuke in Resolution 3160, adopted on 14 December 1973. In 1965, the Assembly had urged Argentina and the United Kingdom to open talks at once on the islands' fate. The call rested on the Charter and on the 1960 vote to end colonial rule, with the good of the island people in mind.

Grave concern fills the text: in eight years, no real step toward a fix had been made. The call for talks is pressed again, with fresh weight. The sovereignty fight that froze here in 1973 would thaw, nine years later, into the Falklands War of 1982.
un-ga-res-a-69-60:
Peace can be built by gathering guns, argues Resolution A/69/60, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its theme is the firming of peace through workable disarmament steps. A whole and joined approach to such steps, the text holds, is often a must before peace can hold and grow in lands torn by war.

The steps are named in plain terms. Arms gained by illicit trade or illicit making must be gathered and dealt with by safe hands, best by destruction. The same goes for arms and rounds that state chiefs declare spare. Such work, done well, lays the base for peace work that lasts past the last cease-fire.
un-sc-res-60: Words on a page were the work of Security Council Resolution 60, passed on 29 October 1948. A small team is formed: the United Kingdom, China, France, Belgium, and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic. Its task is to weigh all changes put to a draft text on Palestine, and, with the Acting Mediator's help, to draw up a fresh draft for the Council. The step was house work inside the long talks on a lasting fix for the land.
un-sc-res-460: The decision entered as Resolution 460 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1968. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1160: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 1160, and the catalog dates it 1993. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1260: Numbered 1260 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1999 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1360: Number 1360 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1999. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1560: Number 1560 in the sequence, this 2004 resolution records a formal decision of the fifteen-member Security Council. Its text comes from the official record through English Wikisource. The paragraphs follow the body's long-standing pattern, moving from noted facts and recalled actions to the specific steps the Council voted to require or request.
un-sc-res-1860:
Resolution 1860 addressed the war in Gaza that began in late December 2008, when Israel launched a major offensive after rocket fire from the strip. Civilians on both sides were suffering, and aid could barely reach Gaza's people. The Council called for an immediate ceasefire.

The text demands a durable truce, open crossings for food and medicine, and an end to weapons smuggling into Gaza. It also restates support for a Palestinian state beside Israel. Its careful wording, and the United States choosing not to block it, make the resolution a much-studied record of wartime diplomacy.
cia-0000136560: A Spanish document dated 5 November 1960, held in the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was training in secrecy that fall for the Cuba landing. The catalog record for this item is the generic series title, with no subject attached. Preserved in the original Spanish, the document is one of the November 1960 layer of exile paperwork. Its contents are not summarized here because the record does not state them.
cia-0000136760: The 2506 Brigade document cache preserves this Spanish text from 6 January 1961. The exile brigade was in training, its April landing three months away. The catalog record names no subject for the item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the first-week-of-January records in the brigade's declassified archive, presented as released.
plos-pone-0000060:
Devon Brewer, John Potterat, Stephen Muth, and co-authors measured what happens after an arrest in a 2006 study of deterrence. Their subject was men arrested for patronizing a prostitute. Criminology calls it specific deterrence when punishment stops the punished person from repeating the act, as opposed to scaring off others in general.

Following arrested men, the team found a large specific deterrent effect: arrest sharply cut repeat offending. That result speaks to a live policy fight over whether these arrests do anything beyond their cost. Evidence either way matters, and this study brought follow-up data, not just opinion, to a debate usually run on instinct.
geneva-bible-1560:
English Protestants who had fled to Geneva under William Whittingham and his fellow exiles produced the Geneva Bible, first printed in full in 1560. It was the first English Bible to divide the text into numbered verses. For decades it was the Bible most English homes actually owned and read.

The translation covers the full Old and New Testaments, with the Apocrypha included. Its clear prose and helpful verse numbers made study far easier than in earlier editions. Shakespeare quoted from it, and the Pilgrims carried it to America. Few English books shaped private faith and plain English reading as much as this one.
un-sc-res-260:
Security Council Resolution 260, adopted on November 6, 1968, recommended Equatorial Guinea for membership in the United Nations. Spain had granted the small west African land independence on October 12 of that year, closing a colonial chapter that ran back to the 1700s. The new state applied for its UN seat within weeks of raising its flag.

The General Assembly admitted Equatorial Guinea on November 12. The council's text is the standard brief form used for new members. But the moment was part of a vast change. Africa's map was being redrawn as colony after colony became a sovereign state. Each such vote added a voice to the Assembly's growing majority of new nations.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d60: Roosevelt wrote to President İsmet İnönü of Turkey on October 26, 1943, a rare entry in a volume mostly passed among four capitals. The letter is Document 60 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Turkey stayed neutral through most of the war, and the allies courted Ankara steadily that autumn. The record names the two presidents and the date. What Roosevelt asked or offered is in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d160: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 23, 1943, in a letter the editors placed in the Moscow Conference section as Document 160 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Its date falls in the middle of the Moscow meeting, when the foreign ministers were testing how far three-power agreement could go. The record gives the date and the two names. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the Moscow papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d260: For an informal Cairo meeting of 23 November 1943, no official record has been found, and the volume prints an editorial note in its place. The gathering, held in the villa occupied by the British Chiefs of Staff, is mentioned in the memoirs of Generals Arnold and Leahy and in Alanbrooke's diary. None of those accounts gives any sign that business was discussed. The editors print the note simply to account for the meeting's place in the conference record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d360:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first plenary session of the Tehran Conference, on 28 November 1943 at four in the afternoon. The three leaders and their staffs sat down together for the first time, and Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin each spoke words of welcome before the war survey began.

Roosevelt, joking that as the youngest present he would welcome his elders, promises complete frankness and nothing made public. Churchill calls the gathering the greatest concentration of power the world has ever seen. Roosevelt then surveys the Pacific war. Over a million American men and most of the navy are there. Supply ships make only three round trips a year. The strategy is attrition: sinking Japanese tonnage faster than Japan can replace it. Keeping China in the war, through the north Burma road, is the western aim.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d460:
British officials kept their own minutes of a meeting on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference closed, and the State Department printed the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume. Where the combined minutes speak for both allies, a United Kingdom minute shows the meeting as London's side saw and filed it.

That single-side view is exactly what makes the record useful. A reader can compare British wording, emphasis, and memory of the discussion with the joint accounts from the same days. Summit history depends on such comparisons, because each capital wrote the alliance's story slightly differently. This minute is one side's version, preserved in the American record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d560:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on March 7, 1944, keeping the March correspondence at full pace. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, among the follow-up papers the editors printed after the conference records proper.

That spring the Western allies were balancing the coming invasion against the demands of Italy, the Pacific, and their Soviet partner. Churchill's letters were the main vehicle for Britain's view on all of them. For readers, this message is part of the long paper bridge between London and Washington over which the coalition's strategy traveled, week by week, until the landings in France.
frus-1944-quebec-d60:
The United States Chiefs of Staff set down this memorandum on September 7, 1944, five days before the Quebec Conference opened. The American chiefs would travel to Canada with the President. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Position papers written just before a conference state what a delegation must win and what it may trade. The American chiefs carried to Quebec the questions of the final German campaign and the balance of effort against Japan. For readers, this memorandum shows the United States military arriving at the summit with its case prepared, in the last days of staff work.
frus-1944-quebec-d160:
Ambassador Winant wrote privately to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944, in one of the most personal letters in the volume. Churchill had arrived ill, though recovering, and regretted Hopkins's absence. Winant then turned to his real subject: Britain's exhaustion after five years of war, and the looming fight against Japan.

Britain was at the bottom of the manpower barrel, he wrote, with men conscripted from 16 to 65 and services visibly aging. Worse, a belief had seeped in that the British Navy was not wanted in the Pacific. If Britain were shut out of smashing Japan, Winant warned, the result would be postwar hatred and schism. A repetition of the tragedy of 1918 would be unforgivable.
frus-1944-quebec-d260:
The draft report of September 14, 1944, encloses the agreed summary of conclusions the Combined Chiefs reached at Octagon. It restates the coalition's war plan in formal language. The over-all objective is the unconditional surrender of the Axis. Europe would be defeated first, while pressure on Japan never slackened. Full resources would then turn against Japan, with Russia if possible.

The basic undertakings follow, including aid to Russia with coordination of forces, aid to China, and help for French, Italian, and other co-belligerent forces. One phrase betrays the week's hardest drafting fight. Moving forces to the Pacific was to have regard to other "agreed and/or inescapable commitments," a compromise welding the British and American wordings together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d60:
Ambassador Averell Harriman answered the President on 17 January 1945 about the food arrangements at Yalta. His telegram from Moscow is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It follows up Roosevelt's request for his own cooks and stewards.

Harriman reports that Foreign Minister Molotov agreed at once. Molotov treated the request as natural, just as it had been handled at Tehran. The President's mess would be set up in the twenty-one room palace at Livadia. Harriman adds that, weather permitting, he will inspect the site on 21 January, taking his daughter Kathleen along since such household matters were her department.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d160:
“Disturbed and deeply disappointed” is how Roosevelt opened his protest to Stalin on 30 December 1944. His top secret message, number 153, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers Stalin's refusal to delay recognizing the Lublin Committee.

No serious trouble, Roosevelt argues, would have followed from holding the purely formal act of recognition for the one month left before the three leaders meet. He had not asked Moscow to cut its practical dealings with the Lublin body. Nor had he asked it to accept the London government as it stands. What he dreads is the effect on world opinion, and on enemy morale, if Moscow crowns one Polish government while most allies still recognize the other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d260:
Stalin named his price for entering the Pacific war on 14 December 1944, and Harriman reported the talk the next day. His top secret message to the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The two men had a map open between them.

The Kurile Islands and the lower half of Sakhalin should be returned to Russia, Stalin said. Japan now holds the approaches to Vladivostok, and every outlet to the Pacific is held or blocked by the enemy. He then drew a line around the southern Liaotung Peninsula, taking in Port Arthur and Dairen. Russia wished to lease those ports and the land around them once more. Harriman recalled the Tehran talk, and answered that the President had seemed to have in mind an international free port instead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d360:
Freed prisoners and civilians drive this letter from Foreign Secretary Eden to Secretary Stettinius, written at Yalta on February 5, 1945. Eden recalled that the conference was to take up a reciprocal agreement with Moscow. It would cover Soviet citizens freed by Allied armies in the west and south, and British and American nationals freed by Soviet forces in the east.

The British chiefs had approved a draft, Eden wrote, and the Combined Chiefs would take it up that day. Speed mattered. Soviet forces were already overrunning the sites of British and American prisoner camps. The letter shows a humane problem becoming urgent diplomacy.

On the Sphere and Cylinder, the Measurement of the Circle, and the Sand-Reckoner stand among its treatises. Archimedes of Syracuse proved results that calculus would not match for nearly two thousand years.

He bounds pi, weighs the crown, and counts the grains of sand that would fill the universe, all with strict proof. Heath's edition adds a famous account of a lost method of discovery. Eureka's author stands here in full: playful, rigorous, and centuries ahead of his readers.
tob-10260:
A short grimoire on calling spirits circulated for centuries under the name of Henry Cornelius Agrippa as a fourth book to his Three Books of Occult Philosophy. Scholars agree Agrippa did not write it. It appeared after his death and fed on his fame.

Unlike Agrippa's learned theory, the fourth book gives practice: names of spirits, seals, hours, and steps for calling them up and questioning them. Magicians copied its rites into later grimoires, and it helped fix the image of the learned magician at work. Readers can compare its plain ritual craft with the deep system of the real Agrippa.
podcast-dannyjones-XmVQFX2Pp60:
Chris and Emily Bledsoe join Danny Jones to talk about a NASA-linked study of UFO contact and what they call spiritual beings. The episode title calls the study forbidden. The Bledsoes are known for close contact claims that drew interest from officials.

The guests tell their story of bright orbs, close sightings, and the officials who came to ask questions. They argue the events point to beings with a spiritual side, not just craft in the sky. Jones lets them lay out the full tale in order. The library files the episode as an archive record, so readers can judge the claims for themselves.
podcast-tuckercarlson-xHjM_aNYI60:
Tucker Carlson warns that the United States is drifting toward civil war. He calls such wars the worst kind any nation can face. The cause, he says, is a gap between groups that no longer share a life.

The title ties his warning to ICE protests and street riots. Carlson argues that clashes over enforcement show how deep the split runs. He urges fast action before violence hardens into habit. The episode is grave from start to finish. It speaks to viewers who already fear the country is breaking apart.
prestwich-flint-implements-amiens-abbevi:
Joseph Prestwich, a respected British geologist, reported on flint tools to the Royal Society in 1860. He had visited gravel pits at Amiens and Abbeville in France, and at Hoxne in England. Worked flints lay there beside bones of extinct animals.

Prestwich confirms the claims of Boucher de Perthes, long dismissed in Britain. His standing made the verdict hard for the Royal Society to ignore. The paper effectively ended the debate over the antiquity of man. From 1860 onward, deep human history was established science in Britain. French workers had been reporting such finds from the Somme gravels for years.
gosse-romance-of-natural-history-1860:
Philip Henry Gosse loved the sea shore and all its wonders, and wrote of them in 1860. The Romance of Natural History treats sea serpents and ocean marvels as romance, in his own word. Gosse was a famed Victorian naturalist who made the aquarium a craze.

He sifts tales of the deep with a believer's heart and a scholar's hand. Oudemans and the serpent men cite his pages to this day. The book shows Victorian science and wonder walking side by side. Gosse's charm is that he will not laugh a good tale out of court.
levi-histoire-de-la-magie-1860:
French mage Eliphas Levi told the long tale of magic in Histoire de la magie, first out in 1860. Levi had been a priest in training, then a sage of the occult. He traces spells, rites, and lore from old Egypt and the East down to his own day in France.

Levi treats magic as a lost branch of deep truth, not mere tricks. His grand sweep gave the new occult wave a past to claim. The book, in French here, is the ground stone of that wave's view of its own roots. Levi wrote in French, and this text keeps that tongue in full. Waite's English take came later and spread the work far past France.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen brings his long tale to its end in Vol. 4 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1860. Four tomes in, the tale of Egypt's place midst the lands of the old world stands full. Wars, trade, faith, and the fall of the pharaohs fill these last parts of the main tale in rich, grave prose.

Bunsen wrote as a man of faith and state, not a dig man. His dates have waned, yet his scope still stuns. One tome of proofs yet stands past this. The tale as tale ends here.
owen-footfalls-boundary-another-world-18:
Robert Dale Owen made the case for ghosts to his land in Footfalls on the Boundary of Another World, out in 1860. Owen was a man of state and print in the United States. He gathers tales of shades seen at death's hour, sounds with no source, and dreams that came true in grim detail from folk he trusts.

His tone is grave, fair, and free of cult zeal. Crowds took the book to heart at once. It gave the new faith a stamp of rank in that land. Few books did more to launch it.
asher-henry-hudson-navigator-1860:
George M. Asher put the journals of Henry Hudson in print for the Hakluyt Society in 1860. Hudson was the English sea captain who sought a north route to Asia. The journals cover his four voyages, the last of which cost him his life.

On June 15, 1608, off Novaya Zemlya, two of his men swore they saw a mermaid. Thomas Hilles and Robert Rayner told of her hair, her tail, and her fall back in the sea. The sober log book tone makes the tale the classic Arctic mermaid report of its age.
hawthorne-marble-faun-1860:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Marble Faun in 1860, his last completed romance of Italy. The tale gives Rome, art, and the Fall in a story of four young friends. Henry James called it the bridge to the international theme in the American novel tradition later.

Donatello, an Italian count with faun-like ears, loves the American artist Miriam in Rome's studios. A model who haunts Miriam is thrown from a cliff, and guilt transforms the glad faun. Hilda, a pure copyist, is crushed by a secret she witnesses and seeks a confessional in Rome. Kenyon, a sculptor, watches love and sin work on his friends across Roman ruins and galleries. Hawthorne asks if a fall can deepen the soul, his old fortunate fall theme.
emerson-conduct-of-life-1860:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published The Conduct of Life in 1860, his late essays on practical philosophy. The set treats fate, power, wealth, and culture in Emerson's most aphoristic and worldly manner of writing. It was his best-selling book in his lifetime, read as a guide to action and character.

Fate grants that heredity and circumstance bind us, then bids thought build altars to them in freedom. Power and Wealth praise energy and economy while warning what each costs the soul that serves them. Culture and Behavior polish the rough individualism of the early essays for society and city life in America. Worship closes the book with a call to moral sentiment over creed, rite, and church form in religion. Mature readers often rank this autumnal volume as Emerson's wisest and most usable work.
voltaire-candide-first-english-translati:
Voltaire's Candide reached English in this anonymous first translation of 1760, as Candidus; or, All for the Best. The London M. Cooper edition predates Smollett's famed version and includes a spurious contemporary Part II in print. Its haste shows the craze Candide caused the year after its French debut in 1759 across Europe.

Candide, taught that all is for the best, is kicked through war, earthquake, and the Inquisition. Pangloss's optimism survives hanging, dissection, and syphilis with its catchphrase absurdly intact at every disaster he meets. Eldorado, a Jesuit state, and a Venetian carnival crowd the picaresque tour of man's follies across continents. The close bids us cultivate our garden, a motto that outgrew the tale that bore it. This first English dress lets readers watch England meet Voltaire's wit at first hand.
eliot-george-mill-on-floss-1860:
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, her most autobiographical novel of a brother and sister. Maggie Tulliver's passionate, doomed devotion to her brother Tom drives the tale of a miller's family. Eliot drew Maggie from herself, the clever girl of a provincial world too narrow for her mind and heart.

Maggie, bookish and intense, is judged by a town that prizes her brother's plodding respectability over her gifts. The Tullivers lose the mill in a lawsuit, and Tom's vow of repayment rules the family's pinched, bitter years at home. Maggie's loves, Philip Wakem and Stephen Guest, end in scandal, renunciation, and a flood that joins brother and sister in death. In their deaths they were not divided, says the tombstone, in Eliot's most quoted epitaph. The novel's psychology of provincial life remains unmatched in English fiction.
ruskin-unto-this-last-1860:
John Ruskin published Unto This Last in 1860, four essays on the morals of economics. Ruskin attacks the idea that wealth is mere buying power and cheap labor a gain. True wealth, he argues, is life itself: health, justice, and noble work. There is no wealth but life is his famous summary.

He defends fair wages, honest goods, and work that honors the worker. The essays first appeared in a magazine and shocked its readers. Gandhi read the book, translated it, and called it a guide for his own life. It became a founding text of ethical economics. Its claims still challenge market orthodoxy.
motley-united-netherlands-vol-1-1860:
John Lothrop Motley published History of the United Netherlands, Volume 1, in 1860. The work continues his Dutch epic after the rise of the republic. This volume covers the years after William the Silent's murder in 1584. The young republic fights Spain while seeking aid from England and France.

The Earl of Leicester's troubled command in the Netherlands fills much of the story. Motley follows diplomacy and war together, in courts and camps. His research and narrative sweep match his earlier volume. The series in time reached four volumes. Readers who finish the Rise will want this sequel. It shows the republic in its golden, perilous age.
childrey-britannia-baconica-1660:
Joshua Childrey was a Hampshire clergyman and naturalist whose Britannia Baconica appeared in 1660. The book catalogs the natural rarities of England, Scotland, and Wales, county by county. Its title honors Bacon, whose call for a natural history of wonders Childrey took up.

Giants' bones, strange springs, fiery exhalations, monstrous births, and echoes in old churches fill his lists with Baconian care. He records what local people reported, sorting the credible prodigies from tales he cannot credit. The book is the Restoration catalogue of prodigies and wonders, a snapshot of a land still marvelous to its own scholars.
holmes-professor-1860:
Oliver Wendell Holmes followed his Autocrat with The Professor at the Breakfast-Table in 1860. The scene returns to the same Boston boarding house, with a new presiding talker. Holmes was then at the height of his powers as doctor, professor, and man of letters.

The Professor's talk runs deeper into theology and human nature than the Autocrat's, with the famous Little Bostonian among the listeners. The volume contains The Chambered Nautilus, Holmes's beloved poem of the soul outgrowing its shells: build thee more stately mansions, O my soul. Serious argument and table wit alternate in Holmes's easy manner. The book confirmed the breakfast-table series as a fixture of American letters.
turgenev-first-love-1860:
Isabel Hapgood translated First Love and its companion stories into English in 1904. Turgenev's title novella, written in 1860, is told by Vladimir, now middle-aged, recalling his sixteenth summer. At a neighboring villa he falls for Zinaida, a young princess who keeps a court of older admirers.

Vladimir spies, dreams, and suffers until he learns that his own father is Zinaida's secret lover. The shock ends his boyhood in a single night of watching. Turgenev called the tale his most personal work, drawn from his own youth. Hapgood's version stands beside Garnett's Turgenev as a distinct translation. The novella remains a classic study of first desire and disillusion.
turgenev-on-the-eve-1860:
On the Eve, Turgenev's novel of 1860, is given here in Constance Garnett's translation. Elena Stahova, a thoughtful young Russian girl, finds the suitors her parents favor too small for her dreams. She meets Insarov, a poor Bulgarian student burning to free his homeland from Turkish rule.

Elena chooses Insarov against her family's wishes, ready to share his cause and his exile. Their marriage takes them toward Italy, where illness waits on the road to war. Turgenev wrote on the eve of the freeing of the serfs in Russia. His new man and new woman point past the gentry world of his earlier books. The novel asks what a life should be spent on.
averroes-destructio-destructionum-1560:
Averroes, the great judge and philosopher of Córdoba, wrote the Tahafut al-Tahafut to answer al-Ghazali's attack on the philosophers. Its Latin name means the Destruction of the Destruction. The text here is the Venice printing of 1560, in the Latin of Calo Calonymos, with the exposition of Agostino Nifo. Two shorter works on the soul travel with it. The book is in Latin throughout.

Point by point, Averroes defends reason against the claim that philosophy breaks faith. He argues for the eternity of the world, the order of causes, and the bliss of the knowing soul. No English version in the public domain exists. The volume is the Latin West's own copy of Islam's greatest debate.
averroes-commentaria-metaphysicam-1560:
Averroes of Córdoba spent his life explaining Aristotle, and his long commentaries on the Metaphysics are the summit of that work. The text here is the eighth volume of the Venice Aristotle of 1560, in Latin. It holds the commentaries on books one through thirteen, with his short epitome of the same work.

Averroes reads Aristotle line by line on being, substance, form, and the first cause that moves all things. His readings taught the Latin schools so deeply that they called him simply the Commentator. No English version in the public domain exists. This is the book that set the terms of debate on God and being for three centuries.
averroes-colliget-1560:
The Colliget is the medical summa of Averroes, the Kulliyat, his book of the general rules of healing. The text here is the ninth volume of the Venice edition of 1560, in the Latin of Joannes Bruyerinus Campegius. With it stand his exposition of the Cantica of Avicenna and three shorter sections gathered by the editors.

Seven books move from anatomy and health to sickness, signs, drugs, foods, and the keeping of health. Averroes writes as both philosopher and court doctor, keen on clear rules drawn from Galen and tested by reason. No English version in the public domain exists. The Colliget was a school book of medicine across Europe for centuries.
sully-memoirs-vol-1-1760:
Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, was Henri IV's great minister, the man who rebuilt France's finances after civil war. His Mémoires of 1638 record that partnership of king and servant. Volume one here opens the English translation printed in 1760, after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756, in a set of five volumes.

Sully writes of war, taxes, roads, and farms with a steward's pride in order restored. The memoir presents Henri and himself as a team that dragged France from ruin to strength. Historians check his boasts, yet no source shows the reign's inner work like this one. Volume one begins the classic ministerial memoir of the age.
sully-memoirs-vol-2-1760:
Volume two continues the English Sully, the Memoirs of Maximilian de Bethune, Duke of Sully, in the printing of 1760. Sully's French Mémoires date to 1638, a generation after Henri IV's murder ended their work together. The English set, after Charlotte Lennox's translation of 1756, runs to five volumes.

In these pages Sully goes on counting what good government costs and what it saves. Campaigns and councils mix with budgets, grain stores, and plans for France's wealth. The minister's voice is brisk, certain, and never shy about his own merit. Readers meet statecraft here as daily labor, not glory. Volume two keeps that practical epic moving.
sully-memoirs-vol-3-1760:
Sully's Memoirs reach volume three in the English translation printed in 1760, after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756. Maximilien de Béthune, duc de Sully, had been Henri IV's right hand in war and finance. His Mémoires of 1638 set down how the two men governed France between them.

Volume three holds more of that double portrait: a king of charm and drive, a minister of ledgers and iron will. Sully recounts reforms in tax and farming, and the plots that ringed the throne. The work became the classic memoir of a great minister, trusted and argued with ever since. Its middle volume keeps the reign's machinery in plain view.
sully-memoirs-vol-4-1760:
Volume four of the English Sully, printed in 1760 after Charlotte Lennox's translation, continues the Memoirs of the Duke of Sully. The French original of 1638 tells how Henri IV and his minister pulled France out of civil war. The English set runs to five volumes, this one standing near its close.

War finance, diplomacy, and court intrigue fill Sully's later pages, all told from the minister's chair. He writes to defend his record, and the defense is detailed enough to test. Few memoirs show so clearly how a state is fed, armed, and kept solvent. Volume four carries that lesson through the reign's high years. The voice stays crisp, proud, and practical.
sully-memoirs-vol-5-1760:
Volume five completes the English Memoirs of Maximilian de Bethune, Duke of Sully, in the printing of 1760. Sully's Mémoires of 1638, Englished after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756, fill five volumes in all. The duke had served Henri IV as soldier, treasurer, and chief adviser through France's recovery.

The closing volume ends the reign and its minister's long service together. Sully's theme never changes: a kingdom thrives when its money is honestly kept and wisely spent. His pride in that record runs through every page, and readers can weigh it against the facts he supplies. The set stands as the classic ministerial memoir of early modern Europe.
virchow-cellular-pathology-chance-1860:
Rudolf Virchow gave twenty lectures in Berlin in 1858 that became Cellular Pathology. Frank Chance translated the German lectures into English in 1860. Virchow's famous rule, omnis cellula e cellula, holds that every cell comes from a cell. Disease, on his account, is disorder at the level of cells.

The lectures walk through sick tissues cell by cell, organ by organ. Fevers, tumors, and decay all get read as cellular events. His method tied the clinic to the microscope for good. The book founded cellular pathology as a discipline. Doctors learned to ask where, in which cells, illness sits. That question still guides medicine.
nightingale-notes-on-nursing-1860:
Florence Nightingale wrote Notes on Nursing in 1860 as a guide for anyone caring for the sick. She states her rule at once: nursing means putting the patient in the best state for nature to act. Fresh air, clean water, light, quiet, and clean rooms form her core teaching. The book founded modern nursing as a skilled practice.

Nightingale writes for homes as much as for hospitals, in plain direct sentences. She teaches close observation of the patient's face, food, and rest. Her stress on sanitation also spread statistical thinking into daily care. The Gutenberg text keeps her sharp voice intact. Few manuals have saved more lives.
burton-lake-regions-central-africa-1860:
Richard Burton led a Royal Geographical Society expedition into East Africa in 1857 to 1859, with John Speke as his second. The Lake Regions of Central Africa, from 1860, is Burton's own account. The goal was the great lakes and the source of the Nile.

Burton reached Lake Tanganyika, while Speke, traveling apart, found Lake Victoria and claimed the prize. Fever, desertion, and quarrels plague the march from the coast. Burton's eye for peoples, tongues, and trade is unmatched, even when his temper shows. The feud born on this trip shaped African exploration for a decade. His appendices on trade goods and routes served later travelers well.
plos-pone-0003460:
Shelley R. Starck and co-authors found a hidden source of cell surface markers in this 2008 paper. Cells display protein fragments on MHC class I molecules for immune checks. Those fragments were thought to come only from normal protein production. Some fragments, though, start at unusual start signals in the message.

The team showed a distinct way of starting protein building makes these hidden fragments. They call the products cryptic peptides. Immune cells can then spot cells making odd proteins. The finding adds a secret supply line to immune surveillance. Hidden protein bits like these may explain some responses doctors could not trace before.
plos-pone-0003560:
Iuliia Vitko and co-authors studied how a helper subunit steers calcium channels in this 2008 paper. Voltage-gated calcium channels pass signals in nerves and muscles. A beta subunit controls the main pore unit's traffic and behavior. Crystal studies had mapped where the two parts touch.

The team showed the beta unit's orientation toward the pore is critical. Twist that angle, and channel regulation changes. How contact leads to control was the open question. Precise geometry thus helps set nerve and muscle signaling. Calcium channels sit at the heart of pain, mood, and heart rhythm drugs.
plos-pone-0003660:
Alessandro Muzzi, Monica Moschioni, Antonello Covacci, and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major disease-causing bacterium. It grips host cells with hair-like pili, whose genes sit together in one operon.

Such grip tools face two pressures: keep working, yet change enough to escape the immune system. The team traced the pilus operon's history and found positive selection and recombination driving it. Their work shows how a pathogen's surface gear can evolve fast while staying useful to the bacterium. That balance helps the germ stay a step ahead of its host.
plos-pone-0003760:
Tobias Mourier and Eske Willerslev published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Retroelements are DNA pieces that copy themselves around the genome. They make up about forty percent of the human genome. Yet large regions of mammal genomes contain none at all.

The authors test whether selection against transcriptional interference keeps those regions clean. A retroelement landing near genes could garble how they are read, and selection may remove such inserts. Their analysis asks whether that pressure, rather than chance, sweeps certain genomic yards clean. Their answer bears on how genomes guard their working genes.
plos-pone-0003860:
Shireesh Srivastava, Linxia Zhang, Rong Jin, and colleagues published this bioinformatics paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. A main goal of microarray analysis is picking the genes that separate one condition from another. Earlier work showed that using prior knowledge about gene function can surface more meaningful hits.

The authors present a method that folds Gene Ontology information into unsupervised clustering and feature selection. The ontology tells the algorithm what each gene is known to do. The approach finds gene groups that make biological sense, not just statistical clusters. The same trick can serve other chip studies beyond this one.
plos-pone-0003960:
Meta Roestenberg, Ed Remarque, Erik de Jonge, and co-authors trialed a malaria vaccine candidate in 2008. The vaccine uses AMA1, a protein of Plasmodium falciparum. The parasite needs AMA1 to enter red blood cells and liver cells. Antibodies that block AMA1 can stop that entry.

Their PLOS ONE article tested the vaccine with three different adjuvants. Adjuvants are added ingredients that boost immune response. The team compared safety and immune response across Alhydrogel, Montanide ISA 720, and AS02. Picking the best partner formula is a required step toward field trials. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004060:
Joan Reibman, Michael Marmor, Joshua Filner, and co-authors linked a stomach germ to lower asthma odds in 2008. Germ exposure early in life may guard against allergic disease. Asthma has risen as many gut microbes have become rarer. Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacterium, has declined in cities.

Their PLOS ONE article reports asthma was inversely tied to H. pylori status. People carrying the germ had asthma less often in this urban sample. The pattern supports the idea that lost microbes changed immune training. It does not by itself prove the germ prevents asthma. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004160:
Ai Ling Wang and colleagues published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of lost central vision in older people. Early in the disease, deposits called drusen form on a membrane behind the retina.

The study looks at the ageing retinal pigment epithelium, the cell layer that feeds the retina. It focuses on two of the layer's cleanup systems. One is autophagy, where cells digest their own worn parts. The other is exosomes, tiny parcels that cells release. The authors weigh how these systems may contribute to drusen formation. Their ideas connect everyday cell housekeeping to a common cause of blindness.
plos-pone-0004260:
Hyun Kwon and colleagues published this smell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Olfactory marker protein is the hallmark of mature olfactory sensory neurons, the nerve cells that detect odors. Since its discovery, what the protein actually does had stayed poorly understood, though knockout mice showed it shapes olfactory signal handling.

The team examined how calcium leaves these neurons after a smell response, a step handled by the NCX exchanger. They report that calcium extrusion by NCX is compromised in mice lacking the marker protein. The result assigns the mysterious protein a concrete job in resetting the sense of smell.
plos-pone-0004360:
Yoshinori Yamakawa and colleagues published this social neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Across cultures, social relationships are often described in spatial terms: close friends, distant relatives, high lords. The authors ask whether this cognitive mapping of social concepts onto physical space arises from shared brain resources for processing social and physical relationships.

Using brain imaging, they studied the evaluation of social distance in the human parietal cortex. That region is famous for handling physical space and number. Finding it also handles social closeness would show the metaphor is built into the brain.
plos-pone-0004460:
Faces carry clues to a person's ancestry, and Yann Klimentidis and Mark Shriver tested how well those clues can be measured in PLOS ONE in 2009. People read ethnicity from faces every day, and those readings shape social life. They may also reflect a long history of human groups living apart and adapting.

In the United States, recent mixing between groups from different continents makes faces a mixed record. The authors estimated ancestry proportions from facial features and checked them against genetic measures. If faces track ancestry with fair accuracy, they become a cheap research tool. The study also raises care points, since reading ancestry from looks can mislead, and has a charged social history.
plos-pone-0004560:
Different steps in a growth signal chain respond with different sensitivity, model Jeongah Yoon and Thomas Deisboeck in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell growth depends on signaling pathways, chains of proteins that pass messages from the cell surface inward. Their regulation is a major focus of cancer research.

The team applied computational methods to the MAPK signaling cascade as triggered by the growth factor EGF. They used a multi-parametric global sensitivity analysis, which varies many factors at once to see which ones control the outcome. They did so without assuming in advance which components matter most. Maps of sensitivity like this tell drug designers where a pathway is fragile and where it will shrug off a single blocked step.
plos-pone-0004660:
Whether two asthma-linked signals can cross the placenta from mother to fetus is tested by Robert Lim and Lester Kobzik in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mechanisms by which prenatal events affect the development of adult disease are incompletely characterized. In a mouse model of maternal transmission of asthma risk, mothers pass a tendency toward asthma to their pups.

The candidate couriers are interleukins 4 and 13, pro-asthmatic cytokines, immune signal proteins. The team sought to test their role by assessing whether they make the transplacental passage. If such signals cross, a mother's immune state could directly tutor the fetal immune system. That would help explain how asthma risk is set before birth, and where prevention might start.
plos-pone-0004760:
Robert Gaeta and colleagues measured gene activity in newly remade oilseed rape hybrids using Arabidopsis chips, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Remade hybrids let scientists watch what happens right after two genomes merge in one plant. Past work showed chromosome swaps in later generations change gene activity by losing or doubling matched genes.

Swaps may also affect genes far from the swap site in indirect ways. The team used chips from a model plant to profile activity in the hybrids. Their data help separate direct from indirect effects. That matters for breeding crops from wide crosses. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
treaty-of-berwick-1560:
England and Scotland conclude the Treaty of Berwick in 1560. Elizabeth's England allies with Scotland's Protestant lords by its terms. French power in the north is the foe both sides fear.

English arms and gold back the Scots against their French-backed regent. The pact helps secure the Scottish Reformation in its cradle year. Old enmity between the two kingdoms starts its turn toward union. A Protestant Britain takes shape along the line this treaty draws. Few short pacts mark so clear a hinge in British history and faith. Within months, Scotland's parliament had cast off Rome and the old mass.
cia-0000009660:
Eleven Vietnamese prisoners of war were released by the Viet Cong at Christmas 1970, a February 1971 CIA report notes. The heading adds a description, cut off in the title, of something connected with the release. Holiday releases were rare breaks in the southern war's captivity.

A release at Christmas carried meaning beyond the eleven men freed. Such gestures served propaganda, morale, and sometimes genuine mercy at once. Analysts weighed which motive dominated before reporting upward. The freed men's accounts could also reveal camp locations and conditions. This file preserves a small act of release inside a long record of holding.
cia-0000012260:
Moving secrets from hand to hand took forms, and a CIA transfer record from August 1960 preserves one. The document transfer and cross-reference forwards a packet for an operation called Compass, and mentions a wheel used in passing secret goods along. Such slips logged what moved, who signed, and where the material went next.

The record shows the humdrum side of spying, where clerks and couriers mattered as much as agents. It ties the Compass packet to other files through its cross-references. For readers, it is the plain paperwork of the covert world, kept with the same care as the secrets themselves.
cia-0000015360: Further word on an FCDA meeting fills a CIA file dated March 5, 1953. The FCDA ran civil defense, the home front guard of the Cold War. Its meetings touched saucers when panic or warning was in play. The file shows the saucer question crossing into the civil defense world. The FCDA meeting file is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015460: Durant's report for the Scientific Advisory Panel on unidentified flying objects survives in a CIA record dated January 2, 1956. The catalog marks the report itself illegible, so its contents cannot be stated here. Durant served as the panel's secretary, a role named in other records of that panel. A key paper that cannot be read is a sharp lesson in archive loss.
cia-0000022360: The text of the indictment against Gary Powers is kept in full in a CIA record dated in 1960. An indictment states charges in the state's own words, count by count. Having the exact text let officials answer Soviet claims line by line. The entry is a primary source for the trial, plainer and harder than any commentary around it.
cia-0000023360: Detained Caucasians were sighted near Loc Ninh, in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1979 reports. Loc Ninh sits near the Cambodian border, north of Saigon. Four years after the war ended, such a sighting stirred the oldest hope of the prisoner issue. It was logged like the wartime reports, for checking against the names still unaccounted for.
cia-0000026760: The Syrian situation has its outlook assessed in a CIA paper dated in 1956. Syria in the fifties changed governments often, and leaned ever closer to Egypt and the Soviet bloc. An outlook paper had to judge a capital where today's rulers might fall by spring. The entry keeps one turn of that restless decade in the agency's own forecast form.
cia-0000036560: On August 1, 1968, the CIA asked for photo comparisons covering cases 9638 through 9645, with the names blanked out in the released record. Photo comparison was a core method in the search for missing American servicemen, and this short request sent one batch of cases to analysts for face matching. Its value lies in scale, since hundreds of such requests moved through the system.
cia-0000037160:

plos-pone-0004860:
Julie Pendergast and colleagues reported robust food anticipatory activity in BMAL1 deficient mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Food availability is a potent cue directing circadian locomotor activity in rodents. Even though nocturnal rodents prefer to forage at night, daytime food anticipatory activity is observed prior to short meals presented at a scheduled time. Persisting even when the central clock gene BMAL1 is absent.

Anticipation survives loss of the master clock gene. A separate food entrainable oscillator must exist. Finding its location remains a major goal. Meal timing affects metabolism broadly. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005460:
David Haskell and Anupam Adhikari tested an old idea of Darwin's in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In his famous book on species, Darwin guessed that the making of new species runs at different speeds in different groups. He also guessed that groups rich in species at one level tend to be rich at other levels too.

Using bird data, the authors found that both guesses hold up. They also showed that the pattern can predict which living birds face the highest risk of dying out. An old hunch, tested with modern data, turns into a tool for protecting birds.
plos-pone-0005560:
Linda Heinemann, Andreas Kleinschmidt, and Notger Müller studied brain responses during visual attention in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When people focus on one spot, the brain's vision areas react even in parts that map places with nothing on screen. The team measured those responses at set distances from the attended spot.

They varied the scene to see what drives the quiet responses in unstimulated areas. Such responses show that attention spreads through the visual field in a structured way. Knowing that spread helps explain how the brain picks out what matters in a busy scene.
plos-pone-0005660:
Fabienne Ripoll and co-authors published the genome of an emerging lung pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mycobacterium abscessus is a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis germ. It causes a stubborn lung disease, above all in people with cystic fibrosis whose lungs are already damaged.

Reading its genome revealed virulence genes borrowed from unrelated germs, not just from its own family. Borrowed genes may explain how a soil and water germ became a lung pathogen. The genome gives drug hunters a full parts list to work from. Its lung disease is hard to cure with current drugs, so each borrowed virulence gene is a possible weak point.
plos-pone-0005760:
Dong Gao and co-authors named a new immune booster protein in 2009. Cells detect viral RNA through sensors such as RIG-I, which then switch on interferon defenses. The team found a ring-finger protein, which they named REUL, that binds this pathway.

REUL acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, a tag-placing enzyme, and it stimulates RIG-I's alarm. Placing the right tags strengthens the signal that produces type I interferons. Those interferons are the body's early antiviral blanket. A new booster in that chain is a fresh lead for antiviral design and for understanding immune faults.
plos-pone-0005860:
Robert Beckman argued in 2009 that mutations which raise the mutation rate can speed tumor growth across many possible fitness landscapes. A tumor needs several genetic changes to become dangerous. Mutator mutations boost genomic instability, supposedly fast-tracking those changes.

The rival view holds that simple repeated selection of faster lineages explains the pattern without mutators. Beckman's analysis tests the mutator idea mathematically across landscapes. If mutators truly help, tumors carrying them may behave and respond differently. The paper is theory, but theory that shapes how oncologists interpret the mutation loads seen in real cancers.
plos-pone-0006460:
Tirta Susilo, Kate Crookes, Elinor McKone, and colleagues compared face reading in children and adults for PLOS ONE in 2009. People tend to recognize faces of their own age better than faces of other ages. Why that happens was unclear. One candidate cause is holistic processing, seeing a face as a whole rather than part by part.

Using the composite task, a test that reveals whole-face processing, the team studied child faces. Their title reports stronger holistic processing in children than in adults for those faces. The result supports the idea that experience tunes face reading. It helps explain why own-age faces feel easier to remember.
plos-pone-0006560:
Gerardo Zardi and co-authors studied a shell-boring parasite and mussel invasions in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stress from other living things may work with harsh settings to slow or aid an invasion. It can also change how invaders and native species compete. The team studied endolithic parasitism, where small organisms bore into shells. They worked on both invasive and native mussels in a place where conditions swing a lot.

A parasite that weakens invaders more than natives could slow an invasion down. One that harms natives more could speed it up. The mussels show why invasion results are hard to guess from species lists alone. Both the place and its parasites shape the outcome.
plos-pone-0009460:
Keizo Takao and a large team tested mice that lack a brain protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is CaMKIV. It helps pass signals from the cell surface to the genes in the nucleus. That relay is thought to lock in long term memory. Mice without the protein went through a wide set of behavior tests.

The tests covered learning, movement, social acts, and responses to fear and stress. Comparing these mice with normal ones shows which acts need CaMKIV and which do not. The full picture helps separate firm memory storage from other brain jobs. It gives later work a clear map of this one relay.
plos-pone-0009560:
Iain MacLeod and Tony Minson studied herpes simplex virus at the cell surface in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus wears several proteins on its coat. Four of them are needed for it to enter a cell. Virus particles missing one of those four cannot enter. They can still stick to the cell's surface, though. The team asked what that sticking alone does.

Binding by itself set off signals inside the cell. The cell responded before any entry took place. So the virus starts talking to its host at first touch. Those early signals may shape how the infection unfolds, and they could be targets for blocking it.
plos-pone-0009660:
Qing Zhou and co-authors compared proteins in a dividing parasite in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness. Inside the parasite sits a structure called the bi-lobe, which must copy itself before the cell can divide. The team compared the parasite's proteins to find new parts of that structure. Their proteomic screen turned up a previously unknown bi-lobe protein.

The new protein proved necessary for the bi-lobe to duplicate and for division to proceed. A part found only in the parasite's machinery is a possible drug target. Blocking division would stop the parasite from multiplying in the blood. The study adds a piece to a machine unlike any in human cells.
plos-pone-0010460:
Nathan Ford and colleagues asked whether early pill-taking habits predict long-term HIV control, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skipping antiretroviral doses lets the virus rebound and gain resistance. Earlier studies linked adherence and virus suppression at single time points. This team followed a patient group for five years. They tested whether adherence measured at the start foretold later failure.

Early habits did carry lasting information about risk. That makes early support for new patients especially valuable. Clinics could flag strugglers sooner and help before failure sets in. Five-year follow-up is rare and gives the claim weight. The study turns a simple measure, early adherence, into a planning tool for lifelong treatment.
plos-pone-0010560:
Dustin Baldridge and colleagues described body-wide connective tissue disease in mice lacking a collagen helper protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in three genes cause brittle bone disease by reducing a key collagen modification. One of those genes makes cartilage-associated protein, Crtap. The team studied mice with Crtap removed entirely. They examined the animals comprehensively, beyond bones alone.

The disease proved generalized, affecting connective tissue across the body. That breadth matches the human condition better than a bone-only view. Mouse models that capture the full picture help test treatments fairly. Collagen is everywhere, so its faults should be too. This study documents that spread in detail for one brittle-bone gene.
plos-pone-0010660:
Mark Vermeij and colleagues showed that baby corals swim toward sound, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Coral larvae drift in open water for days before settling. Choosing the right spot to settle decides whether a larva lives or dies.

In choice chambers, larvae moved toward recorded reef sounds. Healthy reefs are noisy places, full of snapping shrimp and fish calls. Quiet, damaged reefs lack that chorus. Sound may thus guide larvae to living reefs and away from dead ones. The result suggests that protecting reef soundscapes, and even playing sounds back, could help reefs recover.
plos-pone-0010760:
Michael Nickerson and colleagues explained how a gene fault clouds the cornea, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Schnyder corneal dystrophy runs in families and slowly clouds the eye's front window. Fatty deposits of cholesterol build up in the cornea, blurring vision. Faults in the gene UBIAD1 were known to cause it, but not how.

The team showed the gene makes an enzyme that works in mitochondria, adding a tail to a vitamin K related compound. Disease faults changed how that enzyme behaves. Linking a rare eye disease to basic cell chemistry opens paths to a precise diagnosis and, in time, a targeted treatment.
plos-pone-0010860:
Neetu Kumra Taneja, Sakshi Dhingra, Aditya Mittal and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The TB bacterium can lie dormant inside the body for years, and low oxygen is one signal thought to push it into that resting state. A two-part sensor system then switches on a dormancy program.

The team found that vitamin C, at levels found in the body, can trigger the same program. The vitamin mops up oxygen, and as oxygen fell the bacteria switched on their dormancy genes and slowed growth. Early and sustained phases of the response ran through different parts of the sensor system. Taneja and colleagues add a common nutrient to the list of dormancy cues. That matters because dormant TB is the hardest form to kill with drugs.
plos-pone-0010960:
Ben Raymond, Scott Shaffer, Serguei Sokolov and co-authors published this seabird study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sooty and short-tailed shearwaters are among the most numerous seabirds on Earth, roaming the Southern Ocean in huge flocks. Knowing where they feed, and why, matters for managing that ocean's ecosystems, so the team combined bird tracking with ocean data.

They merged tracks from birds breeding in three regions of New Zealand and Australia with at-sea sightings, water measurements, plankton and trawl data, and wind records. Birds from all regions converged on the Polar Front zone, especially one longitude band, and their feeding matched prey and wind patterns there. Raymond and colleagues show how two wide-ranging species share a vast ocean, information conservation planners need as Southern Ocean fisheries and climate shift.
plos-pone-0011060:
Michael Apicella, Deborah Post, Andrew Fowler and co-authors published this tularemia study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Capsule sugars coat many dangerous bacteria and have yielded successful vaccines, but the capsule of Francisella tularensis, the tularemia germ, had been suspected for years without ever being isolated. The authors developed an antibody that recognizes it and used that handle to characterize the material.

The antibody bound a diffuse, very large sugar molecule that stains poorly with standard methods but shows with a glycoprotein stain. The same capsule appeared in all fourteen type A and B strains tested, and it could be purified largely free of other bacterial components. Apicella and colleagues finally pin down a conserved surface feature of a high-concern pathogen. A shared capsule is exactly what a vaccine designer hopes for.
plos-pone-0011160:
Mehla, Bivalkar-Mehla, Zhang and colleagues tested a sea derived compound on HIV in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV can hide in resting cells, beyond the reach of standard drugs. The compound, bryostatin, was tested both for waking hidden virus and for blocking fresh infection.

Bryostatin woke latent virus through two signaling paths inside cells. At the same time, it hindered new infection in a way not tied to cell entry receptors. Pairing a wake up step with a killing step is a leading cure strategy. This dual action makes the compound a useful tool for that research, even before any clinic use.
plos-pone-0011260:
Gertsenstein, Nutter, Reid and colleagues sped up mouse engineering in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making gene altered mice from stem cells of a standard strain was slow and unreliable. The team combined those stem cells with embryos from outbred mice, a mixing method called aggregation, to create chimeras more efficiently.

The chimeras passed the altered genes to their offspring at good rates. That shortcut shortens the path from a lab made gene change to a living mouse line. Faster mouse making accelerates hunts for disease genes across medicine. Labs gain a practical method they can adopt without exotic equipment.
plos-pone-0011360:
Sarah Gold and co-workers traced in 2010 how bluetongue virus gets inside animal cells. Bluetongue is a disease of sheep and cattle spread by biting midges, and its virus must enter host cells to copy itself. Many viruses enter through a standard gateway that uses a cage-like protein coat, but this virus seemed to take another route.

Working with hamster kidney cells, the team showed the virus enters by a gulping process in which the cell swallows fluid and virus together, without the standard coat. That side door explains how the virus can infect cells even when the main gateway is blocked. Knowing the entry route matters for animal health. A drug or vaccine that jams this particular doorway could slow outbreaks that cost farmers heavily in lost livestock.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1260:
Sato reported to Togo on 30 July 1945. The Moscow exchange was nearing its end. Japan had given no answer the Allies would accept, the Soviet door stayed shut, and the war's machinery moved toward its final acts.

An envoy's late reports in a failing mission carry a special weight. Sato wrote as a man who had tested the door often enough to know it would not open. His cables urged Tokyo, in careful shades, to end the war before worse befell it. This dispatch belongs to those last urgings. It closes the July run of the Moscow thread in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1360:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the acting secretary of state from London on 26 July 1945, his third message in this part of the volume. That date fell in the last week of the Potsdam Conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By late July, London itself was changing: Churchill's government fell on 26 July after the election count. Winant's cable came from a capital in political upheaval, reporting to a Washington whose leaders were abroad. Readers who follow the Winant run get the substance of his reports. They also feel how much the alliance depended on steady men in post when events shook the top.
frus-1945-50-intel-d60:
General Craig wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 24 December 1945. A paper dated Christmas Eve shows the War Department's intelligence business running to the year's last days. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Craig had written to the Lovett Committee six days earlier; now he wrote to his own secretary. The two papers together show a staff chief working the question at both levels, study group and department head. Readers closing the volume's 1945 run here should feel the pause that follows. Within a month, the president's directive would settle the contest these papers had waged since August. The Christmas Eve date gives the long autumn a human full stop.
frus-1945-50-intel-d160:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 5" heads a text dated 8 July 1946. The State Department prints it as document 160 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Once a directive went out, staff worked to its terms, and later papers cite its number as their warrant. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d260:
"Office of Special Operations Directive No. 18/5 (Interim)" bears the date 24 February 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 260 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The form is stiff because it has to be: each line is a rule that a named office can be held to. The shelf of such orders, read in order, is the true org chart of the system as it grew. The mark 18/5 ties the order to the Council paper behind the covert tasking. The word interim in the title shows the rules were still being set.
frus-1945-50-intel-d360:
Allen W. Dulles addressed a memorandum to Mathias F. Correa and William H. Jackson on 21 January 1949. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 360, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1861-d60:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 July 1861. The dispatch is document 60 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two days later the Union army broke and ran at Bull Run. Adams's letter left London before that news could cross the sea. It stands in the file as a last report from the brief age when the war was still expected to be short. The next mails would bring the Bull Run news and test every word of this calm. The dread fact, when it came, found Adams ready with a steady hand.
frus-1861-d160:
On 7 November 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton on the last day of the old calm. The letter is document 160 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote the day before a Union warship stopped the Trent off Cuba. His November note to Paris keeps the normal course of the autumn. In the file it reads as the last calm page before news that shook two continents. The Trent lay off Havana that week, on her run toward the English Channel. Calm pages before a storm gain a poignancy that no writer could have planned.
frus-1861-d260:
12 October 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 260 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d60:
Dated 9 May 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 60 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d160:
On 10 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams wrote from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, and the report appears as Document 160 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams was the American minister to Britain, posted there since 1861.

That week a Newcastle speech by Gladstone had stirred talk that Britain might soon treat the South as a separate nation. What Adams heard from British leaders in such days carried real weight in Washington. His report is one piece of the record historians use to judge how near Britain came to changing the war in October 1862. Union consuls in British ports fed the legation word of ships fitting out for the South.
frus-1862-d260:
A Dayton report of 25 March 1862 stands as Document 260 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, wrote it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late March 1862 brought a Union win at Kernstown in the Shenandoah Valley and steady fighting talk in the French press. Dayton's task included countering French claims that the South could not be beaten. His reports home armed Seward with facts about French opinion, which the Secretary then used in his own dealings with the French minister in Washington. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d360:
Document 360, dated 3 March 1862, is Marshal Pelissier's answer to a circular sent out by a Mr. De Long. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume alongside his letter to the French foreign minister of the same date.

An answer to a circular is a formal reply to a question put to many officials at once. And such replies were gathered to guide policy in Paris. Filed in the American volume, this one shows the French government collecting views from its senior men on questions stirred by the war. The record gives no more of De Long than his name.
frus-1862-d460:
On 9 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley in Vienna. The instruction is Document 460 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

October brought Seward better material to work with: Antietam had checked Lee, and the emancipation order had been announced. His instructions that month spread the news and its meaning to every post, Vienna included. Motley could now tell the Austrian court that the war had become openly a war against slavery, a fact that changed European debate. The dispatch is part of the autumn effort to lock in the gains of September. It went out before winter councils in Europe took up the American question again.
frus-1862-d560:
A second instruction dated 6 October 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. It is Document 560 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.
