Two letters in one pouch meant two subjects, handled apart as the Department required. For Brussels in the autumn of 1862 the subjects ranged from Confederate agents in Europe to the court's reading of emancipation. Sanford's energy made his post a clearinghouse, and Washington fed it steadily. Paired with Document 559, this order shows the working granularity of the system. Nothing was bundled. Every question got its own sheet, its own date, and its own answer.
frus-1862-d660:
On 5 February 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to Robert H. Pruyn, the American minister bound for Japan. The letter is document 660 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn was taking over a legation that Townsend Harris had built from nothing.

Seward's early-1862 letters kept adding detail to Pruyn's charge as the new man neared his post. They show a State Department that, war or no war, meant to hold its place in Japan. For a reader, this letter fills in the gap between the naming of an envoy and the start of his real work abroad.
frus-1863p1-d60:
On 22 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams held the American legation in London. The letter is document 60 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Split mail was the legation's habit: short sheets, each on one head of business. Adams had talks, press, and Southern agents to cover, and he kept them apart for clean filing. This letter is the mate to document 59, sent the same day. In line with the run, it shows a post working at full pace in the heart of winter.
frus-1863p1-d160:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 17 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 160 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the set wound up a day spent on the Union's British brief at its most taut. Adams's April letters are the record of a fight won by facts, law, and patience in London. This one ends the 17 April three. It is a working piece of that record, valued now as part of the whole great run.
frus-1863p1-d260: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1863. It is document 260 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d360:
On 12 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 360 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d460:
A dispatch dated 15 April 1863 went from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d560:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 9 June 1863 and wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d660:
The 13 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020160:
Holger Prokisch, Curt Scharfe, David G. Camp, and a large team built a parts list for yeast mitochondria in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. The team combined several methods to name the proteins that work inside yeast mitochondria, then sorted them by job.

A merged list beats any single method, since each one misses some proteins. The catalog gives the field a shared base for testing what each part does. Yeast mitochondria are a stand-in for our own, so the list also guides human work. Many human diseases trace to broken mitochondrial proteins, and a good map is the first step to finding them.
plos-pbio-0020260:
Stewart A. Weber, Jennifer L. Gerton, and Joan E. Polinsky studied chromosome centers in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. The kinetochore is the handle that pulling fibers grab to move chromosomes during division. Cohesin, the glue between sister chromosomes, binds most thickly around that handle's region.

The team found the kinetochore itself boosts that nearby glue binding. So the handle helps load the very glue that resists its pull, a neat balance of forces. Getting this balance wrong leads to lost or extra chromosomes. The study sharpens the picture of how cells make division accurate, a process whose failure is a hallmark of cancer cells.
plos-pone-0000160:
Matthew D. Carling and Robb T. Brumfield published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Population geneticists estimate genetic diversity, written as theta, from samples of genes across many loci. The authors compare gene sampling strategies: how many loci, and how many individuals per locus, give the best estimate for the effort.

Sequencing budgets force trade-offs, and a poor sampling plan wastes money or yields weak estimates. The authors test which designs hold up across multiple loci. Their guidance helps field biologists plan DNA sampling for wild populations, where the estimates feed into conservation and evolution studies.
plos-pone-0000260:
Arja Kaipainen, Mark W. Kieran, Sui Huang, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. PPAR-alpha is a protein that helps control fat metabolism and inflammation. The authors report that when inflammatory cells lack PPAR-alpha, tumor growth is suppressed, showing the protein's role depends on which cells carry it.

A gene can help a tumor in one cell type and hinder it in another. Separating the inflammatory cells' role from the tumor's own cells clarifies that picture. The finding warns drug developers that targeting PPAR-alpha will cut both ways unless the cell type is taken into account.
plos-pone-0000360:
Jesús Gómez-Zurita, Toby Hunt, Fatos Kopliku, and colleagues published this insect evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Leaf beetles, the Chrysomelidae, are a huge family of plant-eating insects. The authors present a recalibrated family tree of the beetles, dated with molecular clocks. They conclude that angiosperms, flowering plants, and their insect herbivores diversified independently rather than in lockstep.

The classic story says beetles radiated because flowering plants did. A recalibrated tree that uncouples the two timelines challenges that story. The paper is a careful piece of evidence in the long debate over co-evolution between plants and the insects that eat them.
plos-pone-0000460:
Evan H. Hurowitz and colleagues sped up an old measurement with a computational shortcut, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. A northern blot is a classic lab test for gene activity, but it is slow and one-gene-at-a-time. Their virtual northern analysis infers the same information for the human genome from existing sequence and expression data.

A virtual method that matches the bench test would let researchers screen the whole genome before spending weeks in the lab. Tools like this mark the point where genome databases became rich enough to answer questions once left to wet experiments. The study checks the shortcut against the real thing.
plos-pone-0000560:
Gustavo T. Rosa and colleagues found a side door a herpesvirus uses to enter cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Murine gamma-herpesvirus-68 is a mouse virus used to model human herpesviruses. The team showed that IgG Fc receptors provide an alternative infection route. When antibodies coat the virus, cells that grab antibodies can pull the virus in.

Antibodies are supposed to neutralize viruses, so a route that turns coating into entry is a trap in the defense. This trick, related to antibody-dependent enhancement, matters for vaccine design, since a vaccine that produces the wrong antibodies could help the virus. The mouse model lets researchers study the route safely.
plos-pone-0000660:
Kamini Singh, Devraj Mogare, Ramprasad Obula Giridharagopalan and colleagues studied a tumor suppressor gone wrong in breast cancer, for PLOS ONE in 2007. SMAR1 is a protein that interacts with p53, the famous cancer guard, and stabilizes it by a phosphate tag at one site. The team shows SMAR1's own production is switched on by p53 through a response element in its promoter.

When DNA damage was triggered by the drug doxorubicin, modified p53 was recruited to that element. The title reports SMAR1 is dysregulated in breast cancer, and the study follows its role in how cancer cells migrate and invade. A broken p53 partner fits the spread story.
plos-pone-0000760:
Jared L. Strasburg, Michael Kearney, Craig Moritz and colleagues combined family trees with range maps for an Australian gecko. Many parthenogenetic organisms, which reproduce without males, seem to have evolved recently and spread rapidly. Those patterns bear on the merits of sexual versus asexual reproduction, yet their interpretation is contested. The team's gecko lives in Australia's arid zone.

Combining phylogeography, the geography of gene lineages, with distribution modeling, they report multiple Pleistocene range expansions. Ice-age climate swings pushed the gecko's range out repeatedly. Each expansion left genetic traces that the combined methods can read. Asexual lineages are often dismissed as short-lived; this one's history is long and dynamic.
plos-pone-0000860:
Mariana de Napoles, Tatyana Nesterova and Neil Brockdorff watched the silent X chromosome wake up early in mouse germ cells, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The inactive X chromosome, characteristic of female body cells, is reactivated during development of the female germ cell lineage. In mouse, analysis of products of X-linked genes and transgenes had indicated when reactivation occurs. Primordial germ cells are the precursors of eggs.

Their title reports an early loss of Xist RNA expression, plus the chromatin modifications of the inactive X, in developing primordial germ cells. Xist is the RNA that coats and silences one X. Losing it early starts reactivation sooner than gene products reveal.
plos-pone-0000960:
Michael Poulsen, Daniel Erhardt, Daniel Molinaro and colleagues studied conflict inside the fungus growing ant partnership, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ants, a fungus they farm for food and other microbes live in a famous mutualism. Theory says conflict inside such partnerships should threaten their stability.

The team focus on antagonistic interactions between bacteria in the system. Rival microbes may, in fact, help shape how host and symbionts relate over time. That twist matters: a partnership can be held together partly by the quarrels of its smaller members. The study adds hard detail to a textbook example of cooperation in nature.
plos-pone-0001060:
Michael Crossland, Steven Dakin and Peter Bex used illusions to reveal blind spots in damaged retinas, in PLOS ONE in 2007. People with retinal disease are often unaware of large gaps in their visual field. The brain fills in the missing area, hiding the loss from its owner.

That filling in makes standard tests unreliable. The team attempt to use illusory stimuli, images that exploit the filling in process, to identify the true blind spots. Finding hidden loss matters because patients who cannot see a gap cannot report or adapt to it. A clever test that outwits the brain's patchwork could change eye screening.
plos-pone-0001160:
What a mother experiences during pregnancy can shape her offspring before birth, though most evidence concerns harm from stress. Alessandro Sale and colleagues tested the opposite idea in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: whether an enriched environment during pregnancy speeds development of the fetus. They studied the visual system of the offspring.

The team reports that maternal enrichment during pregnancy accelerates retinal development in the fetus. The retina is part of the eye that senses light, and its early growth is easy to measure. The result suggests that positive conditions for the mother reach the developing brain, not just harmful ones.
plos-pone-0001260:
HIV-infected children are vaccinated on the same schedule as other children under the Expanded Program on Immunization. Mathurin Tejiokem and colleagues asked whether the protection from those vaccines lasts. Their study, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, covered children living with HIV in Central Africa. Antiretroviral therapy was expected to prolong these children's lives considerably.

The authors report low persistence of antibodies to the program's vaccines in these children. Antibodies that fade early leave children unprotected against diseases the schedule was meant to prevent. Their findings raise the question of booster doses or adjusted schedules for HIV-infected children.
plos-pone-0001360:
Emotional blunting, a diminished ability to respond to emotionally salient stimuli, is a common and disabling feature of schizophrenia. Charmaine Pietersen and colleagues present an animal model of it, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The disturbance may stem from dysfunction of the amygdala, a brain region central to fear responses.

Negative emotional states, such as fear, are where the blunting shows most. A valid animal model lets researchers test the circuit basis of the symptom and screen candidate treatments. The authors describe their model's behavior and its relevance to the human condition.
plos-pone-0001460:
Flavio Rizzolio and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on short stature tied to hormone lack. Lack of growth hormone, alone or with other hormone lacks, causes most such cases. Faults in known genes explain some cases, but many stay unsolved. The team looked at a key region of chromosome 18.

They note stretches of DNA that do not code for proteins but are kept near unchanged across species. Such kept stretches often hold gene switches. Faults there could cause the same ills as gene faults do. The work argues for a shared cause that spans both kinds of DNA change.
plos-pone-0001560:
Jan Alexander Hiss and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how malaria parasites ship proteins out. The parasite lives inside red blood cells and sends proteins out to reshape its home. A short mark on each shipped protein was the known guide. The team ran a computer scan of the parasite's full protein set for that mark.

They found the zones beside the mark hold a kept pattern that varies by protein family. That pattern refines who gets shipped and who stays. A sharper export rule helps labs predict parasite tricks. It may also flag points to jam the shipping line with drugs.
plos-pone-0001660:
Sandra Blanco, Marta Sanz-García, Claudio R. Santos, and their co-authors studied how a human kinase tempers inflammation signals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A cell's response to any trigger reflects a balance among many signaling pathways, and protein interactions tip that balance. The kinase VRK2 can modulate several pathways.

The team reports that VRK2 interacts with JIP1, a scaffold protein that holds signaling parts together. Through that contact, VRK2 changes the gene response driven by interleukin-1, a strong inflammation messenger. The full text gives the interaction tests, the gene activity changes, and the pathway maps. Work like this shows how single protein contacts can retune a cell's answer to inflammation, a process at the heart of many diseases.
plos-pone-0001760:
Junghee Lee, Bradley S. Folley, John Gore, and their co-authors scanned the brains of people with schizophrenia during memory tasks in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Faulty prefrontal function is central to the working memory deficits of schizophrenia, but how activation and memory performance relate was undetermined. Working memory is the mental scratchpad used to hold and use information over seconds.

The team used two imaging methods together, functional MRI and near-infrared spectroscopy, during spatial working memory tasks. The full text gives the activation maps and where patient patterns diverged. Dual imaging cross-checks results, and locating the origin of the deficit helps target cognitive training and drug trials for schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0001860:
Kazuo Okanoya, Naoko Tokimoto, Noriko Kumazawa, and their co-authors trained rodents to use tools in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tool use is defined as manipulating an inanimate object to change the position or form of a separate object. The expansion of cognitive niches and tool-use capabilities probably stimulated each other in hominid evolution, which makes simpler animal cases valuable.

With training, the rodents developed tool use with an optimal motor strategy and functional understanding, per the paper's title. The full text gives the training regimen and the animals' technique changes. Showing that a rodent can learn genuine tool use narrows the gap between human and animal cognition and gives labs a trainable model of it.
plos-pone-0001960:
Anna Syme and Gary Poore wrote a taxonomy study in PLOS ONE in 2008 that sorts out a small sea crustacean and its genus. The animal is an ostracod, a tiny shrimp-like creature in a two-part shell, named Cypridina mariae. Its story was tangled: the first account, from 1850, described only the shell, and that shell was thought lost.

The genus built on it, Cylindroleberis, had a messy naming history as well. The pair give a fuller account of the species and a fresh diagnosis of the genus. Careful naming work of this sort keeps species records stable, so field and lab studies can be sure they mean the same animal.
plos-pone-0002060:
Benoit Doublet and co-authors charted new landing sites of a drug-resistance island in Salmonella, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The Salmonella genomic island 1 is a block of DNA that can move between bacteria. It was first found in an epidemic, multidrug-resistant strain of Salmonella Typhimurium called DT104, and it carries a complex set of resistance genes.

The team report a secondary attachment site where the island can dock in the genome, and tandem integration, where copies line up in a row. Each extra docking route helps the island spread and persist. Tracking them aids the fight against drug-resistant food poisoning.
plos-pone-0002160:
Isabel Porto and co-authors surveyed the tiny algae that live alongside reef macroalgae in the Caribbean, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Symbiodinium are dinoflagellates, single-celled algae best known for living inside corals and feeding them energy from sunlight. That coral partnership has drawn much study as reefs decline worldwide.

Far less was known about Symbiodinium cells that live free or cling to seaweeds rather than coral. The team sampled Caribbean reefs to map where these forms occur and how they spread. Knowing the full range of these algae matters, since free-living stocks may help reefs recover after bleaching.
plos-pone-0002260:
Laure Perrin-Cocon, Sophie Agaugué, Olivier Diaz, and co-authors studied immune cells from people with long-term hepatitis C, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chronic hepatitis C leaves patients with weak antibody and killer cell responses. A defect in dendritic cells, the scouts that start immune attacks, has been suspected. The matter stayed controversial, though.

The team grew dendritic cells from patients' blood cells and stimulated them through a sensor called TLR4. They report that the cells' Th1-driving function, the branch of immunity that fights viruses, was disabled. A defined defect like this points to where immune therapy for chronic hepatitis C might push.
plos-pone-0002360:
Shao-Yin Chen, Yulei Wang, Marilyn Telen, and co-authors read the small RNAs inside mature red blood cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mature red cells have no nucleus or organelles, and it was commonly thought they hold no nucleic acids at all. That assumption had rarely been tested directly with modern tools.

The team analyzed the transcriptome of purified human mature red cells and found microRNAs present and varied. In sickle cell disease, where red cells are the whole story, the microRNA expression pattern differs. Leftover RNA in red cells may help regulate their lifespan and could offer new markers for blood diseases.
plos-pone-0002460:
Müller and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Martina S. Müller, Julius F. Brennecke, Elaine T. Porter, and others. Its subject is perinatal Androgens and Adult Behavior Vary with Nestling Social System in Siblicidal Boobies. Exposure to androgens early in development, while activating adaptive aggressive behavior, may also exert long-lasting effects on non-target components of phenotype.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002560:
Led by Flierl, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Michael A. Flierl, Daniel Rittirsch, Anthony J. Chen, and others. Its subject is the Complement Anaphylatoxin C5a Induces Apoptosis in Adrenomedullary Cells during Experimental Sepsis. Sepsis remains a poorly understood, enigmatic disease.

One of the cascades crucially involved in its pathogenesis is the complement system. Especially the anaphylatoxin C5a has been shown to have many harmful effects during sepsis. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002660:
Work by Martina Buck and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was direct infection and replication of naturally occurring hepatitis c virus genotypes 1, 2, 3 and 4 in normal human hepatocyte cultures. Authorship is credited in the record to Martina Buck and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection afflicts about 170 million individuals worldwide. The authors add a further point. However, the HCV life cycle is only partially understood because it has not been possible to infect normal human hepatocytes in culture. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002760:
Work by David González and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was brucellosis vaccines: assessment of brucella melitensis lipopolysaccharide rough mutants defective in core and O-Polysaccharide synthesis and export. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David González, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The brucellae are facultative intracellular bacteria that cause brucellosis, one of the major neglected zoonoses. The authors add a further point. In endemic areas, vaccination is the only effective way to control this disease. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002860:
Work by Eduardo Lugo and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was ubiquitous crossmodal stochastic resonance in humans: auditory noise facilitates tactile, visual and proprioceptive sensations. The catalog record names Eduardo Lugo first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Stochastic resonance is a nonlinear phenomenon whereby the addition of noise can improve the detection of weak stimuli. The authors add a further point. An optimal amount of added noise results in the maximum enhancement, whereas further increases in noise intensity only degrade detection or information content. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002960:
Patrick Mardulyn, Marie-Anne Vaesen and Michel Milinkovitch grew lab populations with known history in 2008 to test inference methods. Natural populations whose past is known in detail would be ideal for checking tools that reconstruct history from genes. Such populations are extremely rare in the wild.

As an alternative, the team cultured replicate populations in the lab and generated microsatellite data from them. Since the true history was controlled, methods could be scored against fact. Published in PLOS ONE, the setup gives evolutionary biologists a benchmark for tools used on wild populations. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003060:
Nicholas Lesica, Toshiyuki Ishii and Garrett Stanley improved estimates of receptive fields from natural stimuli in 2008. Natural stimuli show that neural responses differ in key ways from responses to artificial ones. Yet natural inputs contain strong correlations and uneven intensity distributions, which bias standard estimates.

A receptive field is the pattern a neuron responds to. The team tackles asymmetric intensity distributions head-on in how they estimate these fields. Published in PLOS ONE, better estimates from real-world stimuli help sensory research leave simple lab patterns behind and still stay exact. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003160:
Yao-Zhong Liu, Scott G. Wilson, Liang Wang and colleagues search for genes behind hip bone size in women in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disease in older people and raises the risk of hip fractures from minor falls, which carry high illness and death rates. Hip bone size is one key measurable risk factor for those fractures.

In a genome-wide association study, the authors identify the PLCL1 gene for variation in hip bone size in females. Readers get a concrete gene lead from a broad scan. Such leads can improve risk prediction and point to the biology of bone growth.
plos-pone-0003260:
Heather B. Jaspan, Lyen C. Huang, Mark F. Cotton and colleagues review bacterial disease in HIV-infected children in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serious bacterial infections are a major source of morbidity and mortality in HIV-infected children. The spectrum of disease is wide, and the germs at fault vary according to setting. Use of antibiotic prophylaxis and emergence of multi-drug resistant bacteria made local data needed.

Their retrospective cohort study covers bacterial disease and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in children in hospital with HIV. Readers get a record for one setting of which bacteria caused illness and which drugs still worked. Such patterns guide first-choice antibiotics where lab testing is scarce.
plos-pone-0003360:
Brigitte Mack and Olivier Gires examine CD44 forms in head and neck tissues in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CD44 splice variants are long known as being associated with cell transformation. Recently, the standard form of CD44 was shown to be part of the signature of cancer stem cells in colon, breast, and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. This was somewhat surprising given the variant history.

The authors compare CD44s and CD44v6 expression in head and neck epithelia. Readers see normal tissue expression set beside tumour-associated claims. Baseline expression matters, because a cancer stem cell marker is useful only if healthy tissue lacks it or uses it differently.
plos-pone-0007460:
C. Patrick Doncaster published a theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how ecologists explain patterns of species abundance. A famous framework, Hubbell's neutral theory, assumes all species have identical vital rates. That simple premise predicts real patterns surprisingly well. Yet many ecologists doubt species are truly interchangeable. Doncaster examined a softer assumption called ecological equivalence.

Under equivalence, species are alike in the ways that matter for the model, not identical in every detail. He argues this is a realistic and testable alternative to neutral theory. Framing it rigorously lets scientists compare the two ideas against field data. The paper is a contribution to theory rather than experiment. It gives a long-running debate a cleaner set of options.
plos-pone-0007560:
Ronald Hancock and Yasmina Hadj-Sahraoui published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on preparing cell nuclei for study. Nuclei are usually isolated in salty solutions that keep them compact. The real cell interior, though, is not a salt bath. It is crowded with large molecules. The authors questioned whether standard ionic conditions distort what nuclei look like and how they behave.

They isolated nuclei using inert macromolecules that imitate the cytoplasm's crowding. The approach preserves nuclear structure under conditions closer to life. A more faithful preparation gives a truer view of the genome's home. Details like chromatin packing depend on the surroundings, so the surroundings should be right. The study offers cell biologists a gentler, more realistic way to handle the nucleus.
plos-pone-0007660:
Heidi Vebø and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Enterococcus faecalis, a bacterium with a double life. It normally lives harmlessly in the human gut. In hospitals, it turns opportunist, causing bloodstream and other infections. The team read the bacterium's full transcriptome, all the genes it switches on, while it grew in blood. That environment is where the commensal becomes an invader.

The blood-grown bacteria ran an adaptive program distinct from gut life. Genes for surviving the bloodstream's defenses and scarcity switched on. Reading that program shows how the turn to pathogen happens. It also lists candidate factors that hospital strains need and gut strains may not use. Such lists guide the hunt for drug and vaccine targets. The study catches a familiar microbe in the act of changing sides.
plos-pone-0007760:
Andrew Ramsay and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It models TB testing services in Malawi under new policies and tools. A recent WHO policy changed how smear microscopy, the basic TB test, should be done. Low-cost fluorescence microscopes were also becoming available.

The team used a hospital laboratory register in Lilongwe as their base. They estimated effects on case detection and laboratory workload. Better microscopes could find more cases without crushing lab staff. Modeling first lets a poor country weigh gains against costs. The study supports smarter roll-out of new TB diagnostics.
plos-pone-0007860:
Vishal Prashar and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It captures a single water molecule at work inside HIV's key enzyme. HIV-1 protease cuts viral proteins into working parts. It is a premier target for AIDS drugs.

Designing blockers requires knowing exactly how the enzyme performs its cut. X-ray analysis revealed a catalytic water molecule sitting in the active site. It was found there alongside a product peptide, the piece just cut. That snapshot sharpens the picture of the transition state. Drug designers can use it to build tighter-fitting inhibitors.
plos-pone-0007960:
Michael Holmes and colleagues took stock of gene-guided prescribing in PLOS ONE in 2009. The field, pharmacogenetics, promises drug choice and dose matched to a person's genes. Their review gathered studies from across the field and judged the strength of the proof behind each claim.

Much of the promise still rested on thin or mixed proof. A few gene-drug pairs stood on firm ground, but many awaited solid trials. The sober survey helps doctors and funders tell ready tools from early hopes, so patients get tests that truly help rather than costly guesses.
plos-pone-0008060:
Federica Crostarosa and colleagues built a monkey model of two infections meeting in one body for PLOS ONE in 2009. Herpes simplex virus type 2 raises the odds of catching and passing HIV, even when no sores show. Testing prevention gels needs a model where both viruses meet as they do in people.

Macaques given vaginal herpes and an HIV-like virus let the team watch the pair interact and test microbicide gels against them. A faithful model can weed out weak gels before human trials. That saves time, money, and risk for the women such gels are meant to protect.
plos-pone-0008160:
Cheryl Olman and colleagues mapped a flaw in brain scans of the memory center in PLOS ONE in 2009. The medial temporal lobe holds key memory structures, but it sits near air and bone. In functional MRI, those borders warp the magnetic field and bend or erase the signal.

The team charted where the bending and loss are worst, and how they shift with scan settings. Honest maps of a flaw are the first step to fixing it. Memory research leans hard on this brain zone, so cleaner scans there mean firmer claims about how memory works.
plos-pone-0008260:
Eva-Liis Loogväli and colleagues examined the mitochondrial molecular clock in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Scientists use mitochondrial DNA changes to date genetic events. Among living humans, the clock seems to tick faster than species comparisons suggest. The rate from human-chimpanzee comparisons looks slower. That mismatch limits how clocks can be calibrated across species.

The authors set out to explain the imperfection of the hominid clock. If the rate changes over time, dates for migrations and splits shift. Fixing the clock affects much of human evolutionary history. Their analysis helps readers judge how firm those dates are.
plos-pone-0008360:
Kerstin Svensson and colleagues presented a PCR array for Francisella in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Francisella bacteria include dangerous pathogens that need precise identification. Clinical and environmental isolates must be typed quickly and reliably. The team built a real-time PCR array for hierarchical identification. Typing markers came from comparisons of many genomes and genes.

Twenty-three canonical single nucleotide differences anchor the typing scheme. Hierarchical typing first places an isolate broadly, then refines it. A robust, rapid, flexible assay serves outbreak response and research. It helps labs tell harmless relatives from true threats.
plos-pone-0008460:
Jessica Saykally and co-authors report a gene effect in female mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Four large human studies had mapped an obesity gene to a part of chromosome 10. That region holds the gene for ZEB1, a factor that controls other genes. ZEB1 also shapes how some cell types mature. The team test its role in body fat.

When ZEB1 is changed in female mice, fat gain is held back. The effect marks ZEB1 as a repressor of adiposity, or fat buildup. The sex-specific result is itself a clue. It opens a new path for study of weight control.
plos-pone-0008560:
Venkaiah Betapudi and co-authors study motor proteins in spreading cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Non-muscle cells express multiple myosin II motor proteins. Forms include myosin IIA, IIB, and IIC, transcribed from different genome loci. Their sequences are significantly homologous, so they were believed to overlap in function. The team test that assumption during cell spreading. As cells spread, they extend flat sheets called lamellipodia at their edges.

They find myosin forms with different functions determine lamellipodia fate. One form may extend a sheet while another retracts it. Distinct motors thus steer a single structure in opposing ways. The result revises the view that these ubiquitous motors are interchangeable.
plos-pone-0008660:
Donal O'Shea and co-authors study natural killer cells in obesity in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Obese individuals who smoke have a fourteen year reduction in life expectancy. Both obesity and smoking are independently associated with increased malignancy risk. Natural killer cells are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity. They are compromised in obese patients. The team measure NK cell function in obese subjects. They also test susceptibility to the effects of cigarette smoke.

They find NK function is impaired in obesity. Smoke exposure further weakens those already compromised cells. That double hit may explain part of the cancer risk. Supporting NK cells could be a target for obese smokers.
plos-pone-0008760:
Siva Panguluri, Shephali Bhatnagar, Akhilesh Kumar, and colleagues listed the genes behind muscle loss driven by inflammation. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A signal called TWEAK can waste skeletal muscle when it stays high. Chronic diseases often raise such signals and shrink muscle. The gene program that carries out the wasting was only partly known.

The team profiled both regular genes and microRNAs in wasting muscle. Patterns emerged for growth, breakdown, and energy pathways. Several microRNAs shifted alongside the classic wasting genes. The combined list gives drug hunters more targets for protecting muscle in chronic illness.
plos-pone-0008860:
Zijun Xiao, Chuanjuan Lv, Chao Gao, and colleagues turned whole cells into factories that recycle their own helpers. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many useful enzymes need a costly helper molecule called NAD in its plus form. Buying the helper at factory scale is prohibitively expensive. Regenerating it inside the cell would cut costs sharply. The oxidized form, needed here, had been harder to recycle than its partner.

Their biocatalyst cells regenerated the helper while making chiral chemicals. Chiral products, with left- and right-handed forms, are prized in pharmacy. Self-recycling cells make green chemistry more practical. Industry gains a cheaper route to fine chemicals.
plos-pone-0008960:
Thomas Hussenet and co-authors named a gene that drives a common lung cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is frequent and aggressive. Cancers often grow by making extra copies of genes that push cell growth. One stretch of chromosome 3 is copied again and again in these tumours.

Scanning that stretch pointed to SOX2, a gene known for keeping stem cells young. Tumours had multiplied SOX2 and switched it on at high levels. Extra copies turned a normal developmental gene into a cancer driver. The finding marks SOX2 as a target worth testing for future lung cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0009060:
Udi Gluschnaider and co-authors found a way to slow prostate cancer cells by blocking their rubbish disposal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prostate cancer is common, and its growth depends heavily on the androgen receptor's signals. Advanced cases are first treated by cutting those signals off. Nearly all patients eventually relapse despite that early success with treatment.

Beta-TrCP is part of the cell's protein-tagging machinery for disposal. Inhibiting it raised levels of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor inside the cells. That rise, in turn, cut the cancer cells' growth in the team's experiments. The result suggests a fresh angle of attack on a very common cancer.
plos-pone-0009160:
Hongxia Ma and co-authors infected rabbits with three hepatitis E viruses to compare them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Farmed rabbits in China had been found carrying a new hepatitis E genotype. Its genome is organised like the mammal-infecting genotypes 1 to 4. Yet its sequence matches them only loosely.

Rabbits are common lab animals, so cross-infection matters practically. The team dosed rabbits with the rabbit virus and with genotypes 1 and 4. Comparing infections showed which strains rabbits can host. The answer guides both animal research and hepatitis E ecology. Each virus was tracked through the infection it caused.
plos-pone-0009260:
Katsuaki Suzuki and co-authors published this rat brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Parkinson's disease is known for movement problems, but depression and thinking troubles often come first. Those early symptoms do not respond to dopamine replacement drugs. Their causes inside the brain are poorly understood.

The team destroyed dopamine neurons in the rat midbrain using a toxin called 6-hydroxydopamine. New cell birth in the hippocampus, a memory center, then decreased. The antidepressant fluoxetine reversed that drop. The result links dopamine loss to a change in the hippocampus, a possible root of Parkinson's mood symptoms.
plos-pone-0009360:
Shweta Bansal and co-authors published this pandemic flu study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu hit school-age children much harder than adults. Older adults seemed to carry some leftover immunity. But that alone might not explain the wide age gap in infections.

The authors modeled how the age pattern of cases shifts during a pandemic. Contact patterns, like children mixing densely at school, play a role alongside immunity. Getting the age pattern right changes practical choices, from school closures to vaccine order. The study shows demography itself as a force shaping an epidemic's course.
plos-pone-0011460:
Cristian Salgado-Luarte and Ernesto Gianoli compared in 2010 how rainforest seedlings cope with being eaten, in sun and in shade. Young plants in a temperate rainforest face hungry herbivores while also competing for light. A seedling can resist attack with defenses, or tolerate it by regrowing, and the better strategy may depend on how much light it gets.

Seedlings in sunny gaps and shaded understory indeed leaned on different strategies, and each strategy succeeded best in its own setting. Light thus reshapes the whole terms of the battle between plant and herbivore. The finding helps explain which species claim which corners of the forest floor. For forest managers and restoration work, it warns that planting a species in the wrong light may strip it of the defense strategy it evolved to use.
plos-pone-0011560:
Iris Müller and co-authors filmed chromosomes in living human cells in 2010 and found a contrast between outer calm and inner motion. During interphase, the long working stage between divisions, chromosomes occupy set territories in the nucleus. Whether those territories are frozen solid or quietly restless inside bears on how genes find partners and regulators.

The chromosomes kept a stable overall morphology while their internal structure reorganized dynamically over time. The genome is thus a restless tenant in a fixed house, its rooms stable but its furniture always moving. That internal motion may be how genes reach the machinery they need without wrecking the nucleus's order. Imaging living cells, rather than fixed dead ones, was essential to see it: fixation would have presented the motion as stillness and the conclusion would have been wrong.
plos-pone-0011660:
Zachary Demorest and co-authors tested a partnership inside the antibody-making machinery, in PLOS ONE in 2010. An enzyme called AID starts three processes that diversify antibodies by altering DNA. AID mostly sits outside the cell nucleus and must enter it to work, and a protein called CIB1 that binds AID looked like a possible helper.

The team disrupted the interaction between AID and CIB1 and checked the antibody processes. Gene conversion and class switch recombination carried on without the partnership. The clear negative result prunes a plausible helper from the model and redirects attention to other partners.
plos-pone-0011760:
Tin Tin Su examined how early embryos respond to DNA damage in a marine cnidarian, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Around the mid-blastula transition, embryos reorganise their rapid cell cycles, adding gap phases and switching from maternal to their own genetic control. Studies in frogs and flies had shown damage responses also change at this stage.

Su exposed embryos of Hydractinia echinata to a DNA-damaging agent and watched their cell cycles respond. The ancient animal's reaction illuminates the deep roots of damage control, showing how very early embryos balance fast division against protecting their DNA.
plos-pone-0011860:
Prakash Vempati, Feilim Mac Gabhann, and Aleksander Popel built a computer model in 2010 of how a growth factor escapes from tissue. VEGF, a signal that promotes blood vessel growth, is often stored bound inside the extracellular matrix, the mesh around cells. Enzymes such as plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases can cut it loose.

The model puts numbers on that release: how fast the cutting happens and how much free VEGF results under different conditions. Vessel growth depends on the timing and amount of this signal, so guessing is not enough. A tested model lets researchers predict how blocking an enzyme would change vessel patterning before trying it in animals.
plos-pone-0011960:
Sarath Kalapala and co-workers tested in 2010 a suspected link between a ribosome change and antibiotic response in a mycobacterium. The bacterium was Mycobacterium smegmatis, a fast-growing stand-in for its tuberculosis-causing relatives. A mutation called K42R in ribosomal protein S12 had been proposed to alter how 16S rRNA mutants respond to a class of antibiotics, the 2-deoxystreptamines.

The team found that the K42R change does not affect that susceptibility. A clean negative result of this kind is valuable: it retires a plausible but wrong idea before more work is built on it. Antibiotic resistance research advances as much by closing false leads as by opening new ones.
plos-pone-0012060:
Jacob van Etten and Robert Hijmans set out in 2010 a way to settle where our crops were first tamed, by making three kinds of proof agree. Work on plant roots in the past has leaned on just one: the seeds and husks dug from old sites, or the genes of crops and their wild kin. Each kind alone leaves gaps, but more and more of both are now on hand.

Their plan folds the dug-up plant past and the gene past into one map-based model that draws the start points and spread routes of tamed plants. A model that must please spade, seed, and gene at once is hard to fool. Knowing where farms were born, and which roads crops took, also shows where their wild kin still live and most need guarding.
plos-pone-0012160:
Stephanie Ortigue, Corrado Sinigaglia, Giacomo Rizzolatti, and co-authors recorded brain activity while people watched others act, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Watching someone grasp a cup gives two kinds of information at once: what the hand is doing, and what the person means by it, such as drinking. The team used dense scalp recordings to follow how the brain's left and right halves handle each kind.

Their high-speed brain maps separate the instant reading of an act from the reading of its intent. Understanding others' actions is the base of learning by imitation, empathy, and social life itself. Work like this also informs care for people whose social reading is impaired, as in some brain injuries.
plos-pone-0012260:
Steven Offer, Qiang Pan-Hammarström, and Lennart Hammarström searched DNA repair genes for the roots of antibody deficiency, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In these syndromes, patients cannot make a full range of antibodies and suffer repeated infections, yet more than nine cases in ten have no known genetic cause. Building diverse antibodies requires B cells to cut and rejoin their own DNA, a process that starts with a deliberate break.

Because that cutting leans on DNA repair machinery, the team examined repair gene variations in these patients and found unique ones worth attention. A repair flaw would explain infections and might also warn of cancer risk. Each candidate gene found gives affected families a possible answer and doctors a new test to offer.
plos-pone-0012360:
Magdalena Gulliksson, Ricardo Carvalho, Erik Ullerås and co-authors asked how low oxygen affects mast cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Mast cells guard tissues and drive allergy and swelling, and inflamed tissue often runs short of oxygen. Yet how oxygen shortage alone changes mast cell survival and the chemicals they release was not well known.

The team grew human mast cells with little oxygen and tracked survival and mediator release. The cells stayed alive and adjusted what they secreted, showing they can keep working in starved tissue. That matters for asthma, wounds, and tumors, where mast cells act in low-oxygen zones and shape how disease unfolds.
plos-pone-0012460:
Juliette Martin, Krishanpal Anamika and Narayanaswamy Srinivasan reclassified the huge kinase family of proteins, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Kinases add phosphate tags to other proteins and run most cell signaling; there are hundreds of them in humans alone. Past family trees used only the kinase region itself, ignoring the rest of each protein.

By classifying kinases on both their kinase and non-kinase regions, the team got a tree that better matches how the proteins actually work. The extra regions often decide what a kinase binds and where it acts. A truer family tree helps predict the job of unstudied kinases, many of which are drug targets in cancer.
plos-pone-0012560:
Morgan Davidson, Jill Larsen, Ian Yang and colleagues documented the loss of a small RNA in a lung cancer type, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that dial down target genes, acting as brakes on growth programs. Losing a brake can free cancer. The team focused on lung squamous cell carcinoma, a smoking-linked cancer with few targeted drugs.

MicroRNA-218 was deleted and downregulated in these tumors, removing its brake on target genes. A lost brake is both a clue to how the cancer forms and a possible marker in tissue or blood. Restoring such microRNAs is an experimental therapy idea this kind of survey feeds.
plos-pone-0012660:
Ahmed and Zerihun surveyed who actually owns and uses treated bed nets in Uganda. Nets treated with insecticide are a proven guard against malaria, above all for young children and pregnant women. Their 2010 study examined the health programme of BRAC, a large local aid group, and asked whether it reaches the poor.

They checked net ownership and use across income groups in the programme's area. A malaria tool only works if the families at most risk really sleep under it. Their equity check shows whether a pro-poor promise holds in practice.
plos-pone-0012760:
Gowen, Wong, Larson and co-authors built a safer arena-virus infection model and used it to test a new drug idea. Several arenaviruses cause severe bleeding fevers and count as emerging public threats. Work on them is slow because the most dangerous ones need top-level containment labs.

Their 2010 Tacaribe virus model offers a workable stand-in for testing treatments. With it they explored an aristeromycin-like compound's power against the virus. A good model that more labs can use speeds the search for drugs against a feared virus family.
plos-pone-0012860:
Liang, Gao, Lin and co-authors silenced an overactive cell-cycle protein to stop breast cancer in mice. Cyclin E is made in excess in many cancers, including breast cancer, and high levels of both its full and shortened forms track with poor outcomes. Their 2010 study used small interfering RNA to target cyclin E in breast cancer cells.

Silencing slowed cancer cell growth in dishes and suppressed tumour development in a breast cancer mouse model. A target that is high in tumours and low elsewhere is exactly what RNA drugs need. The work supports cyclin E as such a target.
pmc-1043860:
Brennecke, Stark, Russell, and co-authors ask how tiny RNAs called microRNAs find the genes they control. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that do not code for proteins, yet they tune gene activity in plants and animals. By 2005 their importance was clear, but the rules for picking targets were not.

The team tested, in a careful and stepwise way, the smallest set of features a target site needs. Their rules help explain how one small RNA can govern many genes at once. The work became a base for later tools that predict microRNA targets from sequence alone.
pmc-10477960:
Members of the GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis group measure the world burden of osteoarthritis from 1990 to 2020. No form of arthritis affects more adults than osteoarthritis does. It brings lasting joint pain and loss of movement, most often after age forty, and it grows more common as people age.

The team built counts for countries and regions and projected the burden forward to 2050. Their work sits inside a world push for healthy aging across the decade to 2030. Solid numbers help health systems plan joint care, pain services, and support for older adults. Counts are given for the world as a whole and for single regions.
pmc-1713260:
Patterson, Price, and Reich present methods for reading population structure from genetic data using eigenanalysis. Sorting people and species into groups by ancestry underlies many studies of history and disease. Older methods, they note, gave no formal test of whether groups truly differ.

Their approach applies principal components analysis, a method first used on genetic data decades earlier, with new statistical rigour. It can reveal structure and test its strength. The work became a standard tool for studies of human ancestry, migration, and the genetics of disease risk.  Eigenanalysis here means reading structure from the largest axes of variation.
pmc-3499260:
Pickrell and Pritchard present a statistical model for inferring population splits and mixtures from genome-wide data. Genetic data hold traces of the historical relationships between populations of a species. Reading those relationships back out of allele frequencies, though, remains a challenging task.

Their model, implemented as TreeMix, builds a population tree and then adds migration events where the tree alone fails. That approach captures both clean splits and later mixing. The method became a staple in studies of human history, animal breeding, and crop origins.  Archaeologists use its migration graphs when testing stories told by ancient DNA.
pmc-3542060:
Hanwell, Curtis, Lonie, and co-authors present Avogadro, an advanced chemical editor and display platform. The project built a molecule editor designed for cross-platform use in chemistry, model work, biology, and materials science. It offers flexible, high-quality rendering of structures.

A powerful plugin system lets users extend the editor for new tasks and file types. Free, fine tools matter because paid chemistry software can be costly for schools and small labs. It became a common teaching and research workbench for building and inspecting molecules.  Students learn molecular modelling on it because the full program costs nothing.
pmc-4001360:
Ru, Li, Wang, and their team built TCMSP in 2014, a database for the study of herbal drugs. Modern drug research and traditional Chinese herbal practice often clash, in part because how herbs act in the body is poorly understood. TCMSP was made to close that gap and speed drug discovery from herbs.

The database links herbs to their chemical parts, the body targets those parts hit, and the diseases tied to those targets. Users can trace a whole chain from plant to molecule to effect. That systems view helps researchers pick the most promising herbs and compounds for lab tests, instead of testing blind.
pmc-4833860:
Menzel, Ng, and Krogh presented Kaiju in 2016 for metagenomic classification. Metagenomics studies microbes from environmental and clinical samples without culturing them. It matters for ecology and for human health, and studies were growing to larger scales.

Recent fast programs compared DNA against genomic references, but Kaiju takes a protein-level approach for sensitivity. It classifies reads by matching translated sequences against a protein database. That catches distant relatives that DNA matching misses. Fast and sensitive classification is the gateway to knowing which microbes are in a sample and what they might be doing.
pmc-5082560:
Burgess, Davies, and Thompson wrote in 2016 about a bias in two-sample Mendelian randomization. Such analyses are often performed using summarized data from two separate samples. In a one-sample analysis, weak instruments bias the causal estimate toward the simple observational association.

The paper examines what happens when the two samples overlap in participants. Overlap can push a two-sample estimate toward the same bias that affects one-sample work. The size of the problem depends on how much overlap exists and how weak the instruments are. Knowing this helps researchers design studies and judge published causal claims with care.
pmc-5756260:
Nina Hessvik and Alicia Llorente reviewed exosome formation and release in 2017. Exosomes are tiny membrane bubbles that cells shed into their surroundings. They form inside a cell compartment and escape when that compartment fuses with the cell surface.

Once dismissed as cell waste, exosomes are now known to carry proteins and RNA between cells. The review gathers what is known about the machinery that builds them and controls their release. It also notes the many open questions about how cargo is chosen. For readers new to the field, it gives a clear map of a fast-moving area.
pmc-7737760:
Rose Oughtred and colleagues described in 2020 the BioGRID, a free public database that collects known interactions between proteins, genes, and chemicals. Every entry is curated by hand from published experiments, rather than scraped automatically. The database covers many species, from yeast, worm, and fly to mouse and human.

By the time of this report it held close to two million carefully checked interactions, and it keeps growing as curators read new papers. Researchers query it to see what a protein partners with, which often hints at what the protein does. In an era of huge automated datasets, BioGRID's value lies in the slow human checking behind each record.
plos-pone-0359860:
Marie Hendrickx, Laure-Anne Kerckhaert, Sara Willems, Rik Crutzen, Vera Verbestel, and Katrien Vanthomme wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a qualitative study set in Flanders, Belgium. Its subject is follow-up that comes too late after cervical screening, when women do not return on time after a result that needs checking.

The authors interview healthcare providers rather than patients, hearing how doctors and nurses see the delays and their causes. Provider views reveal system problems, like reminders or referrals failing, that patient interviews alone might miss. Screening program managers in Belgium and elsewhere can use these accounts to tighten follow-up so fewer women are lost.
plos-pone-0359960:
Nao Suzuki and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It compares the safety of two diabetes drugs, imeglimin and sitagliptin, for patients in Japan who live with type 2 diabetes. The work is a retrospective cohort study based on pharmacy records, looking back at real patients.

Comparing safety in everyday practice matters because trial patients are often healthier than clinic patients. Pharmacy records capture the people actually taking these medicines, including those with other conditions. Doctors choosing between newer and established diabetes drugs in Japan can use real-world safety comparisons like this one alongside trial evidence.
plos-pone-0359660: Qu and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on whether gut microbes change how the body handles ticagrelor, a drug used to stop blood clots. Their work combined lab tests with tests in live animals. The title reports the core result plainly: no such interaction was found in either setting. For doctors who prescribe the drug, that finding eases one worry about how gut health might alter its effect.
plos-pone-0359160: Kam and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on proving identity from the sound of the mouth. The method uses oral acoustic reflections, echoes that bounce inside a person's mouth and carry its unique shape. Such echoes could serve as a biometric, like a fingerprint. A mouth-based check could add a hard-to-copy layer to phone or door security.
plos-pone-0357560:
Mohammad Senisel Bachari, Asgar Khademvatani, and Mahdi Iranfar tackle risk planning for large construction projects in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Big builds face risks that interact, and older planning methods tend to treat each phase separately. Their framework joins the whole chain, from spotting risks and judging them to picking responses, into one system that can weigh fuzzy, judgment based inputs.

A case study on a real liquefied petroleum gas pipeline project puts the framework to work. It sorted twenty distinct risks and twelve possible responses, then used an optimization model to choose the best six responses within the project's limits. That chosen set cut the project's total risk value by more than a third, showing how the method turns expert judgment into a concrete plan.
plos-pone-0340560:
Richmond Balinia Adda and Conrad Pwayirane build a data driven guide to health system resilience for one hundred ninety-five countries, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Readiness scores exist, but governments struggle to turn them into spending priorities. Working from the full 2021 edition of a worldwide health security scoring system covering six domains, the authors distilled a single resilience measure. It captures most of what those domains share. They then asked which domains drive it independently.

Detection, in country health capacity, and prevention carried the strongest independent weight, with detection first. Countries then fell into two broad types: a balanced high performing third, and a larger two thirds group with lower, uneven abilities, weakest exactly in prevention and basic capacity. The typology suggests different strategies: protect strengths in the first group, and fund detection plus core services first in the second. The framework makes resilience investment comparable and concrete.
europmc-pmc8512860: A fresh look at electric impedance (current slowdown) spectroscopy (light analysis): principles, building, and biosensing uses arrived with this 2021 research paper. Electric impedance (current slowdown) spectroscopy (light analysis) is a powerful technique used for the analysis of surface traits related. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9002660: This 2022 research paper covers tesorter: an accurate and fast method to classify ltr-retrotransposons in plant genomes. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7031160: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on mechanisms (the inner workings) of radiation-induced cancer cell death: a primer. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9971660: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on genomes on a tree: a versatile, scalable search engine for genomic and sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) project metadata across. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9192760: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at global, local, and national burden of colorectal (of the colon and rectum) cancer and its risk factors, 1990-2019: a systematic (thorough) analysis. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc9950460: A 2023 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at mitochondria (the cell's power plants) and cell death-linked inflammation (swelling caused by the immune system). The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8121760: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on efficacy (how well something works) of a low-dose candidate malaria vaccine, R21 in adjuvant matrix-m, with seasonal administration to children in burkina. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7039960: A research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) driven by radical oxidation of n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids carries out acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7662460: This 2020 research paper covers solid lipid nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks) for drug delivery (getting medicine where needed): pharmacological and biopharmaceutical aspects. In the golden age of pharmaceutical nanocarriers, we are witnessing a maturation stage of the original concepts and ideas. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7552560: A 2020 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at health-related quality of life in breast cancer patients: review of reviews from 2008 to 2018. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7573460: Shevlin and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on anxiety, depression, traumatic stress and COVID-19-related anxiety in the UK general people during. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7324760: This 2020 research paper covers aimed at the NLRP3 inflammasome in severe. Severe acute breathing syndrome coronavirus 2 is a member of the genus betacoronavirus within the family coronaviridae. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8533760: A research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at ERK: a double-edged sword in cancer. ERK-dependent apoptosis (planned cell death) as a treatment strategy for cancer. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9266760: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at oxidative stress (cell damage from unstable oxygen) in ageing and chronic degenerative pathologies: mechanisms (the inner workings) involved in counteracting cell damage. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7236360: Doctors and scientists took on defining the oral microbiome (microbes living in the body) by whole-genome sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) and resistome analysis: the complexity in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.

Shelley A Adamo leads a team of seven finding a silver lining in starvation for a caterpillar, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Animals must defend against infection even when food runs out, an apparent contradiction the tobacco hornworm helps resolve. After two days without food, the caterpillars' blood chemistry shifted toward a pro inflammatory footing. The melanin based defense pathway ran hotter and darkened wounds faster. Meanwhile a key antioxidant, glutathione, quietly fell.

Boosting that antioxidant back up reversed the inflammation, identifying its decline as part of the trigger. One defense arm, the cell based nodulation response, did weaken. Yet when infected with live bacteria, starved caterpillars cleared more germs from their blood within hours than fed controls did. The twist: raising the antioxidant in starved animals increased their deaths. Chronic inflammation here is not damage but a rationing strategy, buying protection with a different currency.
plos-pone-0358560:
Mélanie Briard leads a team of eight profiling the airways of children with severe asthma at the level of microbes and compounds, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Twenty affected children and ten children without asthma gave lung washings, which underwent bacterial gene sequencing and fine detail chemical mapping. The aim was a local pattern of severe disease in the organ that matters, rather than another blood based guess. A second aim was testing whether subtypes separate chemically.

Severe asthma airways carried more diverse bacteria, not fewer. Several groups were enriched, including streptococci and Moraxella. Their chemistry shifted too: a pathway built on polyamines showed depleted arginine and raised spermine and spermidine, compounds tied to growth and inflammation. Integrated analysis linked the microbial and chemical patterns. The combined signature could eventually sort children whose severe asthma runs on different machinery, a first step toward treatments aimed at mechanisms instead of symptoms.
plos-pone-0358360:
Shuming Cui led a team of five authors who studied how pro basketball has changed, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They used team records and shot location data from twenty-one NBA seasons, spanning 2004 to 2025. Two trends drew their focus: shots clustering at the rim and beyond the arc, and the game's pace settling after 2018.

Cui's group tracked how the mid-range shot faded as teams chased more valued shots. They also charted how pace rose, then steadied. For coaches, analysts, and fans, the study puts hard numbers on a change many viewers sensed. It shows how data-driven choices by teams reshaped the style of the whole league.
plos-pone-0355860:
Elisabetta Versace led a team of eight authors studying how dance is best taught, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Teachers demo moves either facing the class or facing away, and each view poses problems for learners copying the steps. The team tested which viewing angle works better, and how skill level and mental load change the answer.

Versace's study was preregistered, meaning its design and tests were locked in advance. That choice makes the findings more trustworthy as guidance for teachers and choreographers. Dance training is a large field with strong habits but thin evidence. Clear results on something as basic as which way to face can improve lessons for beginners and experts alike.
plos-pone-0356760:
Saad Zahid, Muhammad Nawaz, and Kanwal Zahra analyzed how Pakistani newspapers portray drug addiction, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Media framing shapes public stigma and the policies voters will accept. The team applied a topic modeling method called Latent Dirichlet Allocation to print media coverage of addiction.

Zahid's discovered topic patterns reveal whether coverage informs the public or mainly moralizes about users. Moralizing coverage deepens stigma, which keeps people from seeking treatment. Informative coverage can do the opposite. Media researchers and health advocates in Pakistan gain a map of the current framing, and editors gain a mirror. Automated topic analysis lets the team judge years of coverage at a scale no hand reading could match.
plos-pone-0348860:
Sasha R. Sioni and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a scoping review of digital behavioral addictions among teenagers and young adults. Terms here are a tangle: gaming disorder is a recognized diagnosis, internet gaming disorder awaits study, and heavy social media or smartphone use are research labels, not diagnoses. The review will map how researchers define, measure, and count these problems, and what is known about causes, harms, treatments, and fairness.

The team will search nine databases plus grey sources without date or language limits, focusing on ages ten to twenty-four. Two reviewers will screen and chart everything by hand, with source-language checks for six other languages, so automation never decides eligibility. Instruments will be sorted into evidence tiers, and results kept separate by kind: causes, associations, harms, and treatment effects. The map should give a fast-moving field shared footing.
plos-pone-0357960:
Albert E. Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how physician-scientists fare in the residency match for competitive specialties. MD-PhD graduates are prized for research, but nobody had checked whether sought-after specialties prefer them. The team combined national data spanning 2007 to 2024 for six competitive fields, comparing match rates and representation between MD-PhD and regular MD applicants.

Representation of MD-PhD trainees stayed broadly stable. Dermatology and diagnostic radiology gave them strong match outcomes, while orthopedic surgery's success rate for them declined over the period, and the surgical specialties in between swung inconsistently. Specialty pay and research funding levels explained little. What tracked best with MD-PhD success was the presence of dedicated training programs in the specialty, though even that link was not statistically firm. Aspiring physician-scientists should weigh a specialty's training infrastructure, they suggest, not its prestige or pay.
plos-pone-0357460:
Danwen Zheng and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the tangled body-and-mind symptoms of lung cancer patients receiving immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors improve survival, but symptom mixes vary hugely between patients, and treating them one by one misses the pattern. Nearly a thousand patients were profiled into symptom types, factors modeled, and each type's network mapped for core symptoms and bridges.

Three types appeared: a high-burden group with combined physical and emotional distress, an emotionally dominant group, and a mild, adaptive group covering nearly half the patients. Smoking history, advanced stage, and poor physical function strongly marked the high-burden group, while living with family and combination therapy protected against it. Each type had its own core symptom: fatigue, sleep disturbance, and diminished enjoyment of life. Simulated interventions on the networks suggested different first targets per type, a step toward care matched to the patient.
plos-pone-0357260:
Lu Yuwen and Shuyu Chen tackle a common headache in medical machine learning: rare disease groups have too few patient records to train a good model. Their 2026 framework invents extra records for the small group using a generative model, then improves those records in rounds. Borrowed real-style samples act as anchors so the invented data do not drift away from true patient patterns during the rounds.

Across seven clinical datasets, models trained with the boosted data sorted patients better than models using rival boosting methods. Checks also showed the invented records kept tricky traits of the rare group, such as skewed and multi-peaked value patterns. Yuwen and Chen offer the method for settings where collecting more real rare-case records is slow or impossible.
plos-pone-0356560:
Anup Bhat and fellow clinicians study daily activity and walking capacity in South Asian adults living with bronchiectasis, a lung condition that scars airways and causes breathlessness and tiredness. Most past evidence comes from Western patients, and sex differences in the region are little explored. About fifty stable patients completed activity surveys, breathlessness ratings, a six-minute walk test, and health status forms, alongside records of disease severity and past flare-ups.

Less active patients reported worse breathlessness, while longer time since diagnosis linked to slightly higher activity. Women walked shorter raw distances than men, though not once body-based expectations were applied. Bhat and colleagues say activity support should be part of routine care, with attention to breathlessness as the main brake.
plos-pone-0356460:
Ali Reza Yusefi and fellow researchers interview nurses and supervisors in Iranian hospitals about what makes written nursing records good in suicide care. Notes in such cases carry weight for safety, handovers, and legal protection. Across several hospitals, the team spoke in depth with a varied group of front-line nurses, head nurses, and clinical supervisors, then sorted their accounts into themes.

Eight linked themes emerged, spanning work setting and support, staff knowledge and skill, ongoing training, teamwork and communication, staffing balance, and motivation. Yusefi and colleagues argue that record quality is a system property, not just a personal habit. Hospital leaders who want safer suicide care, they say, must fix staffing and training alongside any form redesign.
plos-pone-0355160:
Simone Kager and a team of clinicians and engineers set out a trial plan, published in 2026. The plan covers a home exercise gym. It helps stroke survivors retrain a weak arm without a therapist in the room. Recovery needs many repetitions, yet outpatient therapy is scarce and travel is hard. Their plan lends each participant three complementary training devices for daily use at home over six weeks, while clinicians watch progress on an online dashboard.

Up to thirty survivors in the subacute and chronic phases will take part at one center. Checks at five points will weigh feasibility, safety, ease of use, arm benefit, and costs.
