Kager and colleagues argue that proving unsupervised home training safe and usable is the step that must come before any large effectiveness trial.
plos-pone-0357660:
Belay Merkeb Zewude and co-authors check stool samples from HIV patients on treatment at public hospitals in Ethiopia's North Shoa Zone, counting gut parasites and hunting their risk factors. Parasites hit HIV patients hard, and local rates in this zone were unmeasured. Several hundred patients gave samples and answered structured questions in the first half of a recent year, with lab checks done by three complementary methods.

About three in five patients carried at least one gut parasite, a high share for people already in regular care. Statistical models linked infection to daily life factors gathered in the survey. Zewude and colleagues argue that parasite screening and water and hygiene support belong inside routine HIV care in the zone, not as an afterthought.
plos-pone-0351160:
Marlon E Cobos leads a team mapping when and where four tick species actively hunt for hosts across the central Great Plains. Several disease-carrying ticks are spreading in the region, and risk follows the ticks' hunting behavior, not just their range on a map. The team fed two years of field surveillance, with both finds and confirmed absences, into new niche models tied to conditions at each sampling moment.

The models revealed seasonal rhythms that differed by species, showing when each tick's hunting range swells or shrinks across the plains. Cobos and colleagues argue that time-aware maps give health agencies a firmer base for timing warnings and control work than static range maps. Their framework also uses absence records that older models usually throw away.
plos-pone-0357360:
Abdulaziz Mohammed Alismail and Abdulaziz Rashed Alghamdi asked school supervisors in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province what keeps them loyal to their work. These supervisors coach teachers and help schools improve. Yet what drives them is rarely studied outside the West. A few hundred rated their inner strength, their sense of real say, their trust in their own skills, and their loyalty to the job. The team then mapped how the parts link.

Inner strength fed both real say and skill trust in a strong way. All three traits fed job loyalty in a direct way as well. Real say did not feed skill trust, so the two paths to loyalty stayed apart. Still, each path carried part of the link from inner strength to loyalty. The pair suggest that districts build inner strength and real say side by side, if they want staff who stay.
plos-pone-0356360:
Rocky E Stroud and colleagues describe the first forty-three thousand participants of NeuroGAP-Psychosis, a case-control study hunting genetic and environmental roots of psychotic disorders in Africa. Their 2026 descriptive paper profiles recruits from Ethiopia, Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda between 2018 and 2023, comparing patients with psychosis against controls across countries.

The mix differed sharply by country. Schizophrenia dominated diagnoses in Ethiopia, while bipolar disorder led in Uganda, and men ranged from under half of recruits in Uganda to two thirds in Ethiopia. The authors attribute much of the variation to recruitment areas, consent languages, and local diagnostic habits rather than biology. The portrait sets up the genetic analyses to come and cautions against treating the four countries as one population.
plos-pone-0356260:
Xiuyang Yuan and colleagues upgraded a lightweight image recognition model so drones can spot cracked and shattered insulators on power lines. The model had to cope with rain, snow, fog, and glare. Their 2026 study assembled nearly four thousand inspection images across weather conditions. Real and synthesized examples were mixed. The detector was rebuilt with a phone-grade backbone, an attention module, and improved feature fusion and box fitting.

The rebuilt model beat its baseline on every accuracy measure across repeated tests. It stayed tiny enough for drone-mounted hardware. It also outscored two rival lightweight detectors. The authors acknowledge the synthetic weather images as a weakness. They plan more real-world collection. Reliable automated inspection would cut the cost and danger of hunting failing insulators by eye.
plos-pone-0355960:
Zonghe Ding and colleagues tackle a guidance problem for automated guided vehicles. These are the driverless carts that ferry goods around warehouses and factories. The problem is that sensors lie. Standard navigation math assumes the lies follow tidy patterns. Their 2026 paper pairs a predictive controller with a set-membership filter. Instead of guessing a probability spread, the filter fences the vehicle's true state inside a shrinking geometric boundary.

That boundary feeds directly into the controller. It acts as a safety margin that breathes with conditions. So the vehicle slows or swerves when uncertainty balloons. In simulations under three kinds of noise, the approach reached its targets more often. It also held up better than two established controllers. For warehouses that cannot afford collisions, guarantees beat averages.
plos-pone-0349360:
Falk Wiegmann and Nancy Ford produce a practical reference for researchers who scan small animals with cone-beam micro-CT, in this 2026 technical note. Reconstructed image quality depends on a filter setting inside the standard reconstruction algorithm, yet papers routinely fail to report it. The authors rebuilt the same scanner data sixteen ways, combining four filter types with four sharpness cutoffs, and measured resolution, noise, and the smallest detectable feature under each.

The trade-off was steep: the sharpest settings roughly doubled measured resolution but multiplied image noise several-fold, while the smoothest settings made even moderate-contrast features several times larger before they became detectable. A mouse lung specimen illustrates the differences visually. The authors offer the side-by-side numbers so imaging scientists can choose settings deliberately and report them properly, instead of accepting defaults blindly.
plos-pone-0355560:
Tinh Tran Phu Do and colleagues examined what lifts farm productivity across twenty-nine Asian countries over two decades. Their 2026 study links harvest output with renewable energy use, digital technology, finance, natural resources, and the quality of institutions. They used long-run statistical methods suited to country panel data, with extra checks for robustness.

Renewable energy, digital access, finance, and stronger institutions each came with higher farm productivity. Natural resource wealth pointed the other way, which the authors read as a resource curse effect. Finance and institutions also fed back into productivity in both directions. The team advises policies that spread clean energy and digital tools in farming, plus credit aimed at green projects.
plos-pone-0354160:
Nakachew Mekonnen Alamirew and co-authors asked how adults in northwest Ethiopia grasp ways to ward off long-term ills. Health literacy means the skill to find, grasp, and use health facts. It shapes whether advice turns into daily acts. Their 2026 study held group talks and deep chats with townsfolk and health staff in the Amhara region.

Four themes showed how literacy links with acts that prevent ills like diabetes and heart disease. Blocks sat in poor access to facts, in language, and in how clinics are run, not just in what folks know. Alamirew and colleagues say health plans must fit local reading skills and local life, or the advice will not land.
plos-pone-0356060:
Benjamin Mbonshi and colleagues measured worm infections in Zambian children who receive HIV treatment. Soil-transmitted worms and HIV overlap in the region, and weakened immunity may invite both. Their 2026 study sampled children aged five to fifteen at clinics in two western districts, testing stool, blood, and treatment records.

About one child in nine carried at least one worm infection, most often roundworm. Infection odds rose as immune cell counts fell and as virus levels climbed. Missed HIV doses carried the strongest risk of all. Clean water access did not explain the pattern once other factors were counted. Mbonshi and colleagues recommend folding routine worm screening and deworming into children's HIV care.
plos-pone-0353360:
Helena Grip and co-authors recorded brain activity and finger motion at the same time to study how fingers move one by one. Independent finger control underlies skilled hand use and depends on both body mechanics and brain control. Their 2026 study scanned twenty-five right-handed older adults while motion capture tracked each finger's bending.

An individuation index scored how cleanly each finger moved without dragging its neighbours along. Brain contrasts between fingers and thumb located control regions specific to each digit. Areas shared by poorly individuated fingers received closer analysis. Grip and colleagues link the paired recordings to rehabilitation, since stroke and injury often steal finger independence first.
plos-pone-0332560:
James John and co-authors examined unmet social needs among families in multicultural and rural parts of Australia. Families facing disadvantage often cannot reach the social and health services meant for them. Their 2026 study re-analysed trial data from culturally diverse communities in South Western Sydney and the rural Murrumbidgee region.

A standard survey counted each family's unmet social care needs. Because need counts varied more widely than simple models allow, the team used a regression form built for overdispersed counts. Parental mental health sat at the centre of the analysis, alongside social and demographic drivers. John and colleagues aim to show services which family traits predict unmet need, so outreach can start where the gaps are deepest.
plos-pone-0355460:
Sujeong Kang and Eunkyung Kim review in 2026 how researchers measure daily stress in the body of typically developing children. Their scoping review covered two decades and searched medical, psychology, and education sources. They separated short sharp stress from longer lasting stress and noted child age, setting, and body markers used.

Fifty seven studies qualified. Short term stress work was more common, and hormone measures, above all cortisol, dominated over nerve, brain, or immune markers. Repeated daily saliva sampling rose for a time then eased. The map shows where evidence is thin and where stronger, broader methods are still needed.
plos-pone-0354460:
Margaret A Kypreos and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a gentler lung biopsy for people with interstitial lung disease, a group of scarring lung conditions. At a Texas medical center, patients underwent freezing-probe biopsies through a bronchoscope using a very thin probe hoped to bleed less than larger ones. Diagnoses before and after the procedure were compared.

The thin probe produced useful answers more often than ordinary forceps biopsies reported elsewhere, though less often than bigger freezing probes, and complications ran higher than expected. Kypreos advises sampling several lobes and taking more pieces to raise the yield.
plos-pone-0353860:
Nia and colleagues, in a 2026 design study, build a candidate vaccine against HPV16, a virus type that drives cervical cancer. Their vaccine strings together short pieces, called epitopes, from the viral E7 protein plus pieces from two heat shock proteins. Heat shock proteins can act as helpers that wake up killer T cells.

The twist is order: the team designed six versions with the pieces arranged in different sequences. They then used computer modeling to see which layout gripped immune receptors best and looked safe and stable. One layout, with the heat shock pieces placed ahead of the viral piece, scored best. The team then built that version in bacteria and cleaned it up for further study. Computer checks predicted it would be non-toxic and unlikely to trigger allergy. The work is an early step: real immune tests in animals and people still lie ahead.
plos-pone-0354260: Menstruation in Bangladesh’s urban slums — unspoken cycles of shame and struggle. This qualitative study explored women’s lived experiences. The intimate accounts demand menstrual health responses that confront stigma — not just distribute pads.
plos-pone-0353460: Energy-dissipating pile-anchor structures — their energy dissipation characteristics simulated. This numerical study examined them. The findings guide engineers designing foundations that absorb seismic fury — buildings that sway without falling.
plos-pone-0354360:
Nilmart and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Thailand, test how three ways of sitting change the body during twenty minutes of smartphone gaming. Young adults often play slumped on the floor or in chairs without back support, and neck pain is a common complaint. Forty-one healthy players each tried chair sitting with a backrest, chair sitting without one, and sitting cross-legged on the floor, in random order.

Neck and trunk angles, measured from photos over time, bent differently depending on position. Neck discomfort was the most common complaint, and it was most frequent in the cross-legged position, though its strength did not differ significantly between positions. A standard ergonomic risk score also rated cross-legged sitting worst. The authors' advice is simple and immediate: for gaming sessions, a chair with a back wins, and the floor position taxes the neck fastest.
plos-pone-0351960:
Saya Kaidarova and seven colleagues examine thyroid cancer patients in Kazakhstan for links between autoimmune thyroid disease and aggressive gene mutations, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. More than half of their two hundred and thirty-one patients also had Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease. The team checked tumours for two mutations known to mark more dangerous papillary thyroid cancers.

The combined high-risk mutation pattern appeared more often in patients without autoimmune disease, alongside larger tumours and spread to lymph nodes. Hashimoto's patients carried fewer aggressive changes, while the small Graves' group showed livelier cell growth. The pattern hints that the type of thyroid autoimmunity may colour how a cancer behaves.
plos-pone-0352960:
Diallo, Ezzinbi, and Outada with Sallet proved results about epidemic math models in a 2026 paper. Their model extends the classic healthy, sick, recovered scheme with stages for exposure, mild and severe illness, hospital care, and intensive care. A version split by age groups was studied as well.

The authors show the model behaves sensibly, work out when an outbreak can take off, and find a unique final size for a single wave. Lasting immunity lets the disease die out under the right conditions, while fading immunity allows a steady state when spread is strong enough. Such proofs give health modelers firm ground for forecasts used in planning.
plos-pone-0352260: Shoulder impingement syndrome — joint mobilization’s clinical efficacy systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed. This paper did so. The findings quantified hands-on therapy’s benefit. The research guided physiotherapy — the evidence for the mobilizing hand.
plos-pone-0353660:
Li, Mendias, and Cao reported a caution for tendon research using a popular mouse line in a 2026 study. The mice carry a switch meant to change genes only in tendon and ligament cells, letting researchers study those tissues cleanly. The team found the switch also fires in male reproductive cells.

Because of that hidden activity, sons inherited the switched gene in every tissue, even without inheriting the switch itself. The effect did not appear through females. A supposedly tendon-only change can thus become a whole-body change in the next generation. The authors urge labs to breed through females with this mouse line and to check offspring carefully.
plos-pone-0353060:
Alsunbul and colleagues built a skin carrier for a common antifungal drug in a 2026 study. The drug treats yeast infections of the skin but sinks in poorly and washes away quickly. Tiny fat-based bubbles, tuned by a statistical design, were loaded with the drug and set into a gel.

Bubble size, charge, and drug capture were measured, and imaging confirmed smooth round bubbles with drug inside. In rats with skin yeast infection, the gel beat a leading store cream at a lower dose, with tissue healing to match. Better skin delivery could cut dose and treatment time for a very common infection.
plos-pone-0353160:
Nasir and colleagues asked whether fatty liver disease and metabolic risks track later thinking decline in a 2026 study. Records from dozens of American health organizations covered two decades. One matched comparison set pitted millions of adults with metabolic risks against healthy controls, and another compared liver patients with risk-only patients.

Outcomes included mild thinking impairment and two kinds of dementia, tracked after matching for age, sex, and background. People with prior brain disease or advanced liver disease were excluded to keep the question clean. If liver disease adds risk beyond shared metabolic factors, brain screening may belong in liver clinics.
plos-pone-0353260:
Fangfang Chen, Cindy Sing Bik Ngai, and Ming Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS One study comparing how Chinese and American government space agencies present themselves on social media. The team gathered posts from Chinese agencies on Weibo and United States agencies on X, then used text-mining tools alongside close reading to compare topics, forms of address, and word patterns.

Chinese agencies came across as state-linked yet friendly guides, mixing mission achievements with patriotism and collective pride. American agencies sounded more strictly professional, stressing research, exploration, and mission success with little mention of the state. The authors read these contrasting voices as products of each country's institutions and culture, and the comparison shows how even technical agencies shape a public identity through routine posts.
plos-pone-0351560:
Dohyeon Lee and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on shrinking huge data files from holotomography. This microscope method maps the inside of living samples without stains or labels. Modern systems produce terabytes of three-dimensional images. Storage and transfer then become real bottlenecks. The team stored data in a cloud-friendly format. They tested thirteen ways to compress the files, across many settings.

They used six datasets from five biological samples. For each method they compared file size, reopening speed, and network speed. One method, Pcodec, gave the most balanced results overall. Two others came close behind. The best choice depends on the bandwidth a lab has. The authors give guidance labs can use when setting up large imaging pipelines.
plos-pone-0352860:
Julia Perlinger and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study translating a burnout questionnaire into German and testing whether burnout comes in distinct flavors. The underlying theory separates workers who are frenetic and overinvolved, those who are underchallenged and bored, and those who are worn out and disengaged. More than six hundred German employees completed the translated questionnaire along with measures of depression, engagement, job demands, and support.

The translation held together statistically, and clustering the answers produced four groups: the three burnout types plus a non-burned-out group. Resources and demands deteriorated in a clear order from frenetic through underchallenged to worn out. The authors argue that naming a worker's subtype points to better-matched help than treating burnout as one uniform condition.
plos-pone-0352760:
Sidharth Samantara and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One engineering paper on a new circuit design for connecting solar panels to the power grid without a transformer. Their switched-capacitor inverter uses three capacitors and twelve switches to produce a seven-level output while tripling the input voltage. The capacitors balance themselves automatically, and the design is built to avoid leakage currents that plague transformer-free systems.

Simulations and a working prototype confirmed the design behaves as intended. Compared with existing transformerless inverters, the authors report fewer parts under less voltage stress for the performance achieved. They frame the work as a contribution to affordable clean energy, since cheaper and more reliable grid-tied converters help solar power spread.
plos-pone-0338360:
Calvin Epidu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of advanced HIV disease in Ugandan children and teens. They used clinic records from forty-eight busy facilities in the west of the country. They followed more than five thousand young people who started treatment between 2016 and 2023. They noted who arrived with advanced disease, and what happened to them.

Nearly one in five had advanced disease. Among children under five, the share was over two-thirds. Just over half of those with advanced disease were still in care at the study's end. About one in twelve had died. Deaths clustered in the first three months of treatment. Malnourished children survived at lower rates. The authors argue for earlier diagnosis and food support, to cut the early death toll.
plos-pone-0352160:
Cillin Condon and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a simple chair-rise test. It asks whether muscle power estimated from that test can flag frailty in older Irish adults. The data come from a national aging study. The team converted how fast people over fifty finished five sit-to-stand reps into a leg power estimate. They checked it against a standard frailty index.

Power fell with age. The fall was steeper in women and in people classed as frail. Cut-off values below which frailty risk rose matched findings from other countries. The power estimate predicted frailty about as well as standard clinic tests, like timed walking. The authors recommend it as a cheap, practical add-on for frailty screening in towns and villages. It complements fuller checks rather than replacing them.
plos-pone-0352660:
Hasan Ekinci and Ahmet Mallı model what makes sports professionals behave innovatively. Their 2026 study surveyed two hundred forty-three sports professionals in eastern Turkey. Feeling supported by others seemed a likely driver of fresh ideas at work. But earlier research had not mapped the mental steps in between. The authors tested motivation and mental flexibility as sequential links in the chain.

Perceived social support showed no direct link to innovative behaviour. Its effect travelled entirely through the two middle steps. Support first raised intrinsic motivation, the inner drive to do the work well. Motivation then fed cognitive flexibility, the ability to switch viewpoints. Flexibility, in turn, predicted innovative behaviour. For sports organisations, the lesson is layered. Backing staff is not enough by itself; work must also feed inner drive and flexible thinking.
plos-pone-0351860:
Xi Chen, Jieqiong Wang, and Xinying Liu trace how one Japanese newspaper frames two related medical traditions. Their 2026 study mines four decades of the Asahi Shimbun, from 1984 to 2025. Kampo is Japan's own adaptation of classical Chinese medicine. Traditional Chinese Medicine is the mainland system it sprang from. Topic modelling and word-embedding analysis reveal the paper's habits of mind.

The newspaper keeps the two traditions clearly apart. Kampo appears inside everyday health concerns and questions of material supply. It sits close to concrete remedies and therapies. Chinese medicine, by contrast, is framed through culture, comparison, and outside reference. Its semantic neighbourhood is abstract: categories, institutions, systems. These frames stayed stable for forty years, flexing only with policy shifts. A shared origin, the authors show, does not guarantee a shared story.
plos-pone-0352360:
Chen Wei and seven colleagues read a harvester drum's workload from its vibrations in this 2026 engineering study. Pepper harvesting machines must adjust on the move. Too much load wastes energy and damages fruit. Vibration signals reveal the drum's structural response. Torque signals reveal the crop pushing back. The authors model the two as one coupled chaotic system, borrowing classic chaos equations. A hybrid algorithm then fits the model's parameters to real behaviour.

Chaos theory supplies the measuring stick. The largest Lyapunov exponent gauges how fast the system's paths diverge, and it shifts with load state. Designed experiments pinned down the best operating settings. The result is a load estimate with a physical story behind it, not a black-box guess. Single signals and simple statistics proved less discriminating. For machine builders, interpretable load sensing promises steadier harvesting, fewer damaged peppers, and settings that adapt themselves in the field.
plos-pone-0352460:
Jonathan Chu, Shreyas Annaswamy, and Sanjay Desai hunted for chemicals that can switch off a calcium pump found in nearly every cell. The pump pushes calcium out of cells, and the version on human red blood cells is tied to sickle cell disease and to how severe malaria becomes. No clean blocker of the pump existed to guide drug work.

The team shrank a lab test using red blood cells and a dye that glows with calcium, then screened more than fifty-two thousand compounds. Almost none interfered with the pump, and none of the early hits held up on retesting. That near-empty result still matters: it suggests the pump offers very few places where a drug can grab hold.
plos-pone-0344860:
Emma Hudgins and co-authors weighed two ways of fighting the mountain pine beetle, a pest chewing through western North American forests and spreading farther as winters warm. The usual policy reacts to fresh sightings and short-term forecasts. Their alternative plans with long-range spread in mind, choosing survey and control spots for the future outbreak they prevent, not just the present one.

In their comparison, the forward-looking strategy shrank the future infested area substantially compared with the reactive approach, in some runs by more than half beyond it. A simpler version that used forecasts without full long-term feedback still beat the standard policy. The numbers make a management point that travels well beyond beetles: money spent reacting to today's map can look efficient while quietly losing the larger war.
plos-pone-0351760:
Chih-Yu Chen, Kuang-Hui Chen, and Kang-Hao Lu checked a piece of gymnastics folklore with hard results. The claim is that performing later in a final helps a gymnast. They mined men's apparatus finals from three Olympic Games and nine world meets. Rankings, scores, and medals were tested against start position on each apparatus.

Almost nothing moved with start order. Rankings, difficulty, execution, and medals were flat nearly everywhere. One exception stood out: pommel horse. Gymnasts drawn in the second half there scored higher on execution and won more medals. Medal shares by continent were even across the board. The overall verdict flatters the judging system. Order effects look like the rare stain, not the fabric of results.
plos-pone-0350560:
A digital program coached by staff helped bowel disease patients manage tiredness, pain, and urgent bathroom needs, yet a large trial found it no better than usual care. Vari Wileman and colleagues dug into what the coaches actually did, in this 2026 PLOS One process study.

Messages between coaches and patients were sampled and scored against a delivery checklist; fidelity stayed high throughout. Nineteen coaches were interviewed before and after about training, supervision, and the work itself. Their accounts explain how faithfully a program can be delivered and still miss its target, a distinction the authors say future digital health trials must plan for from the start.
plos-pone-0351060:
Mohammad Ali and colleagues set out a trial plan, with no results yet, to test heat therapy for long term low back pain in Bangladesh. Deep heat from shortwave machines stays popular in clinics there, even though world guidance counts it as low value. The trial will enrol just over two hundred adults at several Dhaka hospitals and clinics, split by chance into real or sham heat.

Both groups will get standard physiotherapy three times a week for four weeks. Pain, leg pain, activity limits, mood, sleep, and care use will be tracked to six months. A sham arm matters here: only a fair test can show whether a widely loved machine adds anything beyond good standard care.
plos-pone-0349860:
Roberta L Woodgate and colleagues worked with nineteen young people aged fourteen to twenty four across Canada on their mental health journeys through COVID. Youth directed art methods, maps of supports and life paths plus a chosen art piece, joined open interviews online. Themes were built from words and images together.

Three chapters emerged: chaos on entering the pandemic, inward reflection during it, and personal growth after it. Mental health dipped, steadied through self examination, and in many accounts strengthened by the end. Art based work let youth show turning points that interviews alone might miss. Services should honour that growth while staying ready for the next shock.
plos-pone-0349560:
Xiumei Zheng and colleagues built concrete from desert sand and recycled rubble in 2026 work, aiming to cut both river sand mining and construction waste in dry regions of China. A treated mineral additive was added to tune the mix.

Samples varied the additive dose and the shares of desert sand and recycled aggregate. Strength, salt penetration, and pore structure were measured, and a grey theory model linked tiny pore patterns to big performance numbers. The mixes worked together better than expected, and the model predicted performance from microstructure. Such prediction could speed design of greener concrete for desert building.
plos-pone-0350660:
Wenfang Wang and co-authors built a single test in 2026 that detects four targets of the plague bacterium at once. Plague still occurs in pockets worldwide, and fast, certain detection guides both treatment and outbreak control.

The test reads four genes unique to the germ, each in its own channel, and was checked for stray reactions with other bacteria. It detected extremely small amounts and gave repeatable results across strengths. Serum samples from real cases were all caught. One combined run replacing four separate tests could speed plague confirmation in labs with limited staff and time.
plos-pone-0350460:
Juan Carlos Calderón-González and co-authors studied phase angle, a body scan measure proposed as a sign of muscle quality, in young adults in 2026. Whether it truly tracks strength, once lifestyle and body size are counted, was the open question.

More than eleven hundred adults had phase angle, muscle mass, and grip strength measured several ways, including strength scaled to height and low strength judged against world norms. Phase angle stayed linked with strength across methods and adjustments for health, diet, activity, and demographics. A quick, painless scan number that reflects real strength could help clinics screen for weak muscle early.
plos-pone-0325860:
Kazuya Umeno and Yoshihiro Itaguchi explored whether imagining movement with both hands before one hand helps people actually move better, a question with stakes for stroke rehabilitation. Mental practice is known to engage motor brain areas, and two-handed imagery may engage them more strongly. Their 2026 experiment assigned seventy-six healthy young adults to imagery orders or a no-imagery control group, using a palm ball-rolling task.

Only the group that imagined two-handed movement first, then one-handed, improved real performance more than controls. Brain wave measures of motor activation were stronger early on for that group but faded with practice, and they tracked performance only loosely. The authors suggest order matters: two-handed imagery seems to prime the system, while reversing the order adds little.
plos-pone-0350160:
Judit del Río, Norma Ratto, and co-authors used the magnetism locked into ancient kiln walls to re-date the last firing of metalworking furnaces at Quillay, an Inka-era settlement in northwest Argentina. Radiocarbon had placed the kilns in Inka times. Their 2026 archaeomagnetic study sampled five kilns and compared their recorded field direction and strength with models of Earth's past magnetic field.

All five kilns told the same magnetic story, meaning they were last heated together in one short episode. That episode dated not to the Inka occupation but to sometime between the late eighteen hundreds and the mid nineteen hundreds. The authors suggest a later wildfire or deliberate reuse of the chambers to recover copper from slag. The result rewrites part of the site's history.
plos-pone-0336560:
Rachel Mariani and colleagues tested whether shining light through grape leaves and reading the reflection can measure leaf traits that normally require slow laboratory work. They covered twelve wine grape cultivars and twelve traits, including the gas-exchange and water traits that decide how a vine handles heat and drought. The samples varied widely between and within cultivars.

Spectral readings captured that variation, showing the method can detect differences not just between species but between cultivated varieties of one crop. Breeders and growers need trait data at scales no laboratory pipeline can supply, for example when screening hundreds of vines for drought behavior. A leaf scan that substitutes for days of measurement turns that screening from a bottleneck into a routine.
plos-pone-0347160:
Irshad Sikandar Jamadar and colleagues built a computer model of breast cancer treatment that remembers. Ordinary tumour models treat each moment as fresh, but real tissues carry history in scarring, resistance, and immune memory. Their fractional-order model folds that memory into equations covering tumour growth, immune attack, drug resistance, and heat therapy, then runs five treatment schedules across four patient types.

Continuous treatment scored best overall, though the winning schedule shifted by patient: younger patients favoured continuous therapy at one memory strength. Frailer patients did best with adaptive dosing at another. Older patients peaked elsewhere. The immune killing rate proved the most powerful lever, with resistance close behind. Gains over memory-free models were small on average but meaningful in specific pairings. The authors stress that clinical testing must judge whether the theory holds.
plos-pone-0348760:
Ömer Karakoç, Samet Memiş, and Bahar Sennaroglu staged a tournament among thirty-five decision algorithms built on a fuzzy mathematics framework designed for reasoning under uncertainty. Each algorithm classified the same ten public datasets, and the team scored accuracy, precision, recall, and balance. Statistical tests that guard against lucky streaks confirmed the differences.

The fuzzy soft methods held their own against expectations for such abstract machinery. A clear leaderboard emerged, topped by one algorithm, with a small group tied just behind. The authors frame the exercise as a buyer's guide: people facing messy, uncertain classification problems in machine learning now have evidence. It shows which member of this large, confusing family deserves a first try. They also get a structured way to choose among the rest.
plos-pone-0347860:
Yang Cao, Bingchuan Wu, and Miao Wen taught an optimiser to tune itself. Differential evolution is a workhorse method for hard engineering problems, but its behaviour hinges on strategy choices usually set by rules of thumb. Their version puts a reinforcement learning agent in charge of those choices, then polishes promising answers with a classic refinement method, forming a loop of setting, solving, and sharpening.

On a standard international benchmark suite, the self-tuning system proved robust on high-dimensional problems and outscored classic adaptive rivals. It also handled factory scheduling, a very different discrete puzzle, suggesting the framework travels well. The authors offer the design as a template for optimisers that learn online instead of relying on frozen heuristics, aimed at costly problems where every trial counts.
plos-pone-0348060:
Kerem Ersin and Berna Özge Mutlu test how mild electric stimulation of the inner ear affects balance and the feeling that a fake hand is one's own. The balance organs help the brain merge senses into a body sense. Their 2026 study runs forty-eight healthy adults through stimulation, a sham session, and checks at half an hour and an hour afterward.

Standing on one leg dipped at half an hour, then recovered by the hour mark. A stepping-in-place measure improved at both later checks. The fake-hand illusion grew stronger after real stimulation, peaking at an hour, though the sham also nudged it up, hinting at expectation effects. Timing matters if such stimulation is ever used to aid balance therapy.
plos-pone-0336760:
Lokeswara Rao Sajja and colleagues are working on a mechanical heart valve that resists clotting without a lifetime of blood-thinning drugs. Their 2026 laboratory study copies a trick from real blood vessels, whose inner coating carries a slight negative charge that pushes platelets away. A small pacemaker-like device applies a gentle voltage across the valve's surface to imitate that coating.

Nine valves sat in human blood or platelet-rich plasma for half an hour, some switched on and some off. At the strongest setting tested, about ninety-six percent of the surface stayed free of deposits, and the electricity did not damage blood cells or trigger clotting. The team calls this a safe starting point before animal trials.
plos-pone-0348360:
Hongjing Chang, Jing Zhao, Yuhao Sun, and Huan Ding asked ordinary readers to judge four English translations of a poem by Li Bai, the celebrated Tang dynasty poet. Classical Chinese verse is notoriously hard to carry across languages. The four versions of the poem used prose, free verse, rhyme, or word-for-word literal rendering, and four hundred three American readers rated them online.

The rhymed translation won the readers' favour, striking the best balance between meaning and musical beauty. Prose and literal versions conveyed content but pleased readers less. Because only Americans took part, the authors caution that other cultures may respond differently. Still, the study gives translators rare evidence from actual readers rather than theory alone.
plos-pone-0334060:
Anna Fekete and colleagues ran a registered experiment on whether art can dull pain. Forty-two women brought artworks and music they found deeply beautiful to the laboratory, then kept a hand in ice water while experiencing music alone, visual art alone, both together, or neither. The team measured how long participants tolerated the cold, plus stress hormones, heart signals, and self-reports.

Music and the combined experience let women endure the ice water far longer than visual art alone. Yet no art form changed measured stress in the body, and people who easily lose themselves in experiences benefited most. The authors conclude art's pain relief works mainly through absorption and attention, not body chemistry.
plos-pone-0344360:
Megumi Shiomi and her team searched the genes of Japanese patients for the roots of a faulty heart rhythm. The fault comes and goes, so it is hard to catch in time. It can lead to stroke if missed. The team set about a thousand cases next to more than seven hundred controls. They also built a score that adds up many small gene effects.

All strong hits sat in one stretch of one chromosome, near a gene that helps build the heart. The score on its own sorted risk quite well. It did even better when mixed with health facts. The team says gene scores could flag who needs heart checks most.
plos-pone-0341960:
Dinh Duc Truong asked firms in Vietnam a plain question. When green rules press, who spends on clean kit? He used a World Bank survey of firms in the land. He weighed the press of rules, firm traits, and how hard each firm found it to raise cash. The sums let the press and the cash squeeze meet and clash.

Rules did push firms to spend green, but not by much. Tight cash cut green spends on its own. It also dulled the push of rules to near nil for the most squeezed firms. Truong says rules need cheap loans at their side to work at scale.
plos-pone-0348260:
Kitiya Rujimongkon and colleagues tested ivermectin, the familiar anti-parasite drug, against breast cancer cells that respond to hormones and against cells that have learned to resist hormone therapy. Earlier work from the group showed the drug slows these cells and boosts tamoxifen. The 2026 study traced which growth pathways ivermectin switches off.

The drug curbed estrogen-driven growth and lowered the estrogen receptor itself plus HER2, two engines of resistant disease. It also damped signals running through the TGF-beta pathway while sparing a protective partner protein linked to better outcomes. The authors propose ivermectin as a repurposed candidate to prevent or break hormone resistance, pending animal and clinical tests.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Kuwait fell to Iraqi troops before dawn, and the Council answered the same day. On 2 August 1990, it adopted Resolution 660. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. Yemen took no part. The Council voiced alarm at the invasion. It found a breach of world peace and security.

Acting under the Charter, the text condemns the invasion in plain words. It demands that Iraq pull out at once, with no conditions. Iraqi forces must return to where they stood on 1 August. Both states are called to talks on their disputes. The Council backs Arab League efforts to that end. Iraq refused, and this text became the legal base for later steps.

Africa's most populous state joined the world body days after freedom. On 7 October 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 160 without dissent. The Federation of Nigeria had won freedom from Britain six days before. The date, 1 October, was the peak of the Year of Africa. No African state held more people.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Nigeria. Admission followed within days. Nigeria's voice soon carried far in the Assembly. The state grew into one of Africa's top diplomatic powers. It also became a major source of troops for UN peacekeeping. This single line opened that long career.

Children in war zones gained a push from paper rules to real practice in 2003. On 30 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1460 without dissent. It builds on the child-protection texts of 1999 to 2001. The Secretary-General's fresh report lay before it. One legal note stands out in the text. Signing up children under fifteen is now a war crime in the new world court's statute.

The text backs the call for an era of application. Fine words must now be enforced on the ground. States must end impunity and try those who commit crimes against children. UN agencies and warring parties must turn the standards into daily practice. The push fed the watch lists that later named offending forces year by year.

Spain's last African colony won its freedom in October 1968. The small land on the Gulf of Guinea took the name Equatorial Guinea. Its bid for a UN seat moved fast. The bid papers were filed as S/8883. Resolution 260 passed with no dissent on 6 November 1968.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the new republic. The Assembly did so days later. The state's first years were grim. A harsh ruler, Macias Nguema, seized power and drove out much of the skilled class. Oil wealth came far later. None of that was set in stone in 1968. The text records a hopeful first step: a small colony's end, and a new flag over the UN hall.

Long trials strain a court when a judge falls ill. The Hague court for the Balkan wars had no spare bench. If a judge had to quit mid-trial, the case could crack. Its head asked for a fix. Resolution 1660 passed on 28 February 2006. It changed the court's own rulebook.

Stand-in judges could now be named as reserves. A reserve would sit through each phase of a trial. If a judge could not go on, the reserve stepped in. The case would not have to start from scratch. Two parts of the statute were swapped out in full. The text spells out how trial rooms are built and what stand-ins may do. It is dry court craft, yet it saved real trials from collapse.

Cyprus in the summer of 1974 is the setting for Resolution 360, adopted on 16 August by eleven votes to none with three abstentions. A Greek-backed coup had triggered a Turkish military intervention, and a second wave of Turkish operations in mid-August sharply worsened the crisis. The Council had already passed five resolutions on the emergency that summer.

The Council put on record its formal disapproval of one-sided military action against the Republic of Cyprus. It pressed the parties to obey its earlier resolutions, including the call to withdraw foreign military personnel not present under international agreements, without delay. Talks under the earlier ceasefire resolution were to resume at once, and neither side was to let battlefield gains dictate their outcome.

Liberia's slow recovery after civil war frames Resolution 1760, adopted on 20 June 2007. The Council praises the new government's progress since January 2006, notes the end of limits on Liberian timber exports, and welcomes Liberia joining the Kimberley Process, which tracks rough diamonds. Sanctions from Resolution 1521 were still under review, and the Council found too little progress to lift them.

The main step is a new Panel of Experts, with up to three members, to serve for six months and watch the sanctions. The Council says the UN Mission in Liberia still matters for safety and for helping the government control diamond, timber, and border areas. It also finds that Liberia still threatens peace in the region, even with the gains made.

Sexual violence as a weapon of war is the focus of Resolution 1960, adopted on 16 December 2010. Despite repeated condemnation, such violence continued worldwide, in places becoming systematic and brutal, while few perpetrators faced justice. The Secretary-General's November 2010 report documented the slow progress. Command responsibility and the need to end impunity run through the text.

The Council demands that all parties to armed conflict stop all sexual violence at once. It orders a naming system: the Secretary-General's annual reports must list parties credibly suspected of rape and other sexual violence, and that list will guide UN engagement and possible sanctions designations. Parties must make time-bound commitments, with clear orders through their chains of command, and their follow-through will be tracked. It also orders monitoring, analysis, and reporting arrangements in the field, more women protection advisers in peacekeeping missions, and scenario-based training for peacekeepers.

Côte d'Ivoire's peacekeeping force is drawn down in Resolution 2260, adopted on 20 January 2016. The presidential election of 25 October 2015 had passed peacefully. It was a milestone for stability. The Secretary-General's December 2015 report recommended reducing the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI. Progress on reconciliation, justice, and economic recovery continued, though some fragility remained.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides to decrease UNOCI's authorized military ceiling from 5,437 to 4,000 personnel by 31 March 2016. It recalls its request for a report by the same date with recommendations on the mission's future. The request was consistent with Resolution 2226 (2015). The Council says it intends to consider those recommendations promptly. It will do so in light of conditions on the ground.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1760 (XVII), adopted on 31 October 1962, kept up pressure on the question of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly restated the people's right to self-rule and to form an independent African state. It voiced deep regret that Britain had still not called the all-party conference demanded in resolution 1747 (XVI). The conference was to replace the rejected 1961 constitution.

The text warned that forcing that constitution through, and holding votes under it, would worsen an already tense situation. Britain was asked to suspend the constitution and cancel the coming elections. It was asked to grant full voting rights to all without discrimination. It was also asked to let the Acting Secretary-General help bring the sides together.

General Assembly Resolution 3160 (XXVIII), adopted on 14 December 1973, returned to the Falkland Islands, also named Malvinas. The Assembly voiced grave concern that eight years had passed since its 1965 call for talks. The talks were between Argentina and the United Kingdom on who held the islands. No real headway had been made.

The text approved the decolonization committee's chapters on the islands and declared that the talks had to speed up. Both governments were urged to proceed without delay toward a peaceful settlement of the sovereignty dispute. The settlement would end the colonial state of affairs. They were to report the outcome by the next session at the latest.

Resolution 69/60 of the General Assembly backs practical disarmament measures as a way to strengthen peace after conflicts. These include taking in and destroying illicit or surplus small arms and ammunition. They include disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of former fighters. They include mine clearing and keeping stockpiles secure. The Assembly stresses including such steps in peacekeeping missions with the host state's consent. It backs the Programme of Action Implementation Support System for matching needs with resources. It urges giving to the United Nations trust facility for work on arms control.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 1160 — the landmark 1998 resolution imposing an arms embargo on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia over Kosovo. It targeted Belgrade’s war machine. The 1998 Kosovo embargo is the landmark: Belgrade’s Kosovo war machine formally targeted.

Security Council resolution 1260, adopted on 20 August 1999, backs the Peace Agreement signed in Lomé on 7 July 1999. The agreement was between the Government of Sierra Leone and the Revolutionary United Front (RUF). The Council commends both sides and the West African force ECOMOG, and calls on the parties to carry out the agreement in full.

To support the settlement, the Council provisionally expands the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL. It expands it to up to 210 military observers, working under ECOMOG's protection. It strengthens its political, human rights and child protection work. It calls on the RUF and all other armed groups to disarm and join the demobilization programme at once. It notes the agreement's plans for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and a Human Rights Commission.

A shorter renewal than usual is granted to Iraq's oil-for-food programme in this text from July 2001. Earlier renewals had run 180 days. This time the Council chose 150 days, starting 4 July 2001, while it weighed changes meant to improve how aid reached Iraqis.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the core rules first set in 1995 in force for the new period. Priority spending on food, nutrition, and health continued, along with United Nations checks that goods were shared fairly across the country. A full review of the programme was also ordered, a sign that the next renewal could bring wider changes.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's border still had not been marked out, years after the Algiers peace agreements, when their mission UNMEE was extended on 14 September 2004, until 15 March 2005. The Boundary Commission's 2002 ruling was meant to be final and binding, yet demarcation had stalled.

Both parties are called on to cooperate fully with UNMEE and remove all limits on its movement and work at once. They are pressed to work promptly with the Boundary Commission, including paying dues and naming field liaison officers, so marking the border can proceed. Ethiopia is urged to show the political will to accept the boundary ruling without conditions.

A ceasefire in the Gaza war is called for on 8 January 2009. Fighting had escalated after a period of calm was not renewed, and heavy civilian casualties followed. Gaza, it is stressed, is part of the territory occupied in 1967 and of the future Palestinian state, and grave concern is voiced at the deepening humanitarian crisis there.

An immediate, durable ceasefire, fully respected by all sides, is called for, leading to the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza. Unimpeded aid delivery and distribution across Gaza and regular opening of the crossings for goods and people are demanded. All violence against civilians and terrorism is condemned, the relief role of the refugee agency UNRWA is welcomed, and new efforts toward a two-state peace are urged.

Peace came to Rhodesia at the end of 1979, after talks at Lancaster House in London. The talks produced agreement on a constitution for a free and independent Zimbabwe. Genuine majority rule was part of the deal. Britain resumed its role as the ruling power for the transition. Resolution 460 was adopted on 21 December 1979.

The Council welcomed the end of fourteen years of rebellion. In light of the Lancaster House agreement, it acted on sanctions. Member states were called on to end the measures imposed on Southern Rhodesia since 1966. Those measures had been adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The sanctions committee created in 1968 was dissolved. The states that had enforced the sanctions were praised, above all the front-line states. The Council also called for urgent aid to rebuild the country, and for strict respect for the agreement.

Competing drafts for the Council's next step on Palestine were on the table in the autumn of 1948. The draft under discussion was the second revised draft in a Council document. Amendments and revisions had been suggested from several sides. Resolution 60 was adopted on 29 October 1948 to sort the drafts out.

The Council set up a sub-committee of five members. The United Kingdom, China, France, Belgium, and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic sat on it. Its job was to consider every amendment and revision suggested to the draft. It also had to consult the Acting Mediator for Palestine. Together they would prepare a revised draft resolution for the Council to act on. The text is a working step inside the Council's own process, not a decision on Palestine itself.
un-sc-res-660:
Iraqi tanks rolled into Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the Council met the same day. It judged the invasion a breach of international peace and security. It acted under Articles 39 and 40 of the Charter, the parts that cover such breaches. Resolution 660 was adopted that day, by fourteen votes to none.

The Council condemned the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait. It demanded that Iraq withdraw all its forces at once, without conditions. The forces had to return to the positions they held on 1 August 1990. Iraq and Kuwait were called on to begin intensive negotiations at once, to settle their differences. The Council backed efforts toward that end, above all those of the League of Arab States. It also decided to meet again as needed, to take further steps to secure compliance with the resolution.
un-sc-res-1460:
Children caught in war gained a stronger pledge from the Council in January 2003. On 30 January 2003 it backed the Secretary-General's call for an era of application. Old promises to protect children now had to be put into practice. The Council recalled its line of resolutions on children and armed conflict. Reports on women, peace, and security also fed into the text.

Parties that recruit or use child soldiers must stop at once. The Council voiced plans to talk with groups that break the rules. It asked United Nations agencies to coordinate their child protection work. It also pushed for action plans to end the use of children in fighting. Monitoring of abuses formed part of the scheme.
un-sc-res-1660:
The Yugoslav tribunal gained a new kind of judge in 2006. Trials were long, and a judge's illness could stall them for months. On 28 February 2006 the Security Council amended the tribunal's statute. Reserve judges could now be named from the pool of ad litem judges. The tribunal's president made the proposal. A reserve judge would sit through a trial from the start.

If a trial judge could not continue, the reserve could step in. No testimony would need to be heard twice. The annex rewrites two articles of the statute. It sets the chambers at sixteen permanent judges plus temporary ones. The reform served the court's drive to finish its work. It was a practical fix to a real weakness in long trials.
un-sc-res-360:
Cyprus slid deeper into crisis when the Security Council acted on 16 August 1974. Further military operations on the island had gravely worsened the situation after the first Turkish intervention in July. All states had declared respect for Cyprus's sovereignty and independence. The Council called the fighting a most serious threat to peace in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Council recorded its formal disapproval of the one-sided military actions taken against the Republic of Cyprus. It urged the parties to obey all its earlier resolutions, including the withdrawal without delay of foreign military personnel not present under international agreements. Talks called for in resolution 353 (1974) had to resume at once, in a spirit of cooperation. Their outcome was not to be shaped by gains won through military action. The Secretary-General was asked to report as needed, and the Council stayed seized of the question permanently.
un-sc-res-1760:
Liberia's sanctions were kept under expert review on 20 June 2007. The government had rebuilt steadily since January 2006, and its timber rules had ended the log measures. Liberia had just joined the Kimberley Process as a participant. The expert panel's report of 24 May 2007 was before the Council. The arms embargo and asset freeze of resolutions 1521 (2003) and 1532 (2004) had been reviewed against their lifting terms.

The Council found that progress toward those terms was still not enough. The remaining measures therefore stayed in force. It asked the Secretary-General to set up a new Panel of Experts within one month. The panel would follow up the sanctions, check for breaches, and judge the freeze's working. All states and Liberia's government had to cooperate with the panel in full and give it free access. The Council stayed actively seized.
un-sc-res-2260: Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2260, adopted on 20 January 2016. The country had held a calm presidential election in October 2015. Peace, justice work, and the economy were all moving forward, though some weakness remained. A report from the Secretary-General had advised drawing the peacekeeping operation down.
europmc-pmc10182360:
Liu and a large team review immunosenescence, the aging of the immune system, in a 2023 paper. As people grow old, their immune defenses weaken in known ways. Infections hit harder, vaccines work less well, and the risk of cancer and chronic disease climbs, while a low level of inflammation runs in the background.

The review explains the molecular changes behind this decline, in both the fast innate defenses and the slower learned ones. It links those changes to the diseases of old age. It also surveys treatments that aim to restore youthful immune function.
europmc-pmc10287560:
Nassiri and a large trial team report a phase one and two trial of a virus therapy plus an immune drug in recurrent glioblastoma, in a 2023 study. Glioblastoma is a fast-growing brain tumor that nearly always returns after standard care. The treatment paired DNX-2401, a virus engineered to attack tumor cells, with pembrolizumab, a drug that frees the immune system.

The virus was injected into the tumor, followed by the immune drug. The paper reports safety and survival results for the combination. The approach tests whether a virus can turn a cold tumor hot for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc1043860:
Brennecke and co-authors set out the rules in 2005 for how a microRNA finds its target gene. A microRNA is a short RNA piece that does not build a protein. It binds a gene message and dials that gene down. How exact that match must be was still unclear at the time.

The team split target sites into two broad classes. In one class, a strong match at the microRNA's head end suffices, with weak pairing at the tail. In the other class, a weak head match needs a strong tail match to work. Genome-wide data backed both classes in real genes. Each microRNA holds about 100 target sites on average, Brennecke found.
europmc-pmc10477960:
The GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators counted the world burden of osteoarthritis from 1990 to 2020. Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease in adults. It wears down joint tissue, causing chronic pain and loss of movement. It strikes most often after age 40 and climbs steeply with age.

In 2020, 595 million people had the disease, 7.6% of the world population. Case counts had risen 132.2% since 1990. The study covers hand, hip, knee, and other joint sites in 204 nations. Forecasts run to 2050, with knee cases set to rise 74.9%. For people aged 70 and over, the disease ranked seventh as a cause of years lived with disability.
europmc-pmc11164360:
Open2C presents a toolkit that turns raw DNA reads into chromosome contact maps in this 2024 paper. Hi-C and related methods reveal how chromosomes fold by recording which DNA regions touch. These methods pour out massive, varied sequencing data. Turning reads into contact pairs needs fast and flexible processing.

Their suite, pairtools, splits the job into modular command-line steps that can be chained into pipelines. Core steps parse alignments into pairs, sort them, and remove duplicate copies made during copying of DNA. Extra tools handle filtering, quality control, and pair editing. Benchmarks against popular pipelines showed gains in speed and flexibility, the authors report. Special tools cover cut-based protocols, single-cell Hi-C, and maps split by parent of origin. The suite plugs into Python analysis libraries.
europmc-pmc11631760:
Guzman and a large team present an ultra-fast method for measuring proteins by mass spectrometry in this 2024 paper. Mass spectrometry weighs molecules to identify and quantify the full protein set of a sample, its proteome. Speed and coverage usually trade off against each other. Their strategy, called narrow-window data-independent acquisition, pairs high-resolution survey scans with very fast fragment scans.

A new analyser scans fragments at about 200 per second with high accuracy, they report. The setup profiles over 100 full yeast proteomes per day. For human samples it reaches about 10,000 protein groups in half an hour, or about 7,000 proteins in five minutes. That is three times the coverage of the current state of the art. Pre-separated samples give comprehensive human proteome coverage in about three hours. Quantitative precision was shown on a three-species mixture.
europmc-pmc1185560:
Hausdorff wrote a 2005 overview of gait variability, the small changes from stride to stride. Walking looks steady, yet each step differs a bit. Those small shifts can reveal aging and disease effects. They may also track how well therapy or rehab works.

Past work ties stride shifts more closely to falls than average speed does. The overview gathers nine reports on fresh findings. Topics span wearable sensors, math models, and animal studies. One study shows dim light slows some walkers and unsettles others. Hausdorff frames stride shifts as a rich health signal.
europmc-pmc1713260:
Detecting family structure in gene data lacked a formal test of significance. Patterson, Price, and Reich supplied one in 2006, placing principal components analysis on solid statistical ground. The method compresses genetic variation into axes that reveal population splits.

Their theory uncovered a phase change in detectability. Below a threshold of divergence, structure in a fixed data set is essentially invisible. A little above the threshold, detection becomes easy. The flip lets researchers predict how much data a study needs to find structure. Patterson turns a descriptive plot into a testable claim about populations.
europmc-pmc1769360:
Children as young as five can report their own quality of life soundly. Varni, Limbers, and Burwinkle tested that claim in 2007 in 8,591 children aged 5 to 16, using the same PedsQL survey given to parents in a companion study.

Even the youngest children left few items blank. Most self-report scales in each age group, including age five, passed the 0.70 reliability standard. Total scores approached or passed 0.90, the bar for judging single patients. Validity checks held as well. Varni argues the results support hearing the child's own voice in trials, not only the parent's.
europmc-pmc1821060: The Sorcerer II Global Ocean Sampling expedition: northwest Atlantic through eastern tropical Pacific. — a 2005 science paper on the ocean gene trawl route. It maps the sampling route. The paper is the trawl-route study: the findings on ocean germs, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1868760: Phylogenetic and functional analysis of the Cation Diffusion Facilitator (CDF) family: improved signature and prediction of substrate specificity. — a 2005 science paper on the CDF transporter family. It analyzes the CDF family. The paper is the CDF study: the findings on substrate ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2169260: OMERACT: an international initiative to improve outcome measurement in rheumatology. — a 2005 science paper on the OMERACT initiative. It guides the outcome measurement. The paper is the OMERACT guide: the findings on rheumatology, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2211560: Antitumor activity of rapamycin in a Phase I trial for patients with recurrent PTEN-deficient glioblastoma. — a 2005 science paper on rapamycin vs brain tumors. It tests rapamycin on brain tumors for labs. The paper is the brain-tumor trial: the notes on tumor ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2242660: Gene expression profiling and histopathological characterization of triple-negative/basal-like breast carcinomas. — a 2005 science paper on triple-negative tumor maps. It charts the tumor maps for labs. The paper is the tumor-map study: the notes on breast ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2376960: Evaluation of cumulative prognostic scores based on the systemic inflammatory response in patie — a 2008 science paper on swelling scorecards. It grades the swelling scorecards for labs. The paper is the scorecard study: the notes on swelling ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2377260: Prevalence of chronic kidney disease in population-based studies: systematic review. — a 2008 science paper on kidney-disease rates. It reviews the prevalence research. The paper is the rate review: the findings on kidney ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2475660: Multiple multilocus DNA barcodes from the plastid genome discriminate plant species equally wel — a 2008 science paper on plant DNA barcodes. It discriminates the plant species. The paper is the barcode study: the findings on plant ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2478660: The multifunctional FUS, EWS and TAF15 proto-oncoproteins show cell type-specific expression pa — a 2008 science paper on FUS/EWS/TAF15 proteins. It shows the multifunctional expression. The paper is the show study: the findings on protein ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2547860: Gene networks driving bovine milk fat synthesis during the lactation cycle. — a 2008 science paper on cow milk-fat genes. It maps the bovine networks. The paper is the network study: the findings on milk ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2568860: A hierarchy of time-scales and the brain. — a 2008 science paper on the brain's many clocks. It maps the many clocks for labs. The paper is the clock study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2642860: Are animal models predictive for humans? — a 2008 science paper on do animal tests translate. It asks if the animal tests translate for labs. The paper is the translate study: the findings on animal ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2714960: Interplay in the selection of fluoroquinolone resistance and bacterial fitness. — a 2008 science paper on drug-resist trade-offs. It weighs the trade-offs for labs. The paper is the trade-off study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2739160: Mapping the human membrane proteome: a majority of the human membrane proteins can be classifie — a 2008 science paper on the human membrane proteome. It maps the membrane proteins. The paper is the mapping study: the findings on proteome ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2784760: Does neuroinflammation fan the flame in neurodegenerative diseases? — a 2008 science paper on neuroinflammation. It asks if the flame is fanned. The paper is the flame study: the findings on neurodegeneration ills, filed here in full session today twice.
heydon-rosie-crucian-axiomata-1660:
John Heydon's Rosie Crucian Infallible Axiomata appeared in London in 1660, as the monarchy returned to England. The slim book is a rule-book of general axioms, Rosicrucian doctrine in its most concentrated form. Where Heydon's Holy Guide sprawls, the Axiomata compresses the teaching into short, sharp sayings for the adept.

Each axiom states a principle of the Rosicrucian art or life. The Restoration-era statement aims at certainty: infallible is its own chosen word. Heydon marketed himself as the fraternity's English spokesman, and such handbooks were his wares. The Axiomata lets readers hold his whole doctrine in a few pages. It is the Rose Cross boiled down, doctrine as a pocket creed.
plos-pone-0004960:
Birds sing hardest at dawn and dusk. Scientists have proposed many explanations for these choruses. Vincenzo Penteriani and Maria del Mar Delgado added an owl's-eye view in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied eagle owls, which call at dusk. Eagle owls carry a white throat badge that shows during calling.

The owls vocalized most when the badge contrasted most with the fading light. Timing matched the badge's visibility, not just the hour. That suggests the call and the badge form one combined display. The signal is tuned to twilight. The study links song output to a visual signal in a nocturnal bird.
plos-pone-0005060:
Synovial sarcoma is a soft-tissue cancer. A recurrent chromosome swap creates a fusion protein in it. The protein is called SYT-SSX2. Roy Barco and colleagues studied its effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. They found it antagonizes Bmi1. Bmi1 is a key member of the polycomb complex. That complex silences genes.

By jamming the silencer, the cancer protein deregulates polycomb activity. Normal gene control gets scrambled. The finding reveals how one fusion protein rewires the cell's rulebook. It connects a single genetic accident to broad gene chaos. That connection may suggest treatments. Restoring polycomb balance could counter the fusion's effects. The study maps a mechanism, not just a marker.
plos-pone-0005160:
Mitochondria split and fuse to stay healthy. A protein called GDAP1 drives the splitting, called fission. Konstanze Wagner and colleagues studied how GDAP1 reaches its post. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Many such proteins anchor into the mitochondrial outer membrane by a tail. That tail-anchor sits at the protein's end.

GDAP1's targeting and function both depend on its tail-anchor. The tail is not just glue. It modulates what the protein does once anchored. Whether tails tune function was unknown before this. The finding reveals how location and activity intertwine. GDAP1 defects cause a nerve disease in humans. Understanding its anchoring may explain how those defects harm nerves.
plos-pone-0005260:
Flu surveillance often relies on lab reports that arrive late. Phone triage lines, where nurses advise callers, log symptoms much earlier in an outbreak. Yih and colleagues tested those logs as a flu signal in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study asked whether telephone triage data can detect influenza-like illness in the community. Call patterns could act as an early-warning sensor for seasonal flu and for a pandemic. Cheap, fast signals like this help health officials time warnings and stock supplies. Phone lines log each call the day it is made, so a spike in cough and fever calls can warn a city days before lab reports come in.
plos-pone-0005360:
A variant near the TNF gene had already been tied to higher risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. TNF's protein product switches on NF-kB, a master regulator of inflammation. Wang and colleagues widened the search across those gene families in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study tested common variants in the TNF and TNF receptor superfamilies and in NF-kB transcription factors. Each variant was checked for association with lymphoma risk. Since inflammation and lymphoma are linked, a full family scan can reveal which steps in the pathway matter most. Lymphoma care turns on how fast the disease moves, and gene marks tied to risk may one day help sort new cases. Pick the depth of care each one needs at the start.
plos-pone-0005960:
The valve that lets blood leave the heart stiffens as years pass. Eli Weinberg, Frederick Schoen and Mohammad Mofrad built a computer model of that slow change in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers both normal aging of the aortic valve and the disease called calcific aortic stenosis, where hard nodules stiffen the valve flaps.

A model lets the team test how local strain in the tissue may drive the buildup of calcium over time. That link between force and disease is hard to watch in a living heart. The work gives valve science a tool for asking what starts the stiffening, and where a future treatment might step in early.
plos-pone-0006060:
Rotavirus sends crowds of young children to clinics and hospitals each year. Joke Bilcke, Pierre Van Damme, Marc Van Ranst and colleagues gathered the world's counts in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper is a systematic review and meta-analysis of how often symptomatic rotavirus infection occurs, drawing on community studies that followed children where they live.

No pooled estimate of this kind existed before, though the number drives the math on whether vaccines pay for themselves. A firm incidence rate steadies cost-effectiveness studies and health budgets alike. The review gives vaccine planners, above all in poorer countries, a shared figure to plan against instead of scattered local guesses.
plos-pone-0006160:
Prey grow slower when predators are near, and the textbook blames skipped meals. Ulrich Steiner and Josh Van Buskirk tested a rival account in 2009: that predators change prey metabolism itself. Their PLOS ONE paper examines the growth and predation risk tradeoff, which usually assumes reduced activity explains why defense costs growth.

Predator-induced changes in metabolism cannot explain the tradeoff, the title concludes. Ruling out a plausible mechanism is progress, since it sends the field back to behavior and other costs with better focus. The result keeps a classic ecology question open, and open in a more precise place than before.
plos-pone-0006260:
Half of the human protein set still lacks a known job, years after the genome was read. Diana Hooi Ping Low and colleagues characterised one such unknown, a tectonin protein, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its structure folds into repeated propeller shapes that can grip several partners at once.

The protein interacts with ficolin, an immune molecule, and binds LPS, a bacterial surface toxin. Those links place the unknown protein in the body's germ defence. Each solved unknown can reveal new pathways and cascades. The study is a reminder that the genome's parts list is still being annotated.
plos-pone-0006660:
Victoria Morgan and co-authors merged two kinds of brain scans in PLOS ONE in 2009. MRI can map the brain in two ways: how areas wire together and how they fire together. That power sparked wide interest in studying both maps as one. Functional MRI shows which areas turn on at the same time. Diffusion MRI traces the white matter cables that link areas.

By joining the two, the team could study how structure and function relate in brain networks. Strong cables should back strong joint firing, but the two do not always match. Those gaps are of real interest for science and care. Their joint approach helps work on epilepsy and other network ills of the brain.
plos-pone-0006760:
Nowel Azzouz and co-authors mapped partnerships of a major RNA control complex in yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. The complex is called CCR4-NOT. It has nine subunits in yeast, including the deadenylase Ccr4. In the nucleus it connects to transcription. In the cytoplasm it helps break down messenger RNA.

The team showed the complex physically interacts with TRAMP. It also interacts with the nuclear exosome, an RNA shredding machine. Physical contact plus functional effects tie the systems together. RNA quality control thus works as a connected network. Understanding the network explains how bad transcripts are caught and destroyed.
plos-pone-0006860:
Rebecca M. Green and colleagues exposed a tiny worm to cigarette smoke in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smoking is the major cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and lung cancer. Bacterial infections help drive COPD as airway immunity weakens. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans served as a living model. It has a simple innate immune system that researchers know well.

Smoke exposure changed the worms' innate immunity in vivo. The model lets scientists screen immune effects quickly and cheaply. Findings in worms can nominate pathways to test in mammals. That speeds the search for how smoke weakens lung defense. It may eventually support treatments for infection-prone COPD patients.
plos-pone-0006960:
K. G. Guruharsha, Mar Ruiz-Gomez, H. A. Ranganath, and colleagues mapped a muscle gene's control in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Muscle fibers form when myoblast cells fuse together. A gene called dumbfounded, also known as kirre, is an early player in that fusion. It must be switched on in founder cells, which attract other myoblasts to fuse with them.

The team charted where and when this attractant gene turns on. Its regulation proved complex in both space and time. A fixed number of founder cells is chosen from a pool of equals. Precise gene timing is what marks those founders out.
plos-pone-0007060:
Daisuke Nishizawa, Makoto Nagashima, Ryoji Katoh, and colleagues linked pain relief genes to surgery in PLOS ONE in 2009. Opioids are standard drugs for strong pain. Yet people differ widely in how much opioid they need. The team focused on a potassium channel subunit, GIRK2, encoded by the gene KCNJ6.
