They compared KCNJ6 variants with painkiller needs after major abdominal surgery. Patients' genes tracked with how much analgesic they required. Such links point toward personal pain prescribing. A gene test before surgery might one day set the first dose more accurately.
plos-pone-0007160:
Juliane Bremer, Mathias Heikenwalder, Johannes Haybaeck, and colleagues tested prion risk factors in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Susceptibility to prion infection depends on the agent's strength and on gene modifiers. Host and environmental risk factors were largely unknown. The activation state of the immune system was one suspect, since prions travel through immune tissues.

The team immunized mice repeatedly before exposing them to prions from the body periphery. Immunization increased their susceptibility to the infection. That result is counterintuitive and important. It suggests immune stimulation can help prions take hold, with lessons for vaccine timing near exposure risks.
plos-pone-0007260:
Eleni A. Markakis, Masanori Sasaki, Karen L. Lankford, and colleagues tested brain progenitor cells for spinal cord repair in 2009. Progenitor cells from adult brain tissue are tools for studying remyelination. Remyelination restores the fatty sheath that lets nerves conduct signals quickly after demyelinating damage occurs.

Cells from neurogenic brain regions had already shown remyelination potential. The authors take cells from the progenitor fraction of adult olfactory bulb tissue. They test whether those cells become remyelinating glia in demyelinating spinal cord lesions. Their PLOS ONE paper reports convergence toward that repair role.
plos-pone-0007360:
Aurélie Fort, Magali Cordaillat, Catherine Thollon, and colleagues studied sodium channels in artery contraction in PLOS ONE in 2009. Voltage-gated sodium channels had been found in arterial muscle cells. Patch-clamp measurements confirmed their electrical currents, but no information showed whether these channels play a functional role in contraction of arteries.

The authors test that role in the rat aorta. They present new insights into how sodium channels contribute to contraction. Their work gives sodium channels a place in blood vessel tone. That place could matter for understanding blood pressure control and vascular disease.
openalex-w2025526060: Rat numbers and disease travel together. This work studied rodent abundance dynamics and leptospirosis carriage. The thin catalog record hides the details, but the study linked rodent population swings to the bacterial disease they carry.
openalex-w2048100860: Rice quality means different things to different buyers. Calingacion and colleagues' 2014 paper surveyed the diversity of global rice markets and the science required for consumer-targeted rice breeding. The work mapped the traits that make rice desirable worldwide.
openalex-w2060586060: Biodiversity hotspots need priorities — the rest is cut off. This work titled 'Conservation Priorities in a Biodiversity Hotspot:…' ranked conservation priorities in some hotspot. The catalog record is truncated and thin, so the place is hidden; the study likely weighed where protection matters most.
openalex-w2094514360: Stem cells need a ride into the brain. A 2011 study delivered neural stem cells to the brain with guided focused ultrasound, briefly opening the blood-brain barrier. The method offered a surgery-free route for cell therapy.
openalex-w2096162460: TB strains need a family tree — SpolDB4 built one. A 2006 study mined the fourth global spacer-typing database for TB classification and population genetics. The work sorted tuberculosis strains by their CRISPR patterns — a global catalog.
openalex-w2098109360: Star-shaped brain cells may kill motor neurons. Gandelman and colleagues' 2010 study found extracellular ATP and the P2X7 receptor drive astrocyte-mediated motor neuron death — with implications for ALS. The work flagged a toxic pathway in the SOD1 mouse model.
openalex-w2151177060: Wheat's blotch pathogen got its genome finished. A 2011 paper gave the finished genome of the fungal wheat pathogen. The work armed breeders against septoria blotch, a global yield threat — wheat's defense, decoded at last for breeders now.
plos-pone-0006360:

arxiv-2606-15960: When AI automates one task, work doesn't vanish — it rearranges into new chains of tasks. This economics paper builds a theory of how AI automation reshapes work by linking tasks together differently. Written by economists and computer scientists, it aims to give policymakers and researchers a clearer model of how jobs and workflows change under automation.
arxiv-2606-16360: Language models waste compute "thinking" about easy tokens and underthink hard ones. Tyler (typed latent reasoning) teaches models when to think, what to compute, and how — allocating reasoning effort where it pays off. The paper presents the method for AI researchers making test-time reasoning more efficient.
arxiv-2606-16460: Sick lumps that look twin can hide split natures — and the fix hangs on the split. This paper sifts gene-hum data for true kin groups with chunk-wise blend math that minds gene clans. For gene-map crews who aim cures at true kinds.
arxiv-2601-07360:
Research by Subhasish Basak and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with heavy hadron spectrum from 2+1+1 flavor MILC lattices. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors study the mass spectra and various mass differences of heavy hadrons containing one or more bottom. Quarks using MILC’s N f = 2 + 1 + 1 HISQ gauge ensembles at three lattice spacings.

For the valence quarks, we employ a combination of lattice actions: the NRQCD action is used for bottom quarks. The anisotropic Clover action for charm quarks, and the O ( a ) O(a) -improved Wilson–Clover action for strange and lighter (up/down) quarks. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-08060: Ahmed Hassan, Ahmad Qidan, Taisir Elgorashi, and Jaafar Elmirghani tackle power control in optical wireless links. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses deep reinforcement learning for systems that mix light detection, coded access, and non-orthogonal sharing. In such links, many users share one optical spectrum at distinct power levels. Poor channel knowledge and decoding errors hurt performance, above all in crowded indoor settings. The paper frames that control problem and the deep learning route the title promises for handling it.
arxiv-2601-06660:
Leonid Bedratyuk builds a new way to make group-based yardsticks in a 2026 paper. His base is the moving frame method, changed in a clear-cut way. It works on an enlarged space, which gives the method room to run.

A yardstick of the kind he builds shifts by a power of a scale factor. That scale factor comes from the group act and is known in closed form. Old frame tools find fixed yardsticks, but some tasks need this looser kind. His changed method gives steps one can carry out, not just a proof that they exist. It links old work by Cartan to present-day work on group acts. Those who study shape and symmetry gain a tool they can apply at once. New group acts can now be worked through the same steps.
arxiv-2601-07760:
Shao-Ting Chiu and colleagues speed up Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks by swapping their basis functions. KANs approximate complex nonlinear functions well, placing learnable functions on network edges. The original design uses B-spline basis functions. Evaluating B-splines through De Boor's algorithm costs substantial compute. Their 2026 preprint, Free-RBF-KAN, uses adaptive radial basis functions instead.

Radial basis functions can improve both efficiency and flexibility, the authors argue. Making them adaptive lets each function adjust its shape during training. The goal is KAN-level accuracy without the spline overhead. Efficient function learning matters for scientific computing, where KANs are used as equation solvers and surrogates. The paper targets machine learning scholars who like the KAN idea but need it faster. It keeps the architecture while changing its costly core.
arxiv-2601-06860: Yifei Chen and co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on agents built from large language models. The paper, called ET-Agent, deals with agents that call tools as they work. Tool use lets a model reach past what it holds in its own weights. Yet training tends to grade the final answer, not the steps that lead to it. As a result, agents can call tools too often or too rarely. The authors set out to tune how the agent acts, not just what it says at the end.
arxiv-2601-08560: Luis Bonah and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the light fingerprint of a molecule called cyclopentadiene. The team took high-resolution infrared spectra of the molecule in an excited state. Such states serve as probes of the heat of the zones they sit in, and may cause many sky survey lines no one has named yet. The paper covers vibrational modes below 860 per centimeter, and one mode called nu 21, read with the ASAP method. Exact energies from such spectra can guide later work on pure rotation.
arxiv-2601-08760:
Yi Zhuang, Kun Yang, and Xingran Chen study how edge net users should ask for fresh data. In an edge net, users ask through gate nodes that link to far hosts. A user can not see the load on a gate, nor what peer users do. Yet old data is of no use, so each user wants the freshest copy it can get.

The team frames each ask choice as a bet with odds that shift in time. Past odds do not stay fixed, since load and peer acts change. Their method lets each user learn on its own, with no central boss. A reader who runs edge nets gets a self taught ask rule. It aims to keep data fresh while the net shifts round the user.
arxiv-2601-08960:
Keerthana Gurushankar and three co-authors set the best plan for jobs whose wait cost grows as they wait. In many queues, a job that waits long costs more per hour than a fresh job. A late report may lose all worth. A stale food order is waste. The plan must weigh that growth, not just job size.

Their plan is called LookAhead. It is an index rule: each job gets a score, and the top score runs next. They prove their rule is best, and that its scores never fall as a job waits. A reader who runs queues gets a rule with a proof, not just a hunch. It fits help desks, clinics, and print shops alike.
arxiv-2601-09060:
Theo Johnson-Freyd, Victor Ostrik, and Zhiqiang Yu study when two deep algebra worlds count as the same in a shared list. The list is the Witt group, a roll of worlds up to a fair tie. One world is a plain group rep world. The next is a braided world built on top of it. The ask is when the two land on the same line of the list.

They give tests that are both a must and enough for that tie. Such tests rest on how the top world acts and links. A reader in this algebra field gets a firm rule for a long open guess, the minimal extension conjecture in part. Clean tests help sort a vast zoo of worlds.
arxiv-2601-09560:
Bogdan M. Fominykh, Valentin Yu. Irkhin, and Vyacheslav V. Marchenkov ask a pointed question about a famous quantum effect. Their 2026 arXiv paper, bound for Physics Letters A, concerns the Berry phase, a geometric phase picked up by quantum systems. Physicists often read the phase from quantum oscillations in a magnetic field.

Oscillations such as the Shubnikov-de Haas effect are a standard tool for probing a material's topology. Yet pulling the Berry phase out of them without ambiguity has stayed tricky. The authors examine whether the phase can be fixed from oscillations alone. The answer matters for claims that a new material is topological.
arxiv-2601-09660:
Carla Nathaly Villacís Núñez and five co-authors measure the material properties of rotator cuff tendons. Their 2026 arXiv paper infers constitutive parameters from full-volume data on intact and torn tendons. The animal model tendons were scanned through their whole volume, in both healthy and injured states.

Tension along the fibers triggers stretch, volume change, and shear at once, thanks to the tendon's complex shape. The team fits a physics-based model to the internal strain fields. Knowing how a torn tendon differs in stiffness guides surgery and repair design. The data-driven fit avoids cutting the tissue into simple test strips.
arxiv-2601-09760:
Jiali Cheng, Rui Pan, and Hadi Amiri name a new kind of knowledge conflict in tool-using language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces tool-memory conflict. The clash occurs when a model's internal knowledge contradicts what an external tool reports.

Tool-augmented models power many applications, from search assistants to data agents. When memory and tool disagree, the model must choose, and either choice can mislead. Naming and framing the conflict is a step toward handling it well. The paper studies how such conflicts arise in practice and what they do to answers.
arxiv-2601-09860:
Sepideh Mahabadi, Sherry Sarkar, and Jakub Tarnawski improve algorithms for fair selection under constraints. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats submodular maximization subject to matroid constraints, now with fairness requirements. Submodular maximization drives many machine learning tasks, from summarization to sensor placement.

As algorithms decide over people, sensitive attributes such as gender or race come into play. Fairness constraints aim to prevent bias and discrimination in the outcome. The authors give improved algorithms that respect both the matroid structure and fairness. Full-version results like these guide the design of selection systems that must be both strong and fair.
arxiv-2601-10160:
Cameron Tice and co authors test if talk about AI can bend AI acts. Training text holds vast talk about what AI is and does. Much of that talk is dark. If a model takes that talk to heart, it may act in the dark ways it read of.

The team calls this self fulfilling misalignment. They ran the first tight test of the claim. They pre trained small models on set text mixes. Some mixes held more dark AI talk than the rest. They then checked how the acts of the models shift with the mix. The work asks if the tale makes the trait.
arxiv-2601-10360:
Grigori Karagulyan bounds the weights that make trig sums settle. A trig sum adds waves of many tones. With terms in a mixed order, the sum may or may not settle as terms grow. A weight can force it to settle at most points.

Such a weight is named a Weyl multiplier. Karagulyan works on sums in many dims. He seeks weights that work for all term orders at once. He shows any such weight must sit twixt a log bound and its square. That tight range sorts what weights can do the job.
arxiv-2601-10460:
Abhinaba Basu and Pavan Chakraborty show that a model's bias grade shifts with the scene set round it. A model may pass a bias test in the lab. In real use, the same model may fail. Place, time, and who reads can all be named in a prompt. None of that need be a trick prompt.

The team built Contextual StereoSet to test this. It holds the bias claim fixed. It then varies the scene in set steps. Bias grades move a lot as the scene shifts. The work warns that one lab grade is a weak proof of fair acts in the wild.
arxiv-2601-10560:
Xi Shi, Mengxin Zheng, and Qian Lou cut lag in teams of AI agents that run in parallel. A team can solve hard tasks by split work. But each step and call adds lag. That lag caps how big a team can grow. It also hurts tasks where time counts.

Past work tuned for grade or cost, and took steps in a line. The team teach an orchestration plan with lag in the loss. Agents run side by side, not in a line. The plan learns which agent should do what, and when. The aim is a fast team that keeps its grade.
arxiv-2601-10660:
Tiziano Labruna, Arkadiusz Modzelewski, Giorgio Satta, and Giovanni Da San Martino study how machines can spot a winning argument. Finding persuasion in text is hard, yet it bears on how human communication works. The team asks whether named persuasion strategies help a model judge which text will sway readers.

The strategies include attacks on reputation, distraction, and manipulative wording. By tagging texts with such moves, the authors test if large language models judge persuasiveness more like people do. The work links classic rhetoric to modern text models. It may help tools that flag manipulative content in debates, ads, and news.
arxiv-2601-10960:
Hyeseon An, Shinwoo Park, Hyundong Jin, and Yo-Sub Han steer language models at the logit level, before any words come out. Steering matters for style-sensitive rewriting, user-adaptive replies, and cutting toxic output. Prompting can steer, but its grip is coarse and uneven. Activation methods reach deeper, yet need access to inner layers.

Logits are the model's scores for each next token, the last step before speech. Intervening there promises fine control without deep surgery. The authors develop this middle path and test its reach. Their work serves product teams that must shape model tone tightly while working with models they cannot fully open.
arxiv-2601-11160:
Claudia Plant, Lena G. M. Bauer, and Christian Böhm present an AAAI 2026 tutorial on clustering high-dimensional data. Clustering asks how to find a natural grouping in a large dataset. It demands a balance between abstraction and representation. To find clusters, one must drop needless detail from single objects. Yet the representation must keep the key features that make groups distinct.

High dimensions strain that balance: distances blur and noise piles up. The tutorial gathers methods that keep groups visible in such data. It is aimed at researchers and practitioners who cluster genomes, documents, or sensor streams. A clear map of the trade-offs can save teams from groupings that look neat and mean nothing.
arxiv-2601-11860:
Xin Xiong, Zijian Guo, Haobo Zhu, and a cross-lab team tackle decay in clinical AI over time. Tools that work well at launch often fade as data shift. Causes span new patient mixes, code updates such as ICD-9 to ICD-10, and shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

Full retraining is often too costly or blocked by privacy rules. Their frame aims for durable AI that adapts as it moves to new sites and times. It treats drift as a fact to plan for, not a surprise. Sound drift tools could keep care AI safe for longer.
arxiv-2601-12160:
Y. Shen, W. He, J. Sears, and a large team report the first watch of plasmons in low-valence nickelates. Nickelate superconductors opened a new field for the study of electron fluids that pair in odd ways. Plasmons are joint waves of the electron gas, and they hold key facts on charge dynamics.

Such waves had not been seen in nickelates before this work. Their data add a new probe of how charge moves in these materials. That probe can test theories of their odd superconductivity. The team span labs in the US and abroad.
arxiv-2601-11460:
Franziska Herbert and four coauthors teach robots task structure from human demos. Their 2026 preprint builds semantic-geometric task graphs from demonstrations. Long-horizon manipulation is hard for robots to learn raw. Bimanual tasks add two hands whose moves must be ordered.

A good task record must hold two kinds of structure. One is the discrete semantic side: steps and objects used. The other is how object geometry shifts over time. Both sides can vary much from demo to demo. The team's graphs join meaning and geometry in one form. That form supports reasoning about how a task unfolds. Robots can then plan long tasks with clearer steps.
arxiv-2601-11260:
Martin Ortiz builds new theta operators on Shimura varieties in this work. His 2026 preprint deals with Hodge type varieties at hyperspecial level. Theta operators shift weights of modular forms in mod p work. They are differential operators with deep arithmetic uses.

The new family shifts weights modulo a prime p. Basic theta operators come first in the construction. Each is labeled by a positive root of the group. That labeling generalizes Katz's classic theta operator. Katz's case was for modular forms in one variable. Ortiz lifts the idea to the broad Hodge type setting. New operators give new tools for mod p number theory.
arxiv-2601-11560:
Zifeng Wang and seven coauthors launch DeepEvidence for biomedical discovery. Their 2026 preprint builds on biomedical knowledge graphs. Such graphs encode vast, mixed data for the life sciences. Literature, genes, pathways, drugs, diseases, and trials all sit inside.

Using those graphs jointly for discovery stays hard today. Their structures differ from one resource to the next. They evolve over time as new studies land. Cross-resource alignment is limited and needs manual work. That hand work caps the depth and scale of exploration. DeepEvidence aims at deep graph research with less friction. Better tooling could speed drug and disease insight.
arxiv-2601-11660:
Chunshu Wu and four coauthors argue that zeros can be informative. Their 2026 preprint gives a masked binary U-Net for segmentation. Real-time segmentation enables AR, VR, robots, and drones. Tight budgets bind accuracy, latency, and energy on edge devices.

U-Net balances accuracy and efficiency better than big transformers. High-resolution input still strains compute, memory, and power. Binary networks cut weights to one bit for speed. Masking turns many values to zero in the network. Those zeros, the team shows, still carry useful signal. Running on Tensor Cores targets the hardware in edge chips. The aim is real-time masks within strict budgets.
arxiv-2601-13260:
Sawsan Alqahtani and co-authors argue that tokenizers are core design picks, not mere prep steps. A tokenizer cuts text into bits that a large language model reads. The go to cut is byte pair encoding, which joins the most common pairs step by step. It scales well, but the cuts can clash with true word parts.

That clash can waste model room and can grow bias. It hits tongues and fields far from the train mix the most. The team reframes the cut as a model pick in its own right. They urge that it be judged with the same care as net shape or train data. For model builders, the piece is a call to own the first step of the chain.
arxiv-2601-12860:
Youngmin Lee, Subong Lim, and Wissam Raji study the Rankin Cohen bracket for vector valued modular forms. Modular forms are functions with rich symmetry, central to number theory. The Rankin Cohen bracket combines two such forms into a new one. For vector valued forms, the bracket carries extra structure worth mapping.

The team explore how this bracket relates to Petersson inner products. They derive an explicit description of the adjoint map for the bracket operator. The study extends to Jacobi forms and skew holomorphic Jacobi forms. An isomorphism connects their brackets with the vector valued case. Adjoint maps for the extended operators are examined as well.
arxiv-2601-13660:
Aiko Miyamoto and co-authors hunt for changing iron light from the heart of the Circinus galaxy in 2026. They used eight sets of Chandra X-ray data taken over about twenty-two years. Their target is neutral iron-K alpha emission, a sharp X-ray glow from iron atoms. The glow comes from the region near the galaxy's core, about ten to a hundred parsecs out.

Maps and spectra split by place let them track the glow spot by spot. They search for time variability, shifts in brightness over the years. Changes would hint at how light and gas move near a giant black hole. Long records like this are rare and prized.
arxiv-2601-14160:
Ali Hamza Bashir and co-authors adapt language models to German law with synthetic data in 2026. Large language models often struggle in specialized domains like legal reasoning. Limited expert knowledge leads to factually incorrect outputs or hallucinations. German legal question answering is the target task here.

Their method fine-tunes advanced models on novel synthetic data. A generation approach creates training cases in the legal style. Domain adaptation through synthetic data avoids costly expert labeling at scale. Reliable legal assistants could help citizens and junior lawyers find rules fast. The dip was brief, so fast alerts from sky watchers were key. Their quick word let big scopes join in time to catch it.
arxiv-2601-14260:
Xiaoxuan Yang, Peilin Chen, Tergel Molom-Ochir, and Yiran Chen tackle a hardware problem in this 2026 paper. Transformers run most large language models, but they are costly to run at scale. The authors name three main challenges. One is the attention step, which needs huge matrix work.

Attention also forces much data movement. Intermediate results shuttle back and forth between memory and compute units. That traffic drives up both delay and energy use. The team's answer sits in processing-in-memory designs. Such designs place compute inside or near memory chips. The paper works on end-to-end speed-up for transformers on that kind of hardware.
arxiv-2601-15760:
Shubham Patel and Utkarsh Mishra squeeze more from a quantum optimizer in a 2026 arXiv paper. The algorithm is QAOA, built for combinatorial optimization. They test it on MaxCut, a classic graph problem. Three graph families serve as testbeds: 3-regular graphs, Erdős-Rényi graphs, and Barabási-Albert graphs. Their recipe starts with parameter transfer initialization. Good parameters from earlier runs seed the new one.

Targeted single-layer optimization then refines the result. Regularization keeps the search focused, per the title. The abstract reports a mean approximation ratio of 0.9443 for the transfer approach, before the record cuts off. Parameter tuning is QAOA's practical bottleneck. Cheaper tuning widens the problems users can afford to try.
arxiv-2601-15860:
Shui-Hsiang Hsu, Tsung-Hsiang Chou, Chen-Jui Yu, and Yao-Chung Fan build a table representation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Table retrieval finds the most relevant tables for a natural-language query. The search runs over large corpora. Structured tables and unstructured questions differ in form and meaning. That gap makes embedding alignment hard. Recent methods enrich tables with synthetic queries. Many still sample partial tables coarsely and fuse signals simply.

Their method is STAR, a semantic table representation. It uses header-aware clustering and adaptive weighted fusion. Headers carry much of a table's meaning, so the method leans on them. Adaptive fusion weighs parts by their value per query. For search over data lakes, such gains decide whether the right table surfaces at all.
arxiv-2601-15960:
Zihao Wu and a large team report a possible galaxy cluster from the dawn of time in a 2026 arXiv paper. The candidate sits at redshift about 10.5. That distance places it within the first 500 million years, per the title. It contains 18 galaxies with consistent photometric redshifts. They show robust F115W dropouts, the color signature of very distant sources. The group spans 8 comoving megaparsecs in projection.

The data come from the JADES survey with JWST. An overdensity this early is a strong claim. Structure needs time to grow, and 500 million years is little time. A confirmed cluster that young would strain formation models. The authors present it as a candidate, inviting the spectroscopic checks that can settle it.
arxiv-2601-15160:
Yuval Kansal and Niraj K. Jha argue that a knowledge graph can quietly act as a reward model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the reasoning of large language models. The models shine at math and code, but multi-hop reasoning in specialist science stays weak.

The authors propose a bottom-up route. A model first learns firm domain facts, stated like axioms. Signals derived from paths in a knowledge graph then reward good steps. From those facts the model composes answers to complex new tasks that it has never once seen before.
arxiv-2601-15360:
Eichi Uehara repairs a popular estimator for treatment effects that vary by person. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with heterogeneous treatment effects in fields like ad tech and health care. Two problems strike at once: extreme class imbalance and heavy-tailed outcomes.

The X-Learner handles imbalance by cross-imputation. But the author shows it breaks under outlier smearing when squared error rules the fit. A few wild outcomes can poison the estimates. Robust X-Learner swaps in robust methods to stop that smearing. The repair keeps the cross-imputation strength while taming the heavy tails.
arxiv-2601-16360:
Tom Moshaiov and Shaul Zemel give curve forms for group marks on cycles. Their 2026 preprint deals with the symmetric group and its marks. Past work by Cohen and Zemel showed a key size is a curve in n. That size is the span of a group form tied to a set split. The split has a fixed small part and a part that grows with n.

The pair now give like curve forms for marks on cycles. Marks and sizes both turn out as curves of set grade. Curve forms let teams work values for big n at once. No step by step sum is then needed for each n. The work adds firm forms to group maths.
arxiv-2601-16560:
Ruisheng Shi and coauthors test eclipse hits on the Ethereum peer net. Their 2026 preprint deals with hits that cut a node off from true peers. A hit node sees just foe peers and their false tale. Past hits were well read in Bitcoin and Monero nets. How they fare on Ethereum post Merge was far less known.

The team tests if the same tricks can take Ethereum nodes. Post Merge shifts in the peer rules may block or aid hits. Clear risk maps help node hosts set peer guards. Such guards keep the chain tale true for all users. The work brings a known hit to a new net.
arxiv-2601-16960:
Olivia Pal, Veda Duddu, Agam Goyal, Drishti Goel, and Koustuv Saha study student trust in AI answers. Trust and use are oft read as one linked pair. Tune trust right, and fit use should follow, folks say. Their 2026 preprint doubts that link in school work. Students now ask bots for help on a daily basis.

The team frames the doubt as shared mind-read skill. Each side models what the next side knows. Misfit models can leave trust high but use poor. Or trust low while use stays fit. Their work can guide school tools that earn apt trust. It warns grades based on trust polls alone.
arxiv-2601-18260:
Eytan Kats and co-authors teach a model to locate organs inside the body from a photo of its surface. Their 2026 preprint deals with depth images of the patient's outside. Automated patient positioning matters in medical scanning. A well-placed patient shortens the scan and improves throughput and comfort. If a system can infer where organs sit from the surface shape, the scanner can be set up before any imaging dose is spent.

Learning that inside-outside map is the paper's core task. Surface depth is cheap and safe to capture. Organ position varies with body shape, so the map must be learned, not ruled. The work joins computer vision with radiology workflow.
arxiv-2601-18960:
Sofia Cocciaretto and Vittorio Giovannetti study how much quantum data a lossy channel can carry. Most quantum link work rests on qubits, units with two states. Higher level units, called qudits, may carry more and compute better, a point fresh results stress.

They study a family of channels that model energy decay for such multi level signals. The work asks what the quantum capacity of these channels is, that is, how much quantum data can pass safely. Knowing the cap for real loss shapes helps plan links that use bigger units, not just qubits.
arxiv-2601-19060:
Jeonghwan Kim and ten co-authors teach a visual model to fetch facts tied to the exact spot in a photo. Answering questions about images often needs both sharp sight and outside facts. Past systems that fetch facts lack an inner rule for when to fetch and how to aim the search.

Their model, PixSearch, joins region level sight with fetch based reasoning in one end to end system. It can point at the part of the image the question is about, then pull facts for that part. Grounded fetching could cut the made up answers that plague visual question answering today.
arxiv-2601-19360:
Diego Rossini and Lonneke van der Plas find multiword expressions in text with a light, language aware model. Multiword expressions, like idioms, act as one unit of meaning spread over several words. Spotting all their types is a known hard step for language tools.

Their method labels each token as inside or outside an expression, adds linguistic features, and grows the training data by augmentation. Their model tops the prior best on its test set, ahead of far larger systems. A light model that wins on skill, not size, suits real pipelines that process text at scale.
arxiv-2601-19760:
Yuya Koshiba and colleagues report a laser that fires short, strong pulses in the infrared. The device uses a thin disk of holmium-doped YAG crystal, pumped by laser diodes. It was run in two modes: Q-switching and cavity dumping, two standard ways to store and release light in bursts. The output wavelength sits near two micrometres.

The pulses carry more than six millijoules of energy and last only a few nanoseconds. That combination gives a peak power above a megawatt. The beam quality is near the diffraction limit, meaning it stays tight and clean. Such sources serve in materials processing, sensing, and further laser stages. The work shows what thin-disk designs can reach in this wavelength range.
arxiv-2601-20260:
Xingxin Xu and four colleagues present a diffusion method for fusing images from different sensors into one picture. Fusion aims to keep fine detail and high visual quality while joining the strengths of each source image. Diffusion models generate sharp images, but they often lose detail when used for fusion.

The authors design a reversible, efficient diffusion process to cut that loss. Their goal is a fused image that keeps the texture of the inputs, not a smoothed version of them. Better fusion supports night vision, medical scans, and remote sensing, where each sensor alone sees only part of the scene.
arxiv-2601-18360:
Weikang Qian and three colleagues study the shape of a set of plans that show up in hard choice tasks. The sets pair a kind of curved cost rule with caps on how much of each group can be picked. Such sets sit inside tasks in ports, power grids, and work plans. The shape of the set tells a solver which cuts will trim the search with no loss.

The team find a new class of sharp cuts for two such sets. They build the cuts by a step trick that lifts a small true claim to a large one. Sharp cuts can cut run time a lot on real tasks. Their work gives solver teams new tools to add to the kit. It also maps the form of these sets with more care than past work did.
arxiv-2601-18460:
Francisco Gancedo and four colleagues study what can go wrong where two fluids of unlike weight meet and move. The heavy fluid sits on top of the light one in their setup. That stack is not calm: the edge between the fluids tends to grow wild with time. Thick rules of flow, with drag, set how the edge moves.

The team prove that the wild growth does not stop. In their setup the edge grows in length or in curl for all time, with no cap. A proof of that kind rules out hopes that drag alone would calm the stack. It also maps a hard case for teams who model oil, water, or air in tanks. Such proofs keep models honest about what they can and cannot tame.
arxiv-2601-18660:
Jaume de Haro gives a fresh, clear path to a set of marks used to chart a fall into a black hole. The marks are named for Novikov. They ride with bits that fall in a straight line toward the hole. In the chart, time and place are set by those falls, so the chart fits how a fall feels from in-side. Past paths to the marks were long and hard to read.

De Haro starts from falls with a twist: the bits bear a kind of charge that past work tags as less than none. Those falls form a full set that spans the whole of the hole's world, in-side and out. From them the marks drop out in a short, plain way. A clear path could help teach the chart and use it in new work on how holes grow and fade.
arxiv-2601-18760:
Henry Bell and three colleagues argue that the rules used to train language models should rest on why people hold their views, not just on which reply they pick. In the main path now, a model is taught to match a set of writ rules. Those rules are set by a small team. It is not clear how the rules could be set in a fair way with wide voice from all who are touched by the tools.

Picks alone hide the grounds of a view. Two folk may pick the same reply for quite unlike grounds. A rule built on picks may thus miss what folk prize most. The team set out a path that learns rules from grounds and worths. Such rules could claim a fairer base. They could also be checked in the open, ground by ground.
arxiv-2601-21160:
Michael Ibrahim, Nagi Gebraeel, and Weijun Xie study clustering when data stays split across many separate clients. No one knows in advance how many groups exist across all clients. Each client also holds its own mix, and the mixes can overlap or differ.

The authors build a shared learning method that works without pooling the raw data. It extends a classic expectation and maximization routine to the split-data setting. The method has to guess the total number of groups while it learns them. That makes it useful for settings where data must stay local, such as hospitals or banks that cannot share records.
arxiv-2601-21660:
Jingyang Zhao and Mingyu Xiao improve approximation algorithms for vehicle routing with capacity limits. In this classic problem, vans leave a depot to serve customers who each demand some load. Every van has a fixed capacity, and routes should be as short as possible.

The unsplittable version bars splitting one customer's demand across vans, which matches real practice. The authors give better guarantees on how close their routes come to optimal. Routing sits under delivery, repair, and transit services everywhere. Even small gains in the guarantee translate into large savings when the method runs at city scale every day.
arxiv-2601-21760:
Ruian Tie, Wenbo Xiong, and five co-authors downscale climate data to fine grids without any paired training examples. Supervised downscaling learns from matched coarse and fine data, which ties it to the models it trained on. New climate models break that pairing and expose domain gaps.

Zero-shot methods exist but can violate physics or lose their gradient signal at large scale factors. The authors use diffusion posterior sampling to stay both physical and stable. Fine local detail is what impact studies need, from flood risk to heat planning. A method that transfers across climate models saves retraining for every new release.
arxiv-2601-22260:
Tom Gajecki, Jonas Althoff, and Waldo Nogueira work on a clear need: help cochlear implant users pick out one voice in noise. Their 2026 preprint uses brain wave cues to learn which speaker the user wants to hear. An implant turns sound into small electric pulses for the ear.

Their network joins the mixed sound with the brain wave cues in one light step. It then builds a pulse pattern for the wanted voice alone. The method also solves a mix-up that pure sound tools face. It points to implants that track the mind, not just the ear.
arxiv-2601-22360:
B. J. P. Jones works out how light hydrogen atoms bounce off helium at near-freezing cold. His 2026 preprint covers all three forms of hydrogen: plain, heavy, and the rare radioactive form. Both light forms of helium serve as targets.

The rates span a vast range, from near absolute zero up to room heat. The work is driven by a real need: sources of cold tritium for tests of the neutrino's mass. At such cold, each bounce can shift the atoms' paths and spins. Firm rates help teams design those sources with care.
arxiv-2601-22660:
Evan Gibson Smith and Bashima Islam train deep binary networks by freezing layers in stages, with no gradient shortcut. Binary networks use one-bit weights and activations, which makes them tiny and fast. Their 2026 preprint tests progressive freezing in place of the straight-through estimator, the usual trick that fakes a gradient.

Plain global freezing works for binary weights, they find, but fails for full binary nets. Blocked gradients through activations are the cause. The find maps where the trick can and cannot go. Tiny nets matter for phones and sensors. Honest limits guide the design.
arxiv-2601-21960:
Aref Farhadipour and a large team lay out the rules for a shared contest in speaker verification. Systems that confirm a speaker's identity degrade badly when the language changes between enrollment and testing. The field's reliance on English-centered data makes that weakness worse.

The TidyVoice 2026 Challenge, described in this evaluation plan, is designed to confront the language mismatch problem head-on. The plan spells out how systems will be tested so results can be compared fairly. Challenges like this matter because voice verification guards bank accounts and devices worldwide. And a system that fails on non-English speakers fails a large part of the world.
arxiv-2601-20760:
Sarvesh Shashidhar, Abhishek Mishra, and Madhav Kotecha question a basic assumption in how AI models learn from human feedback. Their 2026 paper is about RLHF, the method that trains models with human ratings. RLHF has been effective for AI alignment, the task of making models act as people wish. But it treats all raters as if they respond in the same way.

Real users differ, and the authors put that heterogeneity at the center. If raters want different things, one reward signal may fit no one well. The paper explores what changes when feedback comes from a mixed crowd. It asks how training should handle clashing tastes and values. The work speaks to builders who want models that serve varied users, not an average one.
arxiv-2601-20860:
Babak Vakili asks whether quantum teleportation still works in a universe that expands. The 2026 paper studies teleportation in Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime, the standard model of an expanding cosmos. Two scenarios take center stage. One is a power-law expansion, steady and simple. The other is the de Sitter universe, which expands at an ever-quickening rate. The approach is field-theoretical.

Two comoving observers share an entangled mode of a scalar field. Comoving means they drift along with the expansion. Vakili analyzes the quantum correlations between them. Expansion can stretch and weaken those correlations. The study asks how much fidelity teleportation keeps under such strain. The results matter for quantum information in curved spacetime, a field that joins gravity with quantum rules.
arxiv-2601-21060:
Zhuoyan Li and a large team of co-authors put humans and language models on the same feature-building team. Their 2026 paper studies feature engineering for tabular learning. Feature engineering turns raw columns into inputs a model can use well. Large language models are increasingly used to automate that craft. Given task details, an LLM can propose diverse transformations. Those proposals aim to enhance downstream performance.

The paper's twist is collaboration. Humans and models each bring strengths to the table. Models offer breadth and speed; humans offer judgment and context. The study examines how the pair should work together. Good features often decide whether a tabular model succeeds. This human-LLM workflow could make that step faster and better. The work serves data teams that live in spreadsheets and databases.
arxiv-2512-01260:
Far-off bright cores of galaxies can change in light over time. A team led by Andrew Penton and Hugh McDougall used six years of Dark Energy Survey data to track those changes. They looked for delays between light from gas near a black hole and light from the core itself.

The team found clear time delays for a set of active galaxy cores at large distances. Those delays help show how far the gas sits from the black hole. That distance is a key step toward weighing the black hole. The work adds hard cases at high distance where such tests are rare and hard to do well.
arxiv-2512-01460:
Jozef Kubik, Marek Suppa, and Martin Takac improve sentiment reading in scarce tongues. Models for mood in text are weak when data is thin. Full pre-training is too costly for most teams. Gains must come at the fine-tuning stage instead.

The team tests active learning at that stage. The method picks which texts to label next for best gain. Added schedulers guide that pick with more structure. Smart picks can lift mood scores with far fewer labeled texts. That helps tools for news and social posts in tongues with small data sets.
arxiv-2512-01760:
Anurag Bishnoi, Wouter Cames van Batenburg, and Ananthakrishnan Ravi study the chromatic number of finite projective spaces. That number is the fewest colors to paint all points with no line in one color. Projective spaces over finite fields give a clean but deep setting.

Each point and line follows strict incidence rules. Finding the exact chromatic number is hard as dimension and field size grow. Bounds and builds both advance the hunt. The problem links combinatorics, geometry, and coding theory, where line-free colorings have direct kin. Small cases anchor the hunt, since exact values for tiny spaces expose which bound or build will scale to the next dimension.
arxiv-2512-00460:
Maria Gorelik and Victor Kac wrote a 2025 paper in advanced algebra on modules over Kac-Moody superalgebras. These are large symmetry algebras that extend the Lie algebras used across math and physics. Admissible modules are a special class of representations, introduced by Kac and Wakimoto in the late 1980s.

That theory grew into a well developed subject with many uses, including the representation theory of vertex algebras. Gorelik and Serganova later set it in a more general frame. Gorelik and Kac now work on quasi-admissible modules in that wider setting. Their results extend a tool kit that algebraists use to sort and build representations.
arxiv-2512-00960:
Boran Wen and a large team work on learning from human-object interaction videos in a 2025 computer vision paper. General robots must learn from many kinds of human activity to work robustly in the real world. Ordinary internet videos of people handling objects are nearly limitless and show huge diversity.

The hard part is extracting accurate, scalable 4D interaction data from such wild footage. That means tracking people, objects, and their contact through space and time. Their monocular method uses a single camera view, which is all most online video offers. Reliable extraction could turn the web's video flood into robot training data.
arxiv-2512-01160:
Ahmad Ali rethinks how atomistic models predict energy in a 2025 paper. Density functional theory estimates the energy and behavior of molecules, but it is slow. Machine learning interatomic potentials approximate those energies and forces at a fraction of the cost. Most are trained as regressors that output one energy number.

Ali explores turning the task into classification instead. Energies are placed into categorical bins, and the model predicts a category rather than a precise scalar. The study asks whether that change improves learning for these potentials. A better formulation could make fast molecular models more accurate.
arxiv-2601-23060:
Luo-Jia Kang builds a complete operator basis for the Standard Model Effective Field Theory with modular flavor symmetry. The effective theory extends the Standard Model with higher-dimensional operators that capture unknown heavy physics. Modular symmetries organize the flavor patterns of quarks and leptons.

The setup uses two copies of an A4 flavor group, one for quarks and one for leptons, with separate moduli. Right-handed quarks carry the simplest modular weights. A complete basis tells model builders exactly which operators the symmetry allows. Distinct moduli for the quark and lepton sectors let the symmetry treat the two flavor puzzles separately.
arxiv-2512-03260:
One pixel of a sky survey telescope gets a careful check. Gregory Jaehnig and co-authors report the spectral traits of a 90 GHz CLASS pixel in this 2025 work. CLASS scans the microwave sky to probe reionization and search for inflation signals.

The survey uses telescopes tuned to four frequency bands. Knowing one pixel's exact response helps turn raw signals into clean maps. Small errors in response can mimic faint cosmic signals. Careful calibration is thus key to claims about the early universe and the physics of inflation. Pixel checks like this one underpin trust in maps made from the whole survey.
arxiv-2512-03360:
Working backward from a goal is a natural way to reason. Qingchuan Li and co-authors build a backward reasoning method for language models in this 2025 work. Most current methods reason forward, step by step from premises to conclusions.

Logical reasoning underpins science, math proof, and complex choices, so its quality matters. The authors translate parts of a problem into symbolic form, but only where it helps. Starting from a hypothesis and seeking premises could make model reasoning more focused. It may cut wasted steps in hard problems. Selective translation keeps the speed of neural reasoning where symbols are not needed.
arxiv-2512-03460:
Cell culture batches need watching to stay on track. Johnny Peng and co-authors compare learning methods for that monitoring in this 2025 work. Real-time monitoring tracks cell density, nutrients, metabolites, and product levels through a batch run.

Early detection of deviations supports timely control actions. Yet data and feedback are often limited in bioprocessing. The authors compare methods that learn from limited data and feedback. Better monitoring protects product quality in medicines and other cell-based goods, where batches are costly. Limited feedback is the norm in plants, where each batch is costly and slow.
arxiv-2512-03560:
Enterprise tasks need agents that plan and use many tools. Gianni Molinari and Fabio Ciravegna present Reason-Plan-ReAct in this 2025 work. Single-agent designs force one loop of planning and execution, which causes instability over long trajectories.

Their design splits roles across a reasoner-planner that supervises a ReAct executor. Separation of duties aims to keep complex tasks on track. Firms want agents that coordinate tools and data sources reliably. A supervised structure may reduce the drift and errors seen in monolithic agents. Supervision adds a check on the executor, which can catch tool errors before they cascade through long enterprise workflows and records.
arxiv-2512-01860:
The biharmonic operator governs bending in thin plates and slow flows of thick fluids, and its boundary value problems are famously delicate. Dirk Pauly and Alberto Valli devote a 2025 note to setting these problems up correctly, so that each one has exactly one well-behaved solution.

They develop variational formulations, which recast the equation as an energy-minimization problem, alongside operator-theoretic methods. Special attention goes to Neumann-type conditions and to over- and under-determined problems, where the boundary data are too many or too few. A careful setup like this is the groundwork that later numerical methods for plates and flows must stand on.
arxiv-2512-02260:
Climate change and habitat loss are redrawing where species can live, faster than conservation teams can survey. Hammed Akande and Abdulrauf Gidado propose EcoCast in 2025, a spatio-temporal model for forecasting biodiversity and climate risk continually, with ecologically rich regions like Africa in mind.

Conservation professionals need timely, high-resolution predictions to decide where to protect land and how to intervene. A continual forecaster updates its risk maps as conditions shift, rather than freezing them at publication. Better forecasts of species movement could help limited conservation budgets arrive before the losses they aim to prevent.
arxiv-2512-02460:
Yifan Zhu and four co-authors study groups hidden inside large graphs, such as friend circles in a social network. Two tasks matter here: finding the best group for one query, and splitting a whole graph into groups. Past learning methods treat the two tasks apart, so each new task needs fresh training.

Their 2025 framework, UniCom, handles both tasks in one shared system. It also pays attention to how tight and cohesive each group is. One tool for both jobs could save time for teams that map communities in real world networks of many kinds. One shared tool also makes results from two labs much easier to compare.
arxiv-2512-02660:
Athos Georgiou improves document search so answers point to the right region, not just the right page. Late interaction models like ColPali embed each page as an image and match query words to visual patches closely. Page level results, though, give generation systems more text than they need.

Text extraction tools give exact boxes but judge relevance weakly. Georgiou propagates patch relevance into regions, joining fine matching with precise location. Region level retrieval could make question answering over manuals, forms, and reports sharper, cheaper, and easier for users to verify by eye. A hit at the region scale gives the writer the lines it needs, not the whole file to wade through.
arxiv-2512-02860:
Abdul Hannan and four co-authors revisit how to match a face with its voice across languages. The Face-Voice Association challenge for 2026 tests matching in a multilingual setting. Evaluation uses English and German face voice pairs, so models must cross language lines as well as sense lines.

Their RFOP method rethinks fusion and orthogonal projection, the steps that merge face and voice features. The design focuses the merger on relevant semantic information in both signals. Cleaner matching supports media search, dubbing checks, and identity tools that must work across borders. Pairs in two tongues are a stern test, since a match must cross both the face voice gap and the tongue gap at once.
arxiv-2512-02960:
Arthur D. Yaghjian revisits the old problem of how a charged ball moves as it radiates energy away. A charged sphere of finite size obeys a modified, causal form of the Lorentz-Abraham rule. Let its radius shrink to zero while the mass is fixed, and that rule turns into the Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac form.

Yaghjian then works out the exact terms on speed and outside force that these rules require. Under those terms, momentum and energy stay conserved, as physics demands. Radiation reaction has troubled the theory of charges and fields for a full century now. Clear terms help sort real motions from runaway artifacts that no lab will ever see.
plos-pone-0010060:
The authors were Sanjay Kansra, Shenglin Chen, Madhavi Bangaru, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered hormone drugs and pituitary cells called lactotrophs. These cells make prolactin, and their growth is tied to estrogen receptor alpha. The team had found that receptor matters even when no estrogen is present.

They compared drugs that either break down the receptor or merely modulate it. One drug, ICI 182780, rapidly promoted receptor loss and slowed cell growth. Tamoxifen and raloxifene did not act the same way. The contrast helps explain how anti-estrogen drugs differ, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0010160:
The authors were Justin Valley, Paul Swinton, W. John Boscardin, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study aimed to improve embryo choice for IVF. Picking the best embryo is critical to a successful live birth. Clinics still choose largely by eye, judging shape and development, which is subjective and gives limited information.

The team used light-induced dielectrophoresis, an electric method guided by light, on mouse embryos. The goal was a non-invasive, measured way to grade embryo quality. A reliable physical marker could raise IVF success rates and reduce repeat treatment cycles.
plos-pone-0010260:
The authors were Koji Tsutsumi, Tetsuya Takano, Ryo Endo, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined a brain enzyme called AATYK1. The enzyme is abundant in the brain and helps nerve fibers grow. It is also involved when cerebellar granule neurons die, though its precise function remained unknown to researchers before this study.

The team investigated how another enzyme, Cdk5, modifies AATYK1 by adding phosphate. They found that this modification suppresses a second kind of phosphate tag on the same protein. Layered controls like this fine-tune how nerve cells grow and respond to damage.
plos-pone-0010360:
Naia Morueta-Holme, Camilla Fløjgaard and Jens-Christian Svenning assessed climate risk for a rare mammal in PLOS ONE in 2010. Warming is already shifting where species can live. Animals stuck in a small range have nowhere easy to go. Yet how sensitive such species truly are was not well measured. The team used range models to test that sensitivity.

Their models projected where the animal's climate space would move. They then weighed what that means for protecting it. Small-range species may need help earlier than common ones. Reserves drawn for today's climate may miss tomorrow's refuges. This study gives planners a way to spot that mismatch in advance. It treats one rare mammal as a test case for many.
plos-pone-0009860:
Two lemur species can share one forest yet live on very different energy budgets. Bruno Simmen and colleagues measured energy use and body makeup in both. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lemurs are primates found in the wild only in Madagascar.

Total energy expenditure is all the energy an animal burns in a day. The lemurs were free-living and sympatric, meaning they live side by side in the wild. Comparing neighbors shows how body composition matches lifestyle and diet. Such budgets help explain how similar species divide one habitat.
plos-pone-0009960:
Two large receptor proteins shed their outer parts, and those parts have jobs of their own. Martin Dietrich and colleagues tested what the shed pieces do in living animals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The proteins are LRP1b and LRP4, relatives of the LDL receptor. Their ectodomains are the parts that stick out of the cell. Anchorage independent means working without staying attached to the cell. The team found those domains have anchorage independent functions in vivo. A shed piece, it turns out, is not just waste.
